title: Xiaomi Just Invested in Battery Swapping — But None of Its Cars Can Use It - Memeburn
description:
Xiaomi just dropped $4.4 million on a five-month-old battery-swap company — and not a single car it sells can actually swap a battery.
China’s Battery Swap War Is Heating Up To understand Xiaomi’s timing, look at what’s happening around it.
Between that and this swap investment, the company is quietly building optionality across the entire EV energy stack.
Battery swapping lets you drive into a station and replace your drained EV battery with a fully charged one in about three to five minutes — far faster than fast chargers.
CATL’s Choco-SEB is an open-platform battery swap network designed to work across multiple automakers.
text:
Xiaomi just dropped $4.4 million on a five-month-old battery-swap company — and not a single car it sells can actually swap a battery. Here’s what the company might be planning and why it matters.

What Xiaomi Actually Bought

Through its subsidiary Hanxing Venture Capital, Xiaomi invested 30 million yuan ($4.4 million) in Zhejiang Xinglixing New Energy Technology Co., Ltd., according to corporate registration records reported by EV. That buys a 23.08% minority stake.

Xinglixing was founded in February 2026 in Hangzhou. Its scope covers battery sales, swap facility sales, NEV (new energy vehicle) accessories, and energy R&D. The majority owner — holding 76.92% — is Zhejiang Jinrui Automobile Sales Service Co., a Hangzhou firm running car dealerships since 2007.

That’s the key detail. Xiaomi didn’t invest in a deep-tech startup. It backed a regional operator with people who know how to run physical service locations — a fundamentally different model than what Nio and CATL are building.

Zero Compatible Cars

Here’s where it gets puzzling. Xiaomi’s SU7 sedan and YU7 SUV run on an 800-volt fast-charging platform. They’re pure electric vehicles designed around plug-in charging, not swappable packs. The company also just launched its SkyNomad N70 Max and N90 Max — its first hybrid SUVs — on July 30. Those use a gasoline-electric range-extender (EREV) powertrain, which makes them structurally incompatible with swapping too.

So Xiaomi now has three product lines, zero swap-capable vehicles, and a fresh investment in a swap startup.

Chinese media framed this as a “light-asset” play. Until now, Xiaomi’s energy strategy leaned on third-party charging partnerships — access to over 1.26 million charging piles through deals with Nio, XPeng, and Li Auto, plus its own 600 kW supercharging tech. This investment evolves that approach without committing to the capital-intensive buildout Nio has run for years.

China’s Battery Swap War Is Heating Up

To understand Xiaomi’s timing, look at what’s happening around it. The Xiaomi 18 series arriving in September shows how fast the company moves across categories — and EV infrastructure is no different.

Nio pioneered battery swapping in China starting in 2018. The company now operates roughly 3,991 stations and has delivered over 200 million cumulative charging and swapping services. In 2025, Nio generated about 3.1 billion yuan ($459 million) in swap revenue alone. That’s a real business.

But CATL — the world’s largest battery maker — entered the swap market at the end of 2024 and is moving at a pace that makes Nio’s rollout look cautious. CATL’s Choco-SEB network hit 2,000 stations across 180 cities by June 30, averaging more than 200 new stations per month. The system completes a swap in about 70 to 80 seconds — roughly half the time Nio’s current-gen stations take.

CATL’s approach is also fundamentally open. Its system works with 11 automakers across 18 brands, with 25 swap-compatible models planned. That standardization play could turn battery swapping from a premium perk into a mass-market default.

What Xiaomi Might Actually Be Planning

Xiaomi CEO Lei Jun has over 700,000 EVs on the road. The company targets 550,000 deliveries in 2026 — roughly 34% above last year. At that scale, energy infrastructure stops being someone else’s problem.

This investment isn’t about tomorrow. It’s about keeping a seat at the table while the battery-swap market standardizes. If CATL’s open-platform model wins — and right now, the numbers say it’s gaining ground fast — Xiaomi would rather have an existing relationship with a regional swap operator than start from scratch.

There’s also a vertical integration angle. Earlier this year, Xiaomi registered a subsidiary called Xiaomi Jingxu Technology with a scope that includes battery manufacturing. Between that and this swap investment, the company is quietly building optionality across the entire EV energy stack.

The timing lines up with a broader shift. BYD plans to deploy 20,000 flash-charging stations by the end of 2026. Nio is rolling out fifth-generation swap stations. The energy infrastructure race in China is now as competitive as the vehicle market itself.

The $4.4 Million Signal

In isolation, $4.4 million is a rounding error for a company that posted 19.86 billion yuan in EV revenue last quarter. But small bets placed early in a technology cycle signal where a company expects to go, not where it is today.

Xiaomi has built its entire brand — from smartphones to IoT devices to EVs — on entering markets late with a cost-efficient, ecosystem-driven approach. Battery swapping fits that playbook perfectly. Let the pioneers burn capital. Step in once the standards are settled.

Whether Xiaomi ever builds a swap-compatible vehicle remains open. But the bet is placed — and in China’s EV market, where infrastructure increasingly determines which cars people buy, that might be enough.

FAQs

What is battery swapping for electric vehicles?

Battery swapping lets you drive into a station and replace your drained EV battery with a fully charged one in about three to five minutes — far faster than fast chargers. Automated stations handle the process without you leaving the car. Nio pioneered this technology in China starting in 2018, and CATL’s newer system brings swap time down to about 70 seconds.

How does Xiaomi’s EV lineup compare to Tesla in China?

Xiaomi’s SU7 sedan has outsold the Tesla Model 3 in China, while the YU7 SUV undercuts the Model Y by about $4,350. Cumulative deliveries of both models surpassed 700,000 units as of July 2026. Tesla still leads in global volume, but Xiaomi is closing the gap fast in its home market.

What is CATL’s Choco-SEB battery swap system?

CATL’s Choco-SEB is an open-platform battery swap network designed to work across multiple automakers. Unlike Nio’s proprietary system, CATL’s approach supports 18 brands and 25 planned models. Each swap takes about 70 to 80 seconds, and the company deployed 2,000 stations across China by June 2026.

What is an extended-range electric vehicle (EREV)?

An EREV uses a battery-powered electric motor to drive the wheels, with a small gasoline engine acting solely as a generator to recharge the battery on the go. It’s different from a traditional hybrid because the gas engine never directly powers the wheels. Xiaomi’s new SkyNomad N70 Max and N90 Max are EREVs with up to 1,060 miles of combined range.

Why are Chinese EV makers investing so heavily in charging infrastructure?

Range anxiety remains the biggest barrier to EV adoption. Chinese companies like BYD, Nio, and CATL are spending billions on fast-charging and swap stations because the automaker that controls the refueling experience controls the customer. BYD alone plans to deploy 20,000 flash-charging stations by the end of 2026.

text:
Antora Energy secured $550 million in an oversubscribed Series C round co-led by G2 Venture Partners and Eclipse.

The company will expand U.S. production, establish a second manufacturing hub and accelerate large-scale energy storage deployments.

Antora recently commissioned a 5 gigawatt-hour thermal battery project in South Dakota in less than 12 months.

Antora Energy has raised $550 million to expand its U.S. manufacturing base and deploy large-scale energy storage projects across industrial, data center and power markets.

G2 Venture Partners and Eclipse co-led the oversubscribed Series C round. New investors included Ribbit Capital, Salesforce Ventures, Activate Capital, John Doerr, Westly Group, StepStone Group and Liberty Mutual Strategic Ventures.

Existing backers also participated. They included Decarbonization Partners, Impact Science Ventures, Trust Ventures, Breakthrough Energy Ventures and Lowercarbon Capital.

The financing gives Antora fresh capital as electricity demand accelerates across the United States. Data center growth, domestic manufacturing and grid electrification are placing new pressure on utilities, developers and energy infrastructure.

Antora plans to use the proceeds to deploy projects nationwide, expand production and establish a second U.S. manufacturing hub. It will also invest further in its domestic supply chain.

Energy demand becomes an industrial constraint

Antora develops thermal batteries that store low-cost electricity as heat inside insulated blocks of solid carbon. The systems can later deliver that energy as industrial heat or electricity.

The technology is designed to serve several markets through the same factory-built platform. Potential users include chemical plants, food producers, steelmakers, data centers and electricity networks.

Antora says its systems can store energy for multiple days. They also avoid many supply-constrained critical minerals used in conventional battery technologies.

“From factories to data centers, energy is the bottleneck to industrial growth,” said Andrew Ponec, Co-Founder and CEO of Antora. “Antora has shown we can help break that bottleneck—delivering energy fast, at massive scale, with American innovation. With this funding round, we’re continuing to strengthen our investment in U.S. manufacturing, delivering affordable energy across the country and around the world.”

The company’s expansion strategy comes as energy availability becomes a factor in investment decisions. Manufacturers and technology companies increasingly need faster access to firm power before approving new facilities.

For executives, the constraint is no longer limited to electricity prices. Connection queues, grid congestion, reliability and construction timelines can all influence project economics.

South Dakota project supports scale-up case

Antora recently deployed a 5 gigawatt-hour battery storage system in South Dakota. The company said the project moved from initial construction to energy delivery in under 12 months.

It described the installation as one of the world’s largest battery storage projects. Antora is now seeking to replicate that deployment model through signed agreements with hyperscale technology companies and industrial customers.

“Antora has moved beyond proving the technology to demonstrating it can manufacture and deploy at remarkable speed and scale,” said Joe Fath, Partner and Head of Growth at Eclipse. “The Eclipse team has spent decades helping companies rapidly accelerate manufacturing and deployment, and Antora has the team, technology, and execution capabilities to become a foundational part of America’s energy infrastructure.”

Investors are increasingly focused on technologies that can move from demonstration to repeatable manufacturing. The ability to deploy on schedule and at predictable cost is particularly important for infrastructure customers.

“Our energy system is at an inflection point, and very few companies can meet soaring power demand,” said Jake Tauscher, Partner at G2 Venture Partners “Antora is meeting that demand today. They’re deploying at scale, on budget, and on the rapid timelines customers need. That’s how generational energy companies are built, and it’s why we’re proud to co-lead this round.”

Manufacturing expansion carries policy relevance

Antora operates a three-building manufacturing campus in San Jose, California. The company describes the site as one of the largest battery gigafactories in the United States.

Its workforce includes welders, electricians, pipefitters and machinists. Antora said its manufacturing and construction activities have created or supported hundreds of U.S. jobs.

“This financing unlocks a new phase of growth for Antora,” said Nehali Jain, VP of Strategy and Growth at Antora. “In 2024, we opened our U.S. factory, which is now one of the largest battery factories in the country. Earlier this year, we turned on one of the largest battery storage projects in the world. This funding round is how we deploy more projects, more quickly, across more sectors and geographies.”

The round connects energy security with domestic industrial policy. It also reflects growing investor interest in infrastructure that can support manufacturing, data centers and grid resilience at the same time.

Antora’s next phase will test whether thermal batteries can become a mainstream source of firm energy. Success would give U.S. companies another option for managing power costs, emissions and reliability while electricity demand continues to rise.

Schneider Electric announced a major upgrade to its Charge Pro commercial Level 2 EV charger. The update introduces new capabilities to help property owners and operators deploy, manage and scale EV charging across the United States.

Schneider Electric designed Charge Pro for property owners, fleet operators, and site hosts across a wide range of commercial use cases. Applications include multi-unit dwellings (MUDs), workplaces, public and destination charging locations, and fleet operations. The solution brings together integrated hardware, software and services to reduce deployment complexity, improve uptime and help scale EV infrastructure more efficiently across sites.

The commercial EV charger combines hardware with EV Connect Software+. This a cloud-based charging station management system (CSMS) that enables site owners to monitor performance, manage access and monetize charging stations across multiple locations. Activation includes one year of EV Connect Software+. Additionally, services such as proactive monitoring and driver support to help ensure reliable performance. A five-year hardware warranty helps reduce risk and provides additional assurance for owners and operators. Together, these capabilities help lower total cost of ownership by simplifying operations, reducing maintenance and maximizing charger availability.

“Property owners, fleet operators and workplaces are looking for EV charging solutions that are simple to deploy and dependable at scale,” said Shawn Bonacorsi, Head of Electrification Solutions, Schneider Electric, North America Operations. “They are also prioritizing solutions that can deliver long-term value by helping reduce operational complexity and optimize costs over time. With Charge Pro, everything – from the hardware to the software and firmware – is designed and backed by Schneider Electric, providing a single, integrated solution that performs reliably across sites.”

New features simplify setup, management and charging

Charge Pro capabilities include:

Built-in charging management software: Includes one year of EV Connect Software+ at activation. This enables remote monitoring, access management, usage tracking and driver support.

Faster setup: A simplified commissioning process streamlines installation and reduces setup time, helping bring charging sites online more quickly.

Streamlined charging experience without an app. Drivers can start a session by scanning a QR code — with no app or account setup required.

Designed with security in mind: Built using Schneider Electric’s cybersecurity best practices to help protect charging operations and data.

Expanded connector options support both J1772 and the North American Charging Standard (NACS). Also, flexible configurations up to 80 A support a wide range of vehicles in use today.

Built to support scalable, reliable EV charging

Charge Pro is designed to integrate with Schneider Electric’s broader energy management and electrical infrastructure solutions. By connecting EV charging with electrical infrastructure, customers can better manage energy demand, balance load across sites and make more efficient use of available power as charging needs grow. Charge Pro also integrates with Schneider Electric’s electrical infrastructure portfolio. These integrations include panelboards, switchgear and circuit protection solutions used in commercial EV charging deployments.

Combined with certified installation partners such as Qmerit, Schneider Electric provides a coordinated approach to deploying and expanding EV charging infrastructure.

“EV charging is becoming a core part of how properties, workplaces and fleets support drivers,” Bonacorsi said. “Charge Pro brings together hardware, software and Schneider Electric’s electrical expertise to deliver a more streamlined and dependable charging experience while helping advance energy technology across commercial environments.”

Availability

The Charge Pro Level 2 commercial EV charger is available through Schneider Electric’s network of distribution partners, installers and EV infrastructure integrators.

text:
The U.S. Department of Energy has named North Carolina State University to lead three Genesis Mission projects aimed at using artificial intelligence (AI) to expedite discovery in the fields of high-performance computing, cybersecurity and astrophysics.

DOE’s Genesis Mission is focused on accelerating scientific productivity in the United States. Initial project recipients were announced by DOE July 22.

“NC State has a deep bench of research experience in AI development, application and integration,” says Krista Walton, vice chancellor for research and innovation at NC State. “By leading three Genesis Mission awards, NC State is helping the nation develop the tools needed to thrive in the post-AI era while applying the technology safely to push the boundaries of scientific discovery.”

The three Genesis Mission projects being led by NC State are Phase I projects. These projects all have budgets under $1 million and are designed to be conducted in less than one year. Successful Phase I projects will be eligible for larger Phase II awards in future funding cycles.

Michela Becchi, assistant professor of electrical and computer engineering at NC State, is the principal investigator (PI) on a project that seeks to make next-generation computing hardware more accessible to scientific researchers. The project will develop an AI-powered programming framework that helps generate, debug, and optimize code for emerging AI accelerators—specialized processors originally designed for artificial intelligence that have the potential to benefit demanding scientific and engineering applications beyond AI. Becchi’s collaborators are Sheng Di and Bogdan Nicolae of Argonne National Laboratory.

Xiaorui Liu, an assistant professor of computer science at NC State, is the lead PI on a project focused on defending agentic AI against adversarial attacks. The project will focus on automated scientific AI workflows, with the goal of detecting and preventing attacks that can corrupt results, produce false conclusions, or leak data. The project is being done in collaboration with Fnu Suya and Mahshid Ahmadi of the University of Tennessee, Knoxville, Hui Liu of Michigan State University, and Xinxia Peng of Depict Bio.

Gail McLaughlin, Distinguished University Professor of Physics at NC State, is the PI on a project that will embed AI techniques within large-scale simulations of neutron star mergers and supernovae to model physical processes that are too complex for traditional simulations. The project will deliver new insights into the cosmic origin of the elements and the role of neutrinos in astrophysical explosions. The project is being conducted in collaboration with researchers at the University of Tennessee, Knoxville; Pennsylvania State University; the University of Notre Dame; the University of California, Berkeley; and Oak Ridge National Laboratory.

NC State is also partnering on two additional Genesis Mission projects, both of which relate to nuclear energy. One Phase I project is led by Texas A&M and focuses on using AI to assess and document reactor safety to support human review processes. NC State’s lead on that project is Xu Wu, an associate professor of nuclear engineering.

The second award – dubbed the Prometheus project – is the only Phase II project awarded in this initial round of the Genesis Mission initiative and is receiving $60 million in funding over three years. The Prometheus project is led by Idaho National Laboratory and focuses on accelerating the deployment of nuclear power infrastructure. NC State researchers collaborating on the Prometheus project include Xu; Abhinav Gupta, professor of civil, construction and environmental engineering; and Kevin Han, associate professor of civil, construction and environmental engineering and Edward I. Weisiger Distinguished Scholar.

description:
A renewable energy developer has pulled its controversial permit application to build an industrial-scale solar facility on an Eastern Washington mountain sacred to Indigenous nations.
Avangrid, a powerful player in the Northwest’s push for green energy development, sought for at least five years to build a solar plant on Badger Mountain.
Avangrid continued pushing the project despite a state archaeologist’s warning that the planned development would threaten significant historic sites and current ceremonial activity.

text:
A renewable energy developer has pulled its controversial permit application to build an industrial-scale solar facility on an Eastern Washington mountain sacred to Indigenous nations.

Avangrid, a powerful player in the Northwest’s push for green energy development, sought for at least five years to build a solar plant on Badger Mountain. The project site straddled private as well as public lands. The Confederated Tribes of the Colville Reservation and the Confederated Tribes and Bands of the Yakama Nation have protected rights to practice cultural traditions, such as food gathering and ceremonies, on Badger Mountain and other ancestral public lands.

A 2024 investigation by High Country News and ProPublica found that Avangrid and a consultant it retained, Tetra Tech, had omitted key archaeological and cultural information from a state-mandated review of the site, which would have been used for a solar farm. Avangrid continued pushing the project despite a state archaeologist’s warning that the planned development would threaten significant historic sites and current ceremonial activity. An elected member of the Colville Tribal Business Council told the newsrooms at the time that the project would destroy roughly half the root vegetable harvest in the area.

An Avangrid spokesperson said then that the company had followed “all relevant law and regulation” with regard to the Badger Mountain solar project and had “taken additional steps to accommodate stakeholder feedback where possible.”

It’s unclear whether the company’s decision to cancel the project had anything to do with Indigenous rights. Avangrid declined to clarify its reasoning to HCN.

The Colville Tribes chair, Cindy Marchand, praised the decision in a statement last week. “While the Colville Tribes certainly appreciates the value of renewable energy such as solar power, sacred sites must remain pristine to pass down to future generations.”

After the publication of HCN and ProPublica’s investigation, some members of the Wenatchi-P’squosa, one of the 12 Confederated Colville Tribes, held a demonstration on Badger Mountain, saying that while they support renewable energy, they’re against facilities being built on important cultural sites. Following the demonstration, Avangrid announced that it would pause development to reconsider tribal input and public response. The public comment process is one of the only avenues available for tribal nations to advocate for their rights regarding land development.

At a meeting of the state’s permitting authority council in July, an Avangrid senior director sought a continued pause of the permitting work, pointing to anticipated construction delays affecting the power grid. At the same meeting, the council chair, Kurt Beckett, characterized concerns over the project’s environmental and cultural impacts as “noise,” but he also said tribal objections should be considered in the state’s permitting decision.

Read More

Five days later, Avangrid filed a request to completely withdraw its proposal. And last week, the permitting council formally announced the withdrawal and said it was “closing out existing financial arrangements and notifying interested and agency partners.” It did not provide further comment, referring questions to the developer. The state Department of Natural Resources, which owns the public parcel on Badger Mountain, said it had not received any other requests to develop it for clean energy projects at this time, and a spokesperson did not have additional information about future plans for the site.

No matter the reason for the project’s cancellation at Badger Mountain, the outcome is a good one, said Steven Wynecoop, vice chair of the Wenatchi Advisory Group, an independent body that advises the Colville Tribal Business Council and that organized the 2024 Badger Mountain demonstration.

The mountain is a “very sacred site to us,” said Wynecoop, grandson of the Wenatchi Advisory Group founder Matthew Dick. “Generations, we’ve been going to that mountain for plenty of reasons: medicines, foods like roots and berries.”

text:
U.S. energy company RWE Americas has announced plans to sell its U.S. Distributed Clean Energy (DCE) business to Infrastructure at Goldman Sachs Alternatives.

The transaction covers approximately 348 MWdc of operating distributed renewable assets across 16 states, alongside a 1.2 GW project development pipeline. The deal is subject to regulatory approvals and customary closing conditions, with final closure anticipated in the fourth quarter of 2026.

The divestment represents a strategic pivot for Germany-headquartered RWE’s North American subsidiary, allowing the developer to concentrate resources exclusively on its utility-scale generation and storage activities. RWE Americas currently owns and operates 13 GW of utility-scale power projects across 27 U.S. states and plans to add 9 GW of solar, wind, battery storage, and natural gas projects by 2031.

For Goldman Sachs Alternatives, the acquisition establishes a scaled, institutionally backed distributed generation platform aimed at commercial-scale solar and local power infrastructure.

Following the transaction’s close, the DCE business will operate as an independent standalone entity, retaining its full scope of development, asset management, and operations and maintenance (O&M) capabilities. RWE employees dedicated to the DCE unit are expected to transfer to ensure operational continuity for existing customers.

“Our Distributed Clean Energy business has built a strong platform with high-quality assets, long-standing customer relationships and, above all, an outstanding team,” said Andrew Flanagan, CEO of RWE Americas. “This transaction allows RWE to further sharpen its strategic focus on growing our utility-scale power business in America, while positioning DCE for continued success under new ownership.”

“This acquisition represents a compelling opportunity to build a market-leading distributed generation platform at a pivotal moment for U.S. power infrastructure,” added Teresa Mattamouros, Managing Director within Infrastructure at Goldman Sachs Alternatives. “DCE has a strong foundation of contracted, diversified operating assets and a significant, safe-harbored development pipeline.”

J.P. Morgan Securities plc served as financial advisor and Baker Botts L.L.P. acted as legal counsel to RWE. Jefferies L.L.C. served as financial advisor and Weil, Gotshal & Manges L.L.P. acted as legal counsel to Goldman Sachs Alternatives.

description:

text:
The frontrunner in Michigan’s Republican gubernatorial primary promises to repeal the state’s 2023 clean energy law if elected. The law looks to achieve 100% renewable energy generation by 2040.

U.S. Rep. John James (R-Shelby Township) opposes Michigan’s clean energy law. If elected, repealing it would be his first priority, according to a Bridge Michigan candidate survey.

The GOP candidate’s energy strategy would include “natural gas, nuclear, hydro, renewables where they make economic sense, biofuels and emerging technologies,” he told the publication.

James criticized aggressive “net-zero mandates” during an April House Energy and Commerce Committee hearing, saying they undermine reliability and affordability.

Polling in recent years shows strong support for renewable energy in the state, but energy and the environment are likely to be overshadowed by other concerns this year, Bernie Porn, Michigan EPIC-MRA pollster, told Planet Detroit.

When asked what the top issues are for voters, Porn answered: “Affordability, affordability, affordability.”

Environmental advocates emphasize that renewable energy and affordability are connected issues.

Repealing Michigan’s 2023 renewable energy law would add $5.6 billion in energy costs for Michiganders and result in the loss of 15,588 jobs by 2050, according to an analysis by the energy consulting firm 5 Lakes Energy.

Transitioning away from fossil fuels to clean energy is essential for limiting dangerous global heating, according to the United Nations Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change.

The Michigan governor’s race

James is leading GOP primary contender Perry Johnson in the polls.

The Republican gubernatorial candidates did not respond to requests for comment on this story.

Michigan Senate Minority Leader Aric Nesbitt (R-Porter Township) ended his campaign for governor last month, following President Donald Trump’s endorsement of James.

Former Michigan Attorney General Mike Cox dropped out of the race July 17.

The Cook Political Report changed its classification of the Michigan governor’s race from “toss up” to “lean D” May 21, a change that coincided with former Detroit Mayor Mike Duggan ending his run as an independent.

Michigan Democrat Jocelyn Benson leads Genesee County Sheriff Chris Swanson in Democratic primary polls tracked by The New York Times, and leads the general election polls sponsored by MIRS News Service that are tracked by the newspaper.

Benson and Swanson support Michigan’s clean energy law.

Benson campaign spokesperson Maggie Amjad told Planet Detroit that, “Jocelyn knows if implemented right, the 2023 clean energy law puts Michigan in a position to lead the nation in expanding clean energy and lowering utility costs for families across the state.”

Swanson told Bridge he wants to revisit the energy siting law that gives the state final say over approving renewable energy projects.

Trump, Iran war a drag on Republicans, pollster says

The Michigan House recently passed legislation (HB 5710 and HB 5711) titled “Project Lighthouse” to repeal state clean energy laws, including a rollback of Michigan’s “energy waste reduction” program.

For every dollar this program invests in energy efficiency, residents save roughly $4, according to the environmental group Evergreen Action.

Ed Rivet, executive director of the Michigan Conservative Energy Forum (MICEF), said opposition to renewable energy likely plays well with the Republican base in the primary.

MICEF’s website says its mission is to promote “market-based energy policies that foster competition, diversification and continued technological advancement.”

Candidates will face voters in the general election who hold more favorable views of renewable energy, including many right-of-center voters, Rivet said.

An April poll released by Michigan Energy Michigan Jobs, a coalition supporting clean energy, found 75% of respondents support Michigan’s 2023 clean energy law after hearing a description, with 19% in opposition.

Respondents to the poll were also more likely to blame aging infrastructure and monopoly utilities for rising energy costs than the transition to renewable energy or ongoing reliance on fossil fuels.

Porn said the Trump administration’s war on Iran and the subsequent rise in gas prices will weigh on Republicans in the general election, with Democrats positioning themselves in opposition to Trump.

Conservatives favor ‘all of the above’ energy policy, Rivet says

Rivet, who is a conservative and does outreach on energy issues to candidates from both parties, said Trump is pushing an antirenewable energy agenda that’s contrary to where Republicans have stood in the past.

The administration issued emergency orders to keep aging coal plants like Michigan’s J.H. Campbell plant open and spent billions of dollars to terminate offshore wind leases.

“Conservatives have been more comfortable in the ‘all of the above’ lane,” he said, which he describes as a “pro-market, pro-whatever works” energy policy. Rivet advocates for a diversified energy portfolio that includes renewables and nuclear energy.

General opposition to renewables is unlikely to be a position with broad support, although it may play well in some rural communities that have fought wind and solar projects, Rivet said.

He contrasted this with the widespread opposition to data centers in the state.

“Data centers can be darn near anywhere,” he said, noting the projects are being built in highly populated areas in Wayne and Washtenaw counties.

The scale of land needed for wind and solar projects means they’re largely a rural concern, he said.

Michiganders more likely to blame utilities than renewables for energy prices: poll

Courtney Brady, state advocacy director for the climate action group Evergreen Action, said she’s surprised to see candidates toe the Trump administration’s line on fighting clean energy and going after energy efficiency programs.

“It’s pretty baffling at a time when people are really upset about the affordability impact of Trump’s policies on the state of Michigan,” she said.

Trump’s emergency orders to keep the Campbell coal plant open cost ratepayers $180 million through March, according to Michigan Attorney General Dana Nessel.

The 5 Lakes Energy analysis of a rollback of Michigan’s clean energy law said it would cost the average household $1,360 in additional electric bills by 2050.

Brady said voters are unlikely to respond to Republicans’ messaging on clean energy because they are likely to want to increase the energy supply and see renewables as a resilience measure.

“I don’t think people are mad about clean energy in the way that Republicans want them to be.”

text:
The United States is currently facing a severe housing crunch. One recent Axios analysis (https://tinyurl.com/yww8mkxx) found that the U.S. housing market is short 3.2 million homes, noting “there aren’t enough homes to keep up with the increase in households.”

With energy prices rising and demand for energy-efficient homes growing, builders and developers are increasingly looking for energy-efficient HVAC solutions. Geothermal is over four times more efficient than a furnace or boiler and twice as efficient as an air source heat pump. As a result, geothermal HVAC can help builders and developers meet these demands as they construct the next generation of American housing stock.

When installed in new neighborhoods and developments, the collective savings can be enormous. For example, when Dandelion Energy partnered with Lennar to bring geothermal heating and cooling to new communities in Colorado, the estimated cost savings exceeded $30 million over 20 years (https://tinyurl.com/2mxyk4jz) compared to air-source heat pumps.

Why build with geothermal

Geothermal HVAC allows builders to construct a better product that consumers love. The advantages are multifaceted:

Maximize home price potential: Heating and cooling amount to the most significant utility costs for homeowners. With electricity prices surging and continuing to rise, geothermal technology gives builders a true pathway to deliver a high-end premium product without downgrading the comfort experience that customers expect from conventional fossil fuel systems.

This ability to offer customer-satisfying comfort while meeting modern electrification requirements allows builders to maximize the home’s price potential and deliver a truly future-proof product.

According to one 2025 analysis (https://tinyurl.com/2j38v93m), properties with eco-friendly features sell for nearly 15 percent more than their traditionally built counterparts. Geothermal heating and cooling systems offer a highly efficient and long-term solution to rising energy costs that buyers are willing to pay a premium for.

Unlock financial incentives: The financial landscape for geothermal HVAC is changing as incentives from the Inflation Reduction Act end and provisions from H.R.1, a reconciliation bill incorporating legislation from several congressional committees, take effect.

Under H.R.1, several long-standing programs were revised, and new pathways were introduced to expand access to geothermal energy and reduce its cost.

One of the most significant changes is the authorization of third-party ownership (https://tinyurl.com/yc5zb48e): Qualified companies can now finance, install and own a geothermal system on a homeowner’s property. This unlocks up to a 50 percent federal tax credit and allows the homeowner or building owner to lease the system for a predictable monthly payment. By removing high upfront costs, builders can more readily offer premium, energy-efficient geothermal solutions at greater scale.

Although the federal residential 25D geothermal tax credit ended last year, many state and local governments are rolling out new or expanded incentives. Utilities and public agencies increasingly recognize the long-term value of geothermal systems, from lowering household energy bills to easing demand on the grid.

Added up, federal, state and local policies have made geothermal HVAC more affordable than ever for residential, multifamily and commercial properties. As a result, geothermal systems today can match, or even beat, the cost of traditional HVAC options while delivering the same comfort and reliability.

Use geothermal to future-proof: Integrating geothermal systems from the start is a strategic move to future-proof new construction against regulatory shifts and emerging consumer expectations.

Unsurprisingly, people want to purchase homes constructed with the most efficient, reliable and durable solutions even when housing options are limited. Increasingly, state and local building codes are supporting these priorities, mandating electrification and implementing efficient standards to support consumer outcomes.

Geothermal technology is already positioned to meet the high-performance requirements of an electrified future in ways that air source heat pumps and other technologies can’t.

This approach also avoids locking new homes into outdated energy infrastructure for the next several decades while providing the best HVAC solution available today.

The U.S. needs more housing. Now. This is both a challenge and an opportunity. While there are real hurdles to building enough housing to lower costs and improve accessibility, builders, developers, and HVAC professionals have the chance to equip the next generation of homes with the most efficient, affordable and longest-lasting heating and cooling solutions.

By integrating geothermal HVAC from the ground up, professionals in the building industry can maximize a home’s value, leverage powerful financial incentives and future-proof their projects without sacrificing comfort or harming the environment.

The solutions to our housing crisis must be as durable and efficient as the homes we build. Embracing geothermal technology is a strategic move that delivers on all fronts.

title: Make it here, pay less tax: Gov't unveils production credit for chips, batteries
description:
The Ministry of Finance and Economy put both measures into its 2026 tax revision plan, approved on Monday by the tax policy deliberation committee.
The domestic production tax credit, which officials have compared to the U.S. Inflation Reduction Act, deducts an amount from income tax or corporate tax according to how much a company produces at home.
That structure already applies to the R&D credit and the integrated investment tax credit, and it will be extended to the special tax reduction, which cuts income tax or corporate tax for SMEs by between 5 and 30 percent, and to the credit on video and webtoon production costs.
To encourage venture investment, the age limit for a venture company to qualify for tax support will be loosened to 10 years from founding, up from seven.
A regular ISA exempts interest and dividend income only up to 2 million won, or 4 million won for lower earners.
text:
Companies that make semiconductors, rechargeable batteries and four other strategic products inside Korea will be able to write part of that output off against their tax bills from next year, under a package the government announced Monday.

The package also creates a new individual savings account (ISA) restricted to domestic investments, on which interest and dividend income will be exempt from tax with no ceiling at all.

The Ministry of Finance and Economy put both measures into its 2026 tax revision plan, approved on Monday by the tax policy deliberation committee.

The domestic production tax credit, which officials have compared to the U.S. Inflation Reduction Act, deducts an amount from income tax or corporate tax according to how much a company produces at home. It is aimed at goods that carry high strategic value but have a thin production base in Korea, at a time when countries are competing over technological dominance and supply chains.

Six sectors qualify: solar power, wind power, rechargeable batteries, semiconductors, key materials and AI robot components. The credit runs for 10 years. Which specific goods count will be settled when the enforcement decree is revised in February.

The central condition is that a Korean national has to handle both production and sale within the country. Core processes must be carried out in Korea, and a set share of qualifying production costs must be spent domestically. Those details will also go into the decree. The base credit will be weighted by 1.1 to 1.5 times for production outside the greater Seoul area to support balanced regional development.

Small modular reactor and micro modular reactor technologies will be designated national strategic technologies, which widens the tax credits available on their research and development (R&D) and investment costs. The existing hydrogen category will be broadened into a future energy category.

National strategic technology status lifts the R&D credit rate to between 30 and 50 percent and the investment credit rate to between 15 and 30 percent, both far above the rates for general technologies or for new growth and source technologies.

The package also takes aim at what is known as the so-called Peter Pan syndrome, in which small- and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) avoid growing because they do not want to lose their tax breaks. Until now, a company that outgrew SME status kept its support for a five-year grace period and then lost it outright. A phasedown structure will now apply reduced benefits for a further three years before support ends.

That structure already applies to the R&D credit and the integrated investment tax credit, and it will be extended to the special tax reduction, which cuts income tax or corporate tax for SMEs by between 5 and 30 percent, and to the credit on video and webtoon production costs. To encourage venture investment, the age limit for a venture company to qualify for tax support will be loosened to 10 years from founding, up from seven.

The new account dubbed the productive finance ISA will be established with the intention to draw long-term money into domestic assets. It can hold only Korean stocks and funds, the National Growth Fund and business development companies (BDCs). Its total contribution ceiling is 200 million won ($140,000), double that of a regular ISA, and money can stay in it for 10 years rather than five.

The tax treatment is where the two diverge most sharply. A regular ISA exempts interest and dividend income only up to 2 million won, or 4 million won for lower earners. The productive finance ISA removes the ceiling entirely.

Investors aged 19 to 34 with a total annual salary of 75 million won or less also get an income deduction worth 10 percent of what they pay in.

Dividend income from BDCs, listed public funds that put at least 60 percent of their assets into venture and innovative companies, will be taxed separately at a reduced rate of 9 percent on contributions of up to 100 million won.

name: Clean Energy
title: Clean energy offers least-cost path to meeting electricity demand, says report
description:
To better understand the best pathway to meet the growing demand, EEI examined two scenarios for meeting electricity demand through 2030.
The other pathway models the United States taking full advantage of clean energy to meet growing electricity use.
The report found meeting demand growth in the high fossil case would be $5 billion more than the clean energy approach.
“That’s $5 billion of savings per year with this much more ambitious clean energy future for meeting demand growth,” he concluded.
Price volatility of fossil fuels Fossil fuel prices are very volatile, as seen in 2022 when Russia invaded Ukraine and fuel prices spiked.
text:
Peak electricity demand is projected to increase 24% by 2030, according to Vote Solar, driven by data centers, industrial growth, and widespread electrification. The grid could meet this demand most cost effectively with clean energy rather than with fossil fuels, according to Let the sun in: Clean energy is the cheapest way to meet rising demand, a recent report from Electricity and Energy Innovation (EEI), a nonpartisan think tank.

To better understand the best pathway to meet the growing demand, EEI examined two scenarios for meeting electricity demand through 2030. In one, the United States follows the current federal policy approach, increasing use of fossil fuels as demand accelerates. The other pathway models the United States taking full advantage of clean energy to meet growing electricity use.

The report found that meeting the expected demand growth in the U.S. with a fossil fuel-heavy approach will add $29.7 billion annually to customer bills by 2030. The clean energy scenario, however, reduces overall costs to meet load growth by $5.1 billion annually that year compared to a high fossil scenario, a savings of 17%.

In the high-fossil fuel scenario the researchers blocked any planned coal retirements. In the clean energy model they accelerated the deployment of solar and sustained the deployment of wind out to 2030 to levels that represent what the researchers thought of as “the high end of ambition” for deployment nationally, Brendan Pierpont, director at EEI said in a webinar hosted by Clean Energy States Alliance.

The report found meeting demand growth in the high fossil case would be $5 billion more than the clean energy approach.

“That’s $5 billion of savings per year with this much more ambitious clean energy future for meeting demand growth,” he concluded.

The savings are primarily driven by reduced fuel costs and reduced operation and maintenance costs from retirement of what Pierpont called “expensive, inefficient plants,” as well as offsetting just the usage of many coal and gas plants. The savings, he noted, are somewhat offset by the need for new capital investment and the cost of enabling demand response and energy efficiency at the scale that we’re talking about.

Price volatility of fossil fuels

Fossil fuel prices are very volatile, as seen in 2022 when Russia invaded Ukraine and fuel prices spiked. Natural gas prices jumped by a factor of four, Pierpont said, with coal prices following suit. The study took into consideration price volatility and found that where fuel prices rise to 2022 levels, savings in the clean energy scenario increased by $8 billion per year.

“This really shows that a clean pathway is a significant hedge against that fuel price risk,” Pierpont said. “And that’s important because we are headed, by everything I have read, into a period of more, not less, uncertainty in fuel prices.”

In addition to fuel price uncertainty, the study acknowledges that there is some uncertainty in demand growth as well. Pierpont noted that a lot of load growth proposals are speculative as data centers are not being built as quickly as expected. Some utilities are creating a large load tariff for data centers to make a financial commitment. Pierpont pointed to AEP as an example of one utility that created a long-term contract mechanism for large loads. He said new large loads dropped by nearly two-thirds when it was issued.

This uncertainty was factored into the study, Pierpont said, to determine whether there would be downsides to following the clean energy scenario even if the demand doesn’t grow as expected. Pierpont said that even under this low demand growth case, clean energy will still provide savings.

“The savings are lower because the costs of the system overall are lower. But those savings are still there even if that demand doesn’t show up because even without the scale of demand growth, clean energy still reduces fuel costs, still reduces the operations and maintenance costs and drives those savings.”

Pierpont noted that states can remove some key barriers to the acceleration of clean energy and he pointed to Illinois as an example of improving both state and local permitting processes. The state set minimum standards for local siting that help prevent overly restrictive permit requirements at the county or local level. Illinois has also implemented a process that allows for a check to make sure that those local rules are fair. This is not the state usurping local authority, but it’s making sure that things can happen at the local level in an efficient way, Pierpont said.

Indiana is an example of a state that’s started to tackle the interconnection challenge by requiring that utilities look at the opportunity for surplus interconnection, which Pierpont said is a way of connecting additional resources to existing points of interconnection to make better use of those points.

“We have peaking power plants across the country that may use their interconnections 10% of the time or less, and that’s 90% of the time that all of that equipment…across the grid goes unutilized,” Pierpont said. “And so there’s an opportunity there to make better use of those existing points of interconnection and those existing interconnection rights.”

Other barriers exist including the need to improve electricity planning. Pierpont stressed the need for utilities to validate cost inputs against recent market data. He said for example, new natural gas turbine prices have increased almost two to three times in just a few years while, at the same time, battery storage continues to decline in cost.

Source procurement is one way of doing this, Pierpont noted. This, he explained, is where you go out to the market and say, what would it cost and what are the performance characteristics of a whole bunch of different resources. Those resources can be wind, solar and energy storage or new dispatchable capacity. Or it can be demand side resources like energy efficiency and virtual power plants and other load flexibility options, Pierpont said.

Clean energy confidence

One of the great myths about solar energy is that it’s unreliable because the sun isn’t always shining. The study tested each of the 2030 portfolios in its modeling against seven years of hourly weather data, added any days that at risk of a shortfall of being able to meet demand, then iterated until there were no days with any unserved load in any region across all seven years. Pierpont said the researchers are confident in their findings that clean energy can meet the needs of a growing electricity system.

In addition to certainty around the reliability of clean energy, Pierpont said evidence points certainty that gas prices will continue to rise along with load demand. As we think about meeting demand growth in the future, Pierpont concluded that “it’s important to make the pathway future proof so that we are mitigating these risks as we’re making good decisions.”

name: Clean Energy
title: Data Center Regulation (Or Not) in Pennsylvania: Part 1
description:
The data center boom poses serious energy policy challenges.
Narrowly, they include how to reform markets and rules to ensure that data center costs are not borne by electricity ratepayers.
At this writing, there are 81 active data center development proposals in Pennsylvania.
The only data center legislation that was passed during this year’s budget frenzy was an innocuous requirement tucked into the catch-all fiscal code bill.
One of them, the proposed Wildcat Ridge Data Center Campus, would contain a whopping 588 backup diesel generators to power 14 data center buildings.
text:
The data center boom poses serious energy policy challenges. Narrowly, they include how to reform markets and rules to ensure that data center costs are not borne by electricity ratepayers. In Pennsylvania, the average cost of electricity (a calculation that masks much higher regional variations) increased 14.6% over the past year, and the average electricity bill has increased 20.6% since 2024. A record 387,000 households faced utility shutoffs in 2025.

The impact of data centers on the communities where they are built is no less important. State law requires municipalities to zone for all legal purposes, including data centers, and they can’t legally be banned. At this writing, there are 81 active data center development proposals in Pennsylvania. Counties and municipalities are scrambling to pass moratoria or zoning amendments to deal with the onslaught, and community opposition is growing. So, too, is opposition to utilities’ use of eminent domain to build new transmission lines to serve them.

Arizona, Illinois, Ohio, New York, and Massachusetts are pausing data center incentives or development to consider imposing some rules, and new rules may be coming in Texas.

Pennsylvania lags behind.

There’s been lots of performative talk and voting on bills that would have paused or put some controls on the explosion of data center development, but not one of them has passed.

The House overwhelmingly voted to repeal the state’s open-ended state sales tax exemption for (very generously defined) data center equipment, which is currently projected to cost the state at least $1.9 billion through 2031. That’s in the face of a structural deficit and a projected $5-billion operating deficit this year.

The repeal legislation died in the Senate.

The only data center legislation that was passed during this year’s budget frenzy was an innocuous requirement tucked into the catch-all fiscal code bill. It requires that data centers using more than 10 MW of electricity annually disclose their energy and water usage. The latter will, by definition, be significantly underreported, as it doesn’t include water used at power plants that supply their electricity to data centers.

For his part, Governor Shapiro proposed voluntary standards for data centers. But they would have teeth only if they are legislatively tied to receipt of the sales tax exemption, which many legislators, in the House at least, want to repeal. Efforts to codify the Governor’s proposal also failed before the legislature’s summer recess.

The Governor is now promising executive action. What will that look like—given his limited authority in this space? And will it make a difference?

Measures to reduce or eliminate the significant impact of data centers on electricity rates are urgently needed in Pennsylvania and the 12 other states in the PJM region. In PJM’s last four base capacity auctions, data center-driven capacity charges totaled $29.4 billion—almost half of the $63.6 billion in total capacity charges incurred in that period. PJM’s inability to manage growing demand—largely from data centers—and deal with its chronic interconnection backlog has prompted FERC to announce that it’s poised to impose governance and stakeholder reforms on PJM.

The on-the-ground impacts of hyperscale data centers in host communities have not received the same level of political attention as their impact on electricity prices.

Hyperscale data centers change the character of communities. Lackawanna County, for example, is facing at least 11 major projects, with seven of them proposed in Archbald Borough, population 7,508. One of them, the proposed Wildcat Ridge Data Center Campus, would contain a whopping 588 backup diesel generators to power 14 data center buildings.

Many proposed projects are speculative, and municipalities don’t always make good decisions. But it’s clear that the facilities that are built will have multiple, local, cumulative impacts that state law and regulations do not adequately address.

description:
Hyundai Motor Company and Kia set their highest-ever July sales record in the U.S. market.
Hyundai Motor Company, including Genesis, sold 89,427 vehicles, up 3.7% year on year, while Kia sold 75,857 units, up 6.7%.

text:
Hyundai Motor Company and Kia set their highest-ever July sales record in the U.S. market. Hybrid electric vehicle sales jumped more than 50% from a year earlier, driving earnings growth and pushing the share of eco-friendly vehicles above 30% of total sales.

According to July U.S. sales results released by Hyundai Motor Company and Kia on the 3rd, combined sales rose 5% from a year earlier to 165,284 units. Hyundai Motor Company, including Genesis, sold 89,427 vehicles, up 3.7% year on year, while Kia sold 75,857 units, up 6.7%. Both brands set new July sales records. Genesis, Hyundai Motor Company's luxury brand, also sold 6,947 units, up 3.9% from a year earlier.

The biggest driver of the performance was clearly hybrid models. In July, Hyundai Motor Company and Kia sold a combined 43,727 hybrids in the U.S., up 52.2% from a year earlier. Hyundai Motor Company sold 22,733 units, up 35%, while Kia sold 20,994 units, up 76.6%, showing explosive growth.

Backed by strong hybrid sales, the group's total eco-friendly vehicle sales in July reached 50,937 units, up 24.7% from a year earlier. Eco-friendly vehicles accounted for 30.8% of total sales.

By contrast, pure electric vehicle sales fell 40.5% from a year earlier to 7,210 units. Hyundai Motor Company sold 4,545 units, down 46.1%, and Kia sold 2,665 units, down 27.7%, as the companies were affected by changes in the local market environment, including reduced subsidies.

By model, the sport utility vehicle lineup maintained solid demand. Hyundai Motor Company was led by the Tucson, with 19,714 units, and the Santa Fe, with 13,373 units. Kia was led by the Sportage, with 16,083 units, and the Telluride, with 11,816 units.

The two companies showed mixed results in global sales. Hyundai Motor Company sold 318,454 vehicles worldwide last month, down 5.1% from a year earlier. It sold 48,113 units in South Korea and 270,341 overseas. Kia, meanwhile, continued its growth trend with global sales of 298,037 units, up 13.4% from a year earlier. It sold 54,604 units in South Korea, up 21.3%, and 242,556 overseas, up 11.6%. Special-purpose vehicles totaled 877 units.

Hyundai Motor Company and Kia are strengthening their electrification competitiveness by continuing growth in the U.S. market with hybrids while also rolling out tailored solutions to help popularize EVs in the domestic market.

In particular, Kia expanded its EV lineup on the day by launching five new PV5 variants and updated versions of the PV5 and EV6. It also unveiled a "customer-tailored comprehensive EV solution" covering the entire process, from new car purchases and maintenance to used-car sales and trade-ins.

The company plans to offer transition subsidies to customers who buy an EV after owning an internal combustion engine vehicle. For purchases of the EV3 and EV4, it will provide ultra-low-interest installment financing to reduce the upfront burden. It will also significantly strengthen customer care throughout the EV ownership cycle through a proactive vehicle diagnostics system and trade-in benefits when customers sell their current vehicles.

New EPA Reg. No. 90150-4 authorizes SteraMist® (BIT®) – AgriMist for use up to and including the day of harvest, opening the door to indoor, greenhouse and hydroponic cannabis and hemp operations, along with post-harvest raw agricultural commodity treatment.

FREDERICK, Md., Aug. 03, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- TOMI Environmental Solutions, Inc. (NASDAQ: TOMZ), a global leader in disinfection and decontamination solutions, today announced that the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) has granted a new unconditional registration for SteraMist® (BIT®) – AgriMist (EPA Reg. No. 90150-4), the culmination of a multi-year registration process, expanding the product's labeled use sites to include post-harvest food safety applications, cannabis and hemp cultivation, and greenhouse and hydroponic agriculture.

The new registration allows TOMI's patented SteraMist ionized Hydrogen Peroxide (iHP) technology to be applied directly to a wide range of indoor-grown plants, such as hemp, tobacco, ornamentals, and specialty and medicinal crops for the prevention, control and suppression of common plant pathogens such as powdery mildew, downy mildew, Botrytis, Fusarium and Pythium rot. Notably, the label permits application up to and including the day of harvest, a distinction cultivators have identified as a key operational advantage.

The registration also extends to post-harvest treatment of raw agricultural commodities (RACs), giving food safety and packing operations a tool to help reduce cross-contamination between harvest and shipment. Because of the low hydrogen peroxide, SteraMist's sole active ingredient, which breaks down naturally into oxygen and humidity, treated surfaces require no rinsing or wiping after application.

“This registration expands what SteraMist can do for two of the fastest-growing segments we serve,” said Dr. Halden Shane, CEO of TOMI Environmental Solutions. “We've known for years that SteraMist was capable of this, now the EPA has confirmed it. We've been planning and waiting for this for several years, and it is incredibly rewarding to see it come to fruition. The avocado industry will be thrilled along with cannabis, hemp cultivators, and food safety operators. Everyone needs pathogen control that's rigorous enough to meet EPA standards and simple enough to fit into daily operations. With this label, we offer a technology that works up to the day of harvest, leaves no residue, and requires no rinsing or downtime.”

The expanded label positions SteraMist to serve growers and processors across a range of controlled environment agriculture settings, including greenhouses, indoor cultivation facilities, hydroponic operations, and mushroom production, as well as cut flower and nursery propagation applications covered under the same registration.

name: Congress
title: Opinion | Why I oppose the proposed data center in Lowndes County - Alabama Political Reporter
authors: Terri Sewell, Alex Jobin, Charles Steele Jr
description:
At my recent town hall in Lowndes County, I heard directly from residents about the proposed $1.5 billion data center.
For generations, the people of Lowndes County have faced injustices and hardships that no American community should have to endure.
I have serious concerns that a massive data center could further strain the county’s already fragile water infrastructure.
If this project truly promises opportunity for Lowndes County, then it should withstand rigorous environmental review, transparent public scrutiny and independent analysis.
Until the people of Lowndes County receive the answers, protections and accountability they deserve, I join them in opposing the proposed data center.
text:
Across Alabama’s 7th Congressional District, communities are increasingly being asked to consider proposals for large-scale data centers, from Birmingham and Bessemer to Fairfield and Lowndes County. While residents of all these communities are raising important questions about what these projects will mean for their neighborhoods, infrastructure and quality of life, their concerns seem to be falling on deaf ears.

At my recent town hall in Lowndes County, I heard directly from residents about the proposed $1.5 billion data center. Their concerns reinforced what has become increasingly clear: given the county’s unique history, longstanding infrastructure challenges, and the unprecedented scale of the proposed development, this project demands far greater scrutiny than it has received.

I stand with the residents of Lowndes County in opposing the proposed data center because too many questions remain unanswered, the potential consequences are too significant to ignore, and the people who will live with those consequences deserve better answers than what they have received from the project’s proponents.

For generations, the people of Lowndes County have faced injustices and hardships that no American community should have to endure. Despite playing a pivotal role in shaping our nation’s history during the Civil Rights Movement, they have suffered from chronic underinvestment, strained infrastructure and environmental injustice.

As a Member of Congress, I believe deeply in the promise of innovation. Artificial intelligence has the potential to transform health care, education, manufacturing and countless other sectors of our economy. I want America to lead the world in AI. I want Alabama to compete for the industries of the future. And I want rural communities—including those in Alabama’s Black Belt—to benefit from technological advancement. But innovation cannot come at the expense of the very people it is supposed to serve.

Over the past few months, residents have packed public meetings, signed petitions and sought answers about this proposal. Their concerns are not rooted in fear of technology. They are asking a simple question: Who benefits, and who bears the costs? That question deserves an honest answer.

Across the country, communities are grappling with the rapid expansion of AI data centers. While these facilities promise investment and economic growth, they also require enormous amounts of electricity and water, generate significant noise, place new demands on public infrastructure and local watersheds, and can permanently alter surrounding communities. Experts have warned that the growth of data centers is outpacing the policies needed to protect local residents and natural resources.

For me, the most immediate concern is water. Lowndes County has spent generations fighting for something many Americans take for granted: safe and reliable wastewater infrastructure. Families have lived for decades with failing septic systems and improper sanitation because of racial discrimination, persistent disinvestment, and uniquely challenging soil conditions. I have worked tirelessly to secure millions of dollars in federal funding to help address these longstanding problems, and I am proud of the progress we have made. But anyone familiar with Lowndes County knows our work is far from finished.

I have serious concerns that a massive data center could further strain the county’s already fragile water infrastructure. Before this project moves forward, residents deserve independent analysis of its water demands, its impact on groundwater and its effect on existing infrastructure.

These concerns are not hypothetical, and we need not look far to see the potential for harm.

Just 12 miles away, in Hope Hull, Alabama, Meta’s data center—which is significantly smaller than the one being proposed in Lowndes County—has become the single largest user of water in the Montgomery water system, according to a local official.

In Newton County, Georgia—just a three-hour drive east—residents have reported contaminated drinking water, damage to home appliances, and reduced water pressure following the explosive blasting process used to construct a $750 million data center. Families have been forced to ship themselves bottled water to drink, prepare meals, and bathe, and their water bills are set to increase by 33 percent in the next two years.

These troubling conditions prompted a commitment by the Assistant Administrator of the Environmental Protection Agency to investigate how data center construction impacts local water quality. Lowndes County deserves that same careful scrutiny before decisions are made that cannot easily be reversed.

It is also impossible to ignore the racial and economic dimensions of this proposal.

Lowndes County is rich in Civil Rights history. Situated directly between Selma and Montgomery, the residents of this majority-Black county have made extraordinary contributions to our nation’s ongoing struggle for racial equality. Yet, despite the heart, spirit and fight of its people, Lowndes County has endured more than a century of economic neglect and remains among the poorest counties in Alabama and in the United States.

Too often, low-income Black and minority communities have been expected to shoulder the environmental and economic risks of major industrial projects while others reap the rewards. We cannot allow the AI economy to perpetuate this cycle of injustice.

It is particularly troubling that this development is being proposed in an unincorporated area of the county. Residents have every right to ask whether that location was chosen because it offers fewer layers of oversight and accountability.

This land also has a deep historical significance for many Black Alabamians, including my own family. Our ancestors were sharecroppers in Lowndes County. And like many Black families in rural Alabama, their history stretches back to land once worked by slaves who had no opportunity to own the property they cultivated.

For so many Lowndes County households, their land represents family history and generational sacrifice. Often, it is their greatest financial asset. If this project depresses nearby property values or fundamentally changes the character of these communities, families could suffer lasting financial harm. After generations spent building something to pass on, they should not be asked to gamble it away for promises that have yet to be proven.

Of course, every AI data center site should be evaluated based on its own circumstances. But every community that is being considered deserves transparency and accountability. Far too often, they are given neither.

For all these reasons, I recently proposed the AI Data Center Moratorium Act, legislation that would temporarily pause the construction and expansion of AI data centers until Congress establishes comprehensive safeguards addressing environmental, economic, labor, privacy, and community impacts. The goal is not to stop innovation but to ensure that public policy keeps pace with technological change and everyday people collectively share in the benefits of our new future.

Let me be perfectly clear: I support innovation. I support economic development. What I do not support is asking one of Alabama’s most historically underserved communities to bear disproportionate risks without clear answers, meaningful public engagement and strong, enforceable protections.

If this project truly promises opportunity for Lowndes County, then it should withstand rigorous environmental review, transparent public scrutiny and independent analysis. If developers cannot demonstrate that the county’s water infrastructure, public health, environment and property owners will be protected, then this project should not move forward.

The residents of Lowndes County may not have the financial resources to take on a billion-dollar corporation, but that does not make them powerless. Since this project was proposed, we have seen ordinary people of different racial, political and economic backgrounds come together to make their voices heard. They are asking thoughtful questions because they care about the future of their community. I stand with them.

As we build the economy of tomorrow, we must ensure that no community is left behind. Until the people of Lowndes County receive the answers, protections and accountability they deserve, I join them in opposing the proposed data center.

FREDERICK, Md., Aug. 03, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- TOMI Environmental Solutions, Inc. (NASDAQ: TOMZ), a global leader in disinfection and decontamination solutions, today announced that the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) has granted a new unconditional registration for SteraMist® (BIT®) – AgriMist (EPA Reg. No. 90150-4), the culmination of a multi-year registration process, expanding the product's labeled use sites to include post-harvest food safety applications, cannabis and hemp cultivation, and greenhouse and hydroponic agriculture.

The new registration allows TOMI's patented SteraMist ionized Hydrogen Peroxide (iHP) technology to be applied directly to a wide range of indoor-grown plants, such as hemp, tobacco, ornamentals, and specialty and medicinal crops for the prevention, control and suppression of common plant pathogens such as powdery mildew, downy mildew, Botrytis, Fusarium and Pythium rot. Notably, the label permits application up to and including the day of harvest, a distinction cultivators have identified as a key operational advantage.

The registration also extends to post-harvest treatment of raw agricultural commodities (RACs), giving food safety and packing operations a tool to help reduce cross-contamination between harvest and shipment. Because of the low hydrogen peroxide, SteraMist's sole active ingredient, which breaks down naturally into oxygen and humidity, treated surfaces require no rinsing or wiping after application.

"This registration expands what SteraMist can do for two of the fastest-growing segments we serve," said Dr. Halden Shane, CEO of TOMI Environmental Solutions. "We've known for years that SteraMist was capable of this, now the EPA has confirmed it. We've been planning and waiting for this for several years, and it is incredibly rewarding to see it come to fruition. The avocado industry will be thrilled along with cannabis, hemp cultivators, and food safety operators. Everyone needs pathogen control that's rigorous enough to meet EPA standards and simple enough to fit into daily operations. With this label, we offer a technology that works up to the day of harvest, leaves no residue, and requires no rinsing or downtime."

The expanded label positions SteraMist to serve growers and processors across a range of controlled environment agriculture settings, including greenhouses, indoor cultivation facilities, hydroponic operations, and mushroom production, as well as cut flower and nursery propagation applications covered under the same registration.
