text:
Toyota says the 2027 Highlander EV is delayed because hybrids are selling too fast.

Don't buy the corporate spin.

Deep inside Toyota's supply chain, a much bigger technical headache is unfolding.

The mainstream media is echoing Toyota’s official PR line. They claim an eight-week delay gives buyers more time to purchase gas hybrids. The real story is a mechanical and supply-chain collision between Kentucky and North Carolina.

The Corporate Smoke Screen

Mainstream headlines are treating Toyota's sudden "eight-week production adjustment" as a routine tactical pause. The company publicly insists that skyrocketing consumer demand for gas and hybrid models justified extending current 2026 Highlander production through December.

As reported by Kelley Blue Book, Toyota confirmed that gas and hybrid versions will remain in production while the three-row electric SUV undergoes a minimum eight-week launch adjustment. Furthermore, analysis from Car and Driver emphasizes that current 2026 hybrid inventory will be pushed to maintain dealer volume through early 2027 while engineers make final adjustments.

Having spent over three decades tracking automotive assembly operations, testing pre-production mule vehicles, and working directly with factory logistics managers, I can tell you that explanation crumbles under basic industry logic. Stalling a flagship, three-row electric family SUV hands critical early-mover advantage to key rivals like the Kia EV9 and Hyundai IONIQ 9.

In our original reporting on Toyota's eight-week Highlander delay, it was noted that eight weeks is too long for a simple line tweak, yet too short for a full platform redesign. Additionally, my recent technical breakdown of 2026 Highlander Hybrid software bugs demonstrated how premature launch pushes can result in startup glitches that leave owners stranded with dead screens.

Toyota did not spend billions retooling its massive Georgetown, Kentucky assembly complex just to pump the brakes over strong hybrid sales.

When an automaker announces a minimum eight-week pause right before assembly lines ramp up, it points directly to tooling calibration, thermal testing failures, or supplier readiness issues. The corporate PR machine is masking a brutal pre-production bottleneck. Pushing first deliveries into 2027 is a mandatory soft pause designed to prevent a catastrophic, multi-million-dollar early rollout recall.

Hands-On Experience: The North Carolina Battery Bottleneck

The real pressure point begins 450 miles away from Kentucky at Toyota Battery Manufacturing North Carolina (TBMNC) in Liberty. My technical analysis of Toyota's supply chain reveals that the automaker’s $13.9 billion flagship facility is rushing to ramp up 10 dedicated lithium-ion battery lines for battery-electric vehicles.

Massive 95.8 kWh prismatic cell packs are rolling off brand-new U.S. lines for the first time.

Calibrating energy density consistency across thousands of domestic cells is proving difficult.

Early test packs revealed severe thermal throttling under sustained heavy-load conditions.

Advertising

During my decades evaluating high-voltage battery architecture on test tracks and in dealership service drives, I have witnessed firsthand what happens when heavy EV platforms push thermal envelopes. When installed in a heavy, three-row family SUV carrying seven passengers, initial pack trials generated unexpected heat spikes during rapid DC fast-charging cycles.

Toyota engineers took the right step by refusing to greenlight mass production until cell uniformity and thermal dissipation met strict internal durability standards. Rushing uncalibrated lithium-ion chemistry out the door leads to aggressive software-induced charge throttling, degraded winter range, and premature pack degradation.

Why this matters to buyers: A software-based charge limit patch applied after delivery reduces charging speeds by up to 40 percent to save battery life. Toyota's delay is an engineering intervention, not a sales strategy.

The NACS Native Integration Trap

The Highlander EV is engineered to ship with a native Tesla North American Charging Standard (NACS) port, skipping clunky adapters entirely. While this is a huge selling point for convenience, integrating high-voltage NACS wiring directly into Toyota’s TNGA-K EV platform introduced unexpected floorboard packaging friction.

Engineers had to route heavy 800V-capable wiring and cooling lines through tight unibody rails.

Standard routing compromised rear footwell depth in the critical third-row seating area.

Toyota faced a choice: reduce ground clearance or sacrifice family legroom.

To resolve the floorboard intrusion without lowering ground clearance, factory tooling in Kentucky had to be recalibrated mid-stride. Having inspected modified floorpans across multiple generations of crossover platforms, I have found that modifying physical mounting cradles and high-voltage junction boxes always adds weeks of unexpected factory downtime to a pre-production schedule.

I have inspected numerous floorpan revisions across Toyota's modular platforms over the years. When a high-voltage wiring loom forces a floorpan stamping change, stamping dies must be recut and re-certified for crash safety compliance. That process alone takes at least six to eight weeks of press shop reconfiguration.

Deep Industry Expertise: The Domino Effect On Sub-Brands

This delay isn't isolated to Toyota.

The Highlander EV serves as the core structural foundation for two other upcoming three-row electric crossovers: the luxury Lexus TZ and the Subaru Getaway.

By holding back the Highlander EV, Toyota temporarily froze the rollout pipeline for Lexus and Subaru. The entire tri-brand three-row EV initiative relies on flawless execution from the Kentucky assembly floor.

Advertising

My ongoing conversations with industry technicians and assembly line suppliers confirm that line balancing across joint-venture models is notoriously rigid. If the primary Toyota model experiences structural or cell calibration halts, the secondary luxury and partner variants automatically get pushed down the queue.

Firsthand Consumer Insights: What Family Crossover Buyers Must Do Today

If you are currently waiting on the 2027 Highlander EV, my professional advice is not to expect volume inventory to hit dealership lots until well into mid-2027. First-year production runs will likely be tight, with dealers placing premium markups on early allocations.

Buying a first-run EV off a newly retooled assembly line always carries real consumer risk.

Software bugs, thermal management updates, and initial trim rattles frequently plague year-one builds.

The proven Highlander Hybrid remains the safest, most practical financial bet for the next 18 months.

From a consumer advocacy perspective, Toyota extending 2026 gas and hybrid production is actually a massive win for car buyers. The 243-horsepower Highlander Hybrid delivers an EPA-rated 36 MPG combined without any of the charging or range compromises associated with brand-new EV architecture.

You can still purchase a bulletproof Highlander Hybrid today while Toyota irons out its EV kinks.

Let early adopters absorb the initial software patches and dealer markups on the 2027 EV.

Smart family buyers will wait until year two of production before making the leap to electric.

Toyota's decision to pause production demonstrates a commitment to long-term reliability over short-term PR wins. Taking an extra eight weeks to perfect cell thermal profiles and NACS harness routing saves owners from endless service drive headaches down the road.

Final Verdict For Crossover Buyers

Navigating dealership showrooms during a major powertrain transition requires clear-headed strategy. Do not let salesperson hype push you into placing a non-refundable deposit on an EV that is actively undergoing pre-production tooling adjustments.

If you need a reliable seven-passenger family hauler this year, negotiate hard on an existing 2026 Highlander Hybrid while inventory is strong. If you are set on going 100 percent electric, give Toyota's Kentucky team the time they need to get the 2027 Highlander EV right the first time.

There’s More Here… Also check out my Torque News Home Page for more of my informative Toyota Highlander news articles.

About The Author

Denis Flierl is a 14-year Senior Reporter at Torque News and a member of the Rocky Mountain Automotive Press (RMAP) with 30+ years of industry experience. Explore his full investigative reporting archives and technical guides at DenisFlierl.com.

Based in Parker, Colorado, Denis leverages the Rockies' high-altitude terrain as a rigorous testing ground to provide "boots-on-the-ground" analysis for readers across the Rocky Mountain region, California EV corridors, the Northeast, Texas truck markets, and Midwest agricultural zones.

A former professional test driver and consultant for Ford, GM, Ram, Toyota, and Tesla, he delivers data-backed insights on reliability and market shifts. Denis cuts through the noise to provide national audiences with the real-world reporting today’s landscape demands.

"Continued investment in the Community and Renewable Energy Scheme (CARES) and other support programmes, alongside the significant funding delivered locally by renewable energy projects [in community benefits], will help more communities and local authorities capture the benefits of Scotland's renewable energy industry."
text:
China’s government and an investment vehicle based in the Cayman Islands are among a group of foreign owners whose Scottish wind farms have paid out more than £1bn to shareholders in recent years.

The figures come from a Ferret examination of five years of dividend payments reported in the annual accounts of some of Scotland’s biggest onshore wind projects.

They have been branded “extraordinary” by critics who claim wealth from our natural resources is "filling the pockets of distant private shareholders or other countries’ treasuries” while Scots miss out.

As we reported this year some communities across the country feel they are being short-changed by local wind farms, which are large infrastructure projects which can alter treasured landscapes for decades and cause disruption while being built.

But the renewable sector said it is a major contributor to the economy – supporting over “47,000 jobs” – and the overseas investment it attracted to the country was “delivering lasting value to the Scottish people”.

Our analysis identified 37 projects ultimately owned outside the UK which reported paying £1.15bn in dividends over five years. One of the biggest potential winners identified is IIF International Holdings LP, a Cayman Islands fund managed by the Wall Street banking giant, JP Morgan.

Fifteen wind farms we analysed listed the fund – which owns them through an Edinburgh-based subsidiary called Nadara – as their ultimate parent company.

Together they reported paying more than £450m in dividends over the five-year period. The biggest contributor was the 40-turbine Farr wind farm south of Inverness, which reported paying out almost £110m. Nadara is exploring plans to expand the site with another 10 turbines.

The identities of the investors in the IIF International fund are not made public because of rules in the Caymans, which is considered a corporate tax and secrecy haven. But they reportedly include investors from the US, the Middle East and Japan.

Nadara told The Ferret it has created “strong, lasting relationships” with communities near its turbines and increased its community benefit payments in 2025, alongside offering “shared ownership schemes”. “Nadara adopts a full-lifetime approach to community engagement to create long-term value for our communities as well as for our business,” a spokesperson said.

Developments owned by overseas governments also reported more than £400m in dividends during the five-year period.

Two wind farms owned or part-owned by the French state energy company EDF – Dorenell in Moray and Fallago Rig in the Borders, which it has a stake in alongside US investor Federated Hermes – paid out more than £250m.

Projects owned by Norway’s state-owned renewable company, Statkraft, reported £131m in dividends, while Sweden’s state-owned Vattenfall was in line to receive almost £13m from Clashindarroch in Aberdeenshire.

The Afton wind farm in East Ayrshire, owned by the Chinese government’s State Development and Investment Corporation, reported £26m in dividends. The same organisation ultimately owns the Benbrack wind farm in Dumfries and Galloway, which began generating electricity last year.

Calls for greater Scottish stake

Our analysis does not cover every major onshore wind farm in Scotland, because some do not publish separate company accounts. This includes those owned by major developers such as SSE, and ScottishPower – itself a subsidiary of the Spanish utility company Iberdrola.

Not all the cash paid out by individual projects will necessarily reach the ultimate shareholders. It often first passes through layers of holding companies, which may decide to reinvest it or use it to repay debt.

But the findings provide a snapshot of the money being generated by the onshore wind sector – and where some of it could be ending up – at a time when there are renewed calls for Scotland to take a much bigger stake in its renewable energy industry.

In May, a coalition of campaign groups and think tanks launched the Our Power campaign, which is calling for action to keep more of the money generated by wind, solar and hydro power locally.

Liam Hainey, a spokesperson for the group, said Scots were currently being “shortchanged” with “too much wealth filling either the pockets of distant private shareholders or other countries’ treasuries”.

“If we stick to business as usual and an economy of extraction then we will look back in 20 years filled with regrets.” – Kristopher Leask MSP, Scottish Greens

He added: “We urgently need action to ensure that more of the profits from the renewable sector stay in Scotland and benefit our communities which is why we’re calling on the Scottish Government to take a public stake in future projects and to do everything it can to support council and community ownership.”

The Scottish Government has supported community energy through its CARES scheme, which provides funding and advice to groups seeking to develop or have a stake in renewable projects.

It also launched a pilot scheme last year giving communities the first opportunity to lease and repower 10 wind farms on publicly owned land. Repowering involves replacing a project’s turbines at the end of their operational life.

Meanwhile, the UK Government’s clean energy investment company, GB Energy, published its Local Power Plan this year, which said it “refused to accept that the days when Britain owned things are in the past”.

It committed up to £1bn over three years to help more communities own local energy projects, which it claimed could become a “long-term engine for local economic growth and community wealth building”.

Part of the rationale for the plan was that community-owned energy projects have been found to deliver more for communities than the current model of ‘community benefit’ payments – where developers make voluntary payments to support local initiatives near their turbines.

The industry points out that community benefits are a “unique feature” of the renewable sector and claims “no other industry has chosen to take such a positive role in our society”.

Communities receive £55m from community benefits from all Scottish onshore renewable projects per year. The Farr wind farm, ultimately owned by the IIF fund, paid out nearly £95m in 2023 alone.

One 2021 study found community-owned projects provide 34 times more money to communities than the average community benefit package. GB Energy also pointed to evidence that public support for the transition to cleaner energy increases when local people own projects and see their economic benefits firsthand.

But currently only around one per cent of Scotland’s onshore wind capacity is owned by communities. That lags far behind countries like Denmark, where, since 2008, developers have been required to offer communities at least a 20 per cent stake in new wind farms. In Germany, one study estimated that 40 per cent of renewable capacity is citizen-owned.

“The UK squandered our oil and gas wealth – we cannot repeat the same mistake with renewables.” – Laurie Macfarlane, Future Economy Scotland

“There is nothing inevitable about a system where Scotland’s natural assets are controlled by overseas governments and multinational corporations,” the Scottish Greens MSP for the Highlands and Islands, Kristopher Leask, told The Ferret.

Leask, who worked for the charity Community Energy Scotland before being elected to parliament in May, added: “Scotland has an enormous renewable energy potential, but too often our communities are seeing the disruption without sharing in the rewards.

“If we stick to business as usual and an economy of extraction then we will look back in 20 years filled with regrets.”

That view was shared by Laurie Macfarlane, the co-director of think tank Future Economy Scotland. “The UK squandered our oil and gas wealth – we cannot repeat the same mistake with renewables,” he said. Macfarlane claimed it was “extraordinary” that £400m in dividends had flowed from projects owned by the French, Chinese, Swedish and Norwegian governments, “while the Scottish exchequer has received nothing”.

He added: “If the Scottish Government is serious about delivering a just transition, it must take bold steps to expand both public and community ownership of our renewable resources. The people of Scotland deserve a real stake in our energy future.”

But a spokesperson for Scottish Renewables, the body that represents the whole of the country’s green energy sector, argued it continued to attract “significant inward investment, delivering lasting value for the Scottish people, the economy and energy security”.

"Renewable energy supports more than 47,000 jobs in Scotland, creating opportunities for businesses and workers while helping to grow a strong domestic supply chain. These benefits are felt far beyond individual projects, bringing investment, skills and opportunities to communities across the country,” they continued.

"Continued investment in the Community and Renewable Energy Scheme (CARES) and other support programmes, alongside the significant funding delivered locally by renewable energy projects [in community benefits], will help more communities and local authorities capture the benefits of Scotland's renewable energy industry."

text:
Walmart Expands Proprietary Fast-Charging Infrastructure Across U.S. Retail Footprint

Walmart Inc. is accelerating the deployment of its proprietary electric vehicle charging network, transitioning from third-party host partnerships to an in-house branded model across its retail locations. Through mid-2026, the retailer established 46 high-speed charging stations incorporating 380 individual ports, bringing total charger availability to approximately 326 of its 4,600 domestic stores. An estimated 300 additional locations are currently under construction, positioning the company as a rapidly scaling direct-operated charging network provider trailing only Tesla in second-quarter infrastructure expansion.

The strategy leverages store footprint accessibility, where ninety percent of the domestic population resides within ten miles of a facility, to capture charging dwell-time traffic and stimulate adjacent retail revenue. By operating native direct-current fast-charging equipment at competitive utility rates, the network targets plug-in electric vehicle drivers, particularly those without residential Level 2 charging access. The infrastructure expansion aims to build out public power delivery capabilities across underserved regional corridors while enhancing core store utilization metrics.

title: Trump's environmental rollbacks have come to New Jersey
description:
Donald Trump has declared war on environmental protections from Washington, but in New Jersey, the problem isn’t just what Trump is doing.
Oregon passed an Environmental Protection Act that freezes federal environmental standards at pre-Trump levels.
Adopt a state Environmental Quality Review Act requiring environmental impact statements.
New Jersey spent decades building some of the strongest environmental protections in the country.
Our elected leaders have a choice: They can strengthen New Jersey’s environmental protections before federal safeguards disappear, or become complicit through inaction.
text:
As Washington weakens environmental protections, Trenton takes apart New Jersey’s own safeguards.

Donald Trump has declared war on environmental protections from Washington, but in New Jersey, the problem isn’t just what Trump is doing. The problem is what New Jersey is doing that allows those attacks to have an impact here at home.

The Trump administration isn’t simply rolling back a few regulations around the edges. It is carrying out the largest dismantling of environmental protections and standards in American history. The cumulative effect isn’t one bad policy. It’s more than 530 administrative actions, a death by a thousand cuts.

For New Jersey, these aren’t abstract policy debates. They translate into dirtier air, more flooding, stalled toxic cleanups, higher utility bills, and greater public health risks.

Gov. Mikie Sherrill can go on cable television and criticize Donald Trump all she wants. She can refuse to hand over voter rolls and denounce attacks on democracy. But if New Jersey weakens its own environmental protections, cuts DEP funding, fast-tracks permits, raids clean energy funds, and delays climate rules, then we aren’t building a wall against Trump. We’re building an on-ramp.

You can’t fight Trump with one hand while handing his agenda a permit with the other.

For decades, New Jersey’s environmental laws acted as a shield against federal rollbacks. We had stronger wetlands protections, stricter flood regulations, and a DEP that wasn’t afraid to tell polluters, “No.” Today, that shield is developing more holes than the Pulaski Skyway.

Trump is swinging a wrecking ball at environmental protections nationally. The question is: Why is New Jersey helping carry it?

Operation FAST: DEP or drive-thru?

Gov. Sherrill’s Executive Order 5, “Operation FAST,” is being sold as government efficiency. In reality, it puts environmental protection on a stopwatch.

The permitting dashboard and “permit czar” impose mandatory timelines on state agencies, particularly the DEP, forcing staff to process permits at record speed.

They’ve turned the Department of Environmental Protection into the Department of Excessive Pollution.

When you limit public input and scientific review, you’re not cutting red tape. You’re cutting public health and safety. Toxic contamination, wetlands destruction, flooding impacts, and pipeline hazards don’t operate on political timelines.

Scientists don’t find pollution or health problems faster because politicians are impatient.

New Jersey already has more Superfund sites than any other state in the nation. We should be hiring inspectors, scientists, and enforcement staff, not asking them to review complex permits like contestants on a game show.

At this rate, DEP’s new motto may as well be: “Would you like a pipeline with that permit?”

Breaking open the piggy bank

For years, politicians have treated environmental funds like an ATM. The Clean Energy Fund and the Regional Greenhouse Gas Initiative, or RGGI, were created to fight climate change, not to plug holes in state budgets.

Raiding $190 million from clean energy programs and hundreds of millions more from RGGI plays directly into Trump’s hands.

That money was supposed to lower utility bills, expand renewable energy, and help vulnerable communities adapt to climate change. Instead, it is being used to balance budgets, a political choice that deepens both the climate crisis and the leadership crisis.

It’s the political equivalent of selling your fire extinguisher to pay your electric bill while your kitchen is on fire.

The reactionary energy response

New Jersey should be leading the transition to renewable energy. Instead, we’re hearing an “all-of-the-above” energy strategy that sounds suspiciously like “everything except moving quickly on renewables.”

The Power NJ Act lifted New Jersey’s 50-year moratorium on new nuclear plants while gas plant expansions continue receiving support.

This isn’t an energy transition. It’s an energy regression.

Natural gas plants lock us into decades of emissions. Nuclear leaves behind radioactive waste that will outlive every politician currently in office. Yet somehow we’re told this is “clean” and “innovative.”

Apparently, every bad energy idea becomes acceptable if you attach the words “data center” to it.

New Jersey’s biggest problem: The holes we never fixed

The dirty little secret is that Trump’s environmental rollbacks are having an impact in New Jersey because we never fixed the damage done years ago.

New Jersey still hasn’t repaired or strengthened many of the Christie administration’s rollbacks to flood hazard rules, stream encroachment protections, wetlands regulations, Category One buffers, water quality planning, headwaters protections, and ecological connectivity standards.

Climate change doesn’t care whether a loophole was created by Christie, Trump, or anyone else. Floodwater doesn’t stop at party lines.

Every loophole in state law becomes an open invitation for federal rollbacks.

Those gaps aren’t theoretical. They affect decisions being made right now, including whether New Jersey adopts stronger climate standards for future development.

Climate rules delayed when we need them most

The REAL (Resilient Environments and Landscapes) rules were designed to make New Jersey climate-ready by requiring developers to account for future flooding and sea-level rise.

The rules would:

Require the use of current climate science instead of outdated FEMA maps.

Mandate higher flood elevation standards.

Reduce future flood losses.

Better protect communities from sea-level rise and extreme weather.

Instead, implementation has been delayed until 2027.

Environmental protection delayed is environmental protection denied.

We’re telling people whose basements have flooded three times in five years that they’ll have to wait while developers finish building tomorrow’s flood victims.

Climate change isn’t taking a year off. Why are we?

What New Jersey doesn’t have

New Jersey’s environmental laws were built on the assumption there would always be a federal floor.

That floor is disappearing. If the state truly wants to protect itself from Trump’s environmental agenda, it can no longer pretend its existing laws are enough.

While the federal government argues it no longer has an obligation to regulate climate pollution under the Clean Air Act, New Jersey has largely relied on the EPA to do the heavy lifting.

That means New Jersey has:

No enforceable CO₂ limits.

No methane regulations.

No mandatory greenhouse gas reductions for major polluters.

No comprehensive state climate regulatory program.

Unlike California, New York, Oregon, Washington, and Massachusetts, New Jersey lacks several critical protections:

A state Environmental Quality Act (“mini-NEPA”) requiring environmental impact statements for major projects.

An Environmental Backstop Act that automatically preserves stronger federal standards when Washington rolls them back.

Strong methane and carbon dioxide regulations independent of federal standards.

Comprehensive habitat protections under the Endangered and Nongame Species Conservation Act.

A meaningful Climate Superfund law to make polluters pay.

Stronger environmental justice protections without loopholes.

Updated PFAS and toxic chemical standards that automatically keep pace with science.

New Jersey’s Environmental Justice law has loopholes big enough to drive a garbage truck through. It cannot directly deny many permits, and public hearings have limited legal effect.

Our Endangered Species law protects animals but not necessarily the habitats they need to survive.

That’s like protecting birds while cutting down all the trees.

Other states are fighting back

While New Jersey has done little to build a firewall against Trump’s environmental agenda, other states already have.

Oregon passed an Environmental Protection Act that freezes federal environmental standards at pre-Trump levels. If Washington weakens protections, Oregon simply says, “Not here.”

California and New York have state environmental review laws that can stop or delay projects regardless of what happens in Washington.

Washington maintains independent carbon caps.

Massachusetts and California have led lawsuits against the EPA and the Trump administration over environmental rollbacks.

Meanwhile, New Jersey continues challenging Trump on other issues while largely ignoring his attacks on the environment.

At some point, the Garden State risks becoming the Paved-Over State.

The federal threat we cannot ignore

Some threats New Jersey cannot stop on their own.

Trump’s cuts to EPA funding hit us particularly hard because a significant portion of DEP’s budget comes from federal dollars.

Federal Superfund cuts threaten cleanup projects on the Passaic River, Berry’s Creek, and dozens of other toxic sites.

Federal offshore wind and offshore drilling decisions affect projects in federal waters.

Pollution from Ohio and Pennsylvania still blows into New Jersey regardless of our laws.

And when the federal government weakens protections for endangered species crossing state lines, New Jersey cannot put a fence around the Delaware Bay.

But that’s exactly why state protections matter.

What New Jersey should do

If New Jersey wants to build a real firewall against Trump’s environmental agenda, it should:

Pass an Environmental Backstop Act modeled after Oregon.

Adopt a state Environmental Quality Review Act requiring environmental impact statements.

Pass climate legislation with strong, enforceable standards.

Adopt the REAL rules immediately and strengthen flood protections.

Restore and strengthen Christie-era environmental protections.

Strengthen methane, greenhouse gas, and climate regulations.

Expand endangered species protections to include habitat, breeding, and foraging areas.

Eliminate loopholes in the Environmental Justice law.

Fully fund the DEP and hire additional scientists, inspectors, and enforcement staff.

Stop treating environmental funds like a political slush fund.

Update standards for toxic chemicals like PFAS and accelerate toxic site cleanups.

Pass a Climate Superfund law.

Donald Trump is dismantling environmental protections at the federal level. That’s bad enough.

What’s worse is voluntarily dismantling them ourselves.

New Jersey spent decades building some of the strongest environmental protections in the country. At the very moment Washington is retreating from environmental responsibility, Trenton should be strengthening that legacy, not weakening it.

You can’t call yourself the Garden State while allowing it to become a polluted wasteland.

If we continue down this road, we won’t become the Garden State. We’ll become Texas on the Hudson.

Or worse, we’ll be Florida with worse traffic and more flooding.

Our elected leaders have a choice: They can strengthen New Jersey’s environmental protections before federal safeguards disappear, or become complicit through inaction.

History won’t remember the strongest press releases. It will remember who stood up and fought.

authors: Emily Anderson Stern, The Salt Lake Tribune, Emily Anderson Stern, The Salt Lake Tribune, Alixel Cabrera, Will Ruzanski

text:
Utah is a finalist to host a U.S. Department of Energy campus that would attempt to close the nuclear fuel cycle, which the federal government says would bring billions of dollars and thousands of jobs — but with it would come a significant portion of the nation’s nuclear waste.

In exchange, as the state negotiates a potential deal with the agency, Utah Office of Energy Development Director Emy Lesofski told The Salt Lake Tribune it is asking for help in addressing one of Utah’s most pressing environmental crises: the drying Great Salt Lake.

“(The agreement) has to be something that is a good deal for us and that makes sense for us, and that also helps us solve some of the challenges that we have,” Lesofski said in an interview. “We think that the Great Salt Lake is a really important national treasure, as well as Utah treasure, and so we want to make sure that anything we’re doing, we can utilize it to provide some measure of assistance for that.”

The proposed site for the campus in Tooele County’s remote West Desert is roughly 10 miles from the Great Salt Lake, which could hit a record low again this year, resulting in more toxic dust storms for the heavily populated Wasatch Front.

Utah is one of five states — including Idaho, Louisiana, Oklahoma and Tennessee — that are contenders for a “nuclear lifecycle innovation campus,” DOE announced Tuesday, which would aim to host facilities for the full nuclear fuel cycle in one place, co-locating fuel fabrication and enrichment with reprocessing used nuclear fuel and disposition of waste.

Sites may also host nuclear reactors and data centers, according to the agency.

Lesofski said federal officials have previously indicated that they could select three states of the more than two dozen that applied for a campus. At the behest of Gov. Spencer Cox and the Republican-led Legislature, Utah joined the competition for a federal nuclear hub in April.

DOE did not respond to questions about the number of states it will select and how it plans to approach negotiations with finalists.

Cox signed a memorandum of understanding with U.S. Energy Secretary Chris Wright on Monday, obtained by The Tribune, in which the parties agreed to “cooperate in good faith” to realize their “shared vision … to unlock the full value of the nuclear fuel cycle.”

But Lesofski emphasized the governor’s signature does not mean Utah is sold on building a campus.

“If we are in a position where we don’t think it’s safe and we don’t think it’s good for Utah, we won’t do it,” she said, adding, “And we have no reason to think we won’t be able to get there — DOE’s been a good partner, and we work well together, but we always reserve the right to say it’s not the right thing to do.”

According to the memorandum, if both parties do not sign onto a host agreement by Sept. 30, “either party may terminate this MOU.”

That two-month timeline, Lesofski said, is “a big lift, but we’re committed to working through it responsibly and safely and thoroughly. The state energy director added that she wasn’t sure if the end of September was a final date for approval.

Will Utahns be involved?

There are lengthy permitting processes that both the state and federal government must go through before beginning development on a campus, Lesofski noted, and they include opportunities for the public to weigh in.

In Monday’s agreement, both federal and state entities said they would “work collaboratively with local communities, including counties, municipalities, and other governmental entities, to coordinate development activities and ensure robust community engagement and transparency.”

Lesofski said her office has been working to engage Utahns on the issue for months.

As part of Cox’s “Operation Gigawatt” seeking to double the state’s electricity generation, with a focus on fast-tracking nuclear development, it put $1.8 million toward a public relations campaign to convince Utahns of the value of nuclear energy, The Tribune reported last year.

Even if a host site deal comes with help for the Great Salt Lake, environmental advocates remain wary of how storing spent nuclear fuel could impact the health of Utahns and the lake itself.

“Make no mistake, as part of its obligation to protect its citizens, the federal government should absolutely provide meaningful and effective support to save Great Salt Lake,” said Carmen Valdez, a senior policy associate for Healthy Environment Alliance of Utah. “But this trade-off is not worth the price.”

“Practically,” Valdez added, “accepting the nation’s nuclear waste would mean transporting high-level radioactive waste by rail and road, through communities across Utah and around the lake, and storing highly radioactive materials within its watershed, dramatically increasing the potential for leaks or accidents, possibly in perpetuity.”

The proposed campuses across the country come as President Donald Trump’s administration looks to quadruple nuclear energy production, but has not found a solution for the radioactive waste.

A leaked White House plan indicates he is pushing federal lawmakers to abandon plans to store high-level nuclear waste at Yucca Mountain in Nevada, POLITICO reported, and pass laws allowing the waste to be sent to campus host states.

Ahead of any hubs being built, Lesofski noted, “because Yucca Mountain is the law of the land, there are things that have to be changed on the federal level, and that’s something that we are watching closely.” She said her office has been working with Utah’s Sen. Mike Lee on the issue.

Lee chairs the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, giving him an influential role in where policy conversations land. His office did not respond to a request for comment.

text:
Sacramento just landed the first sodium-ion battery plant of its kind, a grid-storage bet that could reshape how cities store power

Peak Energy will build what it calls America’s first factory dedicated to grid-scale sodium-ion energy storage at Sacramento’s Metro Air Park. The 183,000-square-foot plant is designed to produce up to 4 gigawatt-hours of battery systems each year, and the company expects production and shipments to begin in the first quarter of 2027.

The real test is whether a less flammable battery chemistry can help utilities store more renewable power, steady the grid during peak demand and ease the electric bill without creating a safety fight for nearby residents. The proposed plant sits less than a mile from a Natomas neighborhood.

A factory built for the grid

Peak says the Sacramento facility will make enough storage systems each year to serve nearly four million homes. Co-founder Cameron Dales said the batteries will enter electricity networks in Sacramento through SMUD and reach customers across the country.

These are not batteries for phones or cars. Peak plans to assemble large units about 30 feet long, built to absorb electricity when supply is plentiful and release it when homes, businesses, or power-hungry data centers need more. The batteries work like a reservoir for the grid.

That matters as solar and wind become a larger part of the power mix. Renewable energy can be abundant at one hour and scarce at another, so storage helps utilities shift that electricity across the day instead of building a new power plant for every demand spike.

Why sodium changes the equation

Sodium-ion batteries move ions during charging and discharging in much the same way as lithium-ion batteries, but they use a different chemistry. Sodium is widely available, and supporters say the technology can operate across a broader range of temperatures with less system complexity.

Peak’s design uses passive cooling rather than the active refrigeration commonly needed by large lithium-ion installations. The company says that can cut energy-storage costs by 20%, support 99% guaranteed uptime, and allow systems to operate for more than 20 years without scheduled maintenance.

Those are company projections, not yet a verdict from years of operating the Sacramento plant. Still, they explain the business case. Less cooling equipment can mean less noise, fewer maintenance points, and less electricity spent cooling the batteries instead of serving customers.

Safety will shape local trust

Battery projects can face fierce community resistance, and Sacramento is not operating in a vacuum. A January 2025 fire at the lithium-ion storage facility in Moss Landing led to a roughly 24-hour evacuation of about 1,200 residents, a reminder that emergency planning is not an abstract concern.

Dales called Peak’s sodium-ion system “a much simpler, safer, more resilient technology.” Sodium-ion chemistry is generally less prone to overheating than lithium-ion, but chemistry alone does not erase risk. Plant design, fire separation, monitoring, worker training, and a clear response plan will still matter to families living nearby.

That may be the project’s most important local test. A first-of-its-kind factory has to earn trust in everyday terms, not just in a laboratory report or a ribbon-cutting speech.

Jobs beyond the factory floor

The facility represents up to $71 million in capital investment and is expected to create 239 local jobs over the next 18 months. Peak says the average annual wage will exceed $90,000, while suppliers, contractors, logistics companies, and service businesses could see additional work.

“These are jobs that are accessible to people in our neighborhoods,” Greater Sacramento Economic Council President and CEO Barry Broome said. The council is already helping retrain workers laid off by Blue Diamond for battery-sector roles.

That detail matters. Advanced manufacturing often sounds distant or highly specialized, but many positions can become reachable with focused technical training. For workers trying to replace a lost paycheck, the clean-energy transition only feels real when it leads to a stable job.

Why Sacramento won

Peak searched nationwide before selecting Metro Air Park. The company cited Sacramento’s manufacturing workforce, its access to California’s expanding storage market, its proximity to Silicon Valley, and support from local and state partners.

The project also received a $10.5 million California Competes tax credit in May 2026. Sacramento offers another practical advantage through SMUD, which is a key partner and already provides electricity to the industrial site.

For local customers, the promise is straightforward. More storage could help SMUD use renewable electricity when it is cheapest and most abundant, then deliver it later when demand rises. That does not guarantee a smaller electric bill, but it gives the utility another tool to control system costs.

GM adds industrial weight

Peak recently formed a strategic partnership with General Motors, backed by an investment from GM Ventures. The companies plan to pair GM’s next-generation sodium-ion cell technology with Peak’s grid-storage platform, giving the startup access to deep battery engineering and industrial expertise.

There is an important limit, however. Peak’s Sacramento factory will initially assemble storage systems using cells sourced from Asia, according to CEO Landon Mossburg, rather than immediately manufacturing every battery component in the United States.

The GM partnership could help close that gap over time, but a fully domestic supply chain is still a goal rather than a finished product. That nuance does not diminish the factory’s scale. It shows what Sacramento is actually getting first, a major system-assembly hub and a possible bridge toward U.S.-developed sodium-ion cells.

What happens next

Peak already reports more than 6 gigawatt-hours of customer commitments, including agreements with Jupiter Power, Energy Vault, and RWE Americas. Initial production and shipments are planned for early 2027, while a local report said the broader site is expected to be fully operating by the end of that year.

Now comes the hard part. Peak must install the production line, hire and train workers, meet customer schedules, and prove that its cost and safety claims hold up at commercial scale.

Sacramento’s bet will be judged by reliable batteries, good jobs, safe operations, and whether households feel any benefit on the electric bill.

text:
Support CleanTechnica's work through a Substack subscription, on Patreon, or on Stripe. Help us produce all of the high-quality, original content we publish week after week despite the challenges of content-scraping AI, antisocial media, inflation, and other hurdles.

As the all-important midterm elections draw closer, Democrats are fine-tuning their economic messaging while Republicans are…well, panicking. That doesn’t mean the 2026 mid-term results are a foregone conclusion, though. If economic messaging is all the Democrats to offer, they are missing an opportunity to motivate a key demographic, namely, voters who recognize that Congress must pick up the climate action ball dropped by US President Donald Trump.

Spokane Is Burning

The latest news on the climate front indicates that the global warming chickens have come home to roost, with a vengeance. On top of a series of record setting heat waves across the country, smoke from Canadian wildfires engulfed much of the US Northeast last week, and this week Mother Nature has followed up with three wildfires burning their way through Spokane County, Washington. So far they have consumed more than 600 buildings, many located within the borders of the City of Spokane. Thousands have been forced to evacuate, with some under urgent “leave now” and “last notice” warnings.

Meanwhile, the impact of wildfire smoke on human health is coming into sharper focus. Too bad US Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has chosen this moment to launch a cooking show on teevee (roadkill, much?) instead of employing his media amplifier in the service of CDC health advisories, but such is the world we live in today.

Fortunately, the information gap has been filled by science. In addition to an ongoing advisory remaining on the CDC website, the journal Frontiers in Environmental Health has just published a research paper showing that an increase in wildfire smoke over the past 16 years has offset the public health gains of reducing pollution from transportation and industry. The new study pinpoints low birthweight and pre-term births among the rise in negative health outcomes related to the impact of wildfire smoke on pregnant women.

“Even in regions that are not strongly associated with wildfire, such as the southeast region of the U.S., wildfire pollution rates grew substantially during that time period,” summarizes the news organization Stateline.

What’s With All The Climate-Hushing?

In a nutshell, wildfire smoke is now the single leading pollutant impacting pregnant women in the US, on top of the direct, destructive impact of wildfires on homes, businesses, and communities. Moreover, wildfire hazards are just one of many climate-related impacts to hit the domestic electorate over the head on an up-close-and-personal basis beyond the oft-cited sea level rise metric, including increasing cycles of heat waves, drought, and flooding. Regardless of how far or near they are to a seacoast, more US voters are getting to know climate change on a painfully intimate level.

Clearly, if climate change is not the primary economic issue of all time, it is among other major economic issues left unaddressed (to put it kindly) by the current Republican majority in Washington, on up to and including the impact of the Iran war on fuel prices.

Nevertheless, word on the street is that Democratic strategists are encouraging candidates to avoid talking about climate change. A research team at the University of California – Santa Barbara, for example, cites multiple advisory groups and pundits that have advised against including climate change in campaign messaging.

“Candidates have listened: an Inside Climate News analysis of press releases from congressional Democrats finds that mentions of climate change have dropped 80 percent since 2021,” the researchers note.

Why Not Talk About Climate Change?

Rather than dwell on the situation as-is, the USC researchers took it upon themselves to investigate whether or not climate-hushing is sound advice for Democratic candidates this year. They summarize the climate-hushing argument in three parts:

Claim 1 Climate is not a top issue Voters care more about costs, health care, jobs and other issues.

Claim 2 The phrase “climate change” is polarizing The same policies labeled with climate will divide people along partisan lines.

Claim 3 Emphasizing climate change loses votes This does NOT necessarily follow from Claim 2.

In support of the climate-hushing argument, the USC team found that Claim 1 is true. Climate clawed itself up only as far as the #12 spot out of 15 in an exercise designed to test voter priorities, and there it sat. Meanwhile, the top three priorities, predictably, were the cost of living, the economy, and health care.

If you spotted the missed opportunity, there it is. To the extent that climate solutions address the cost of living, the general economy, and public health, climate action should be part and parcel of economic messaging.

More to the point, the study contradicts Claim 2. “Saying the word climate does not polarize. Identical policies drew the same support when framed as climate versus energy or clean air. Voters care more about the policy mechanism than the policy’s goal,” the USC team summarized, indicating that it’s important to provide a context and solutions rather than simply bandying “climate change” about.

A similar finding applies to Claim 3. “Climate supporters are far more motivated to vote on climate than climate opponents. Emphasizing climate actually increased support for candidates rather than lowering it,” the researchers explained.

For the record, the USC researchers tested each of the three claims through two national surveys totaling approximately 3,500 adults this past summer.

Now What?

It remains to be seen where the Democrats go with climate messaging as the 2026 election cycle heats up, so to speak. If anything, climate action provides candidates with a common-ground argument and a solid track record of recent support to pull on, considering the ambitious programs set in motion by the Biden administration.

That kind of universal messaging is sorely needed at a time when divide-and-conquer forces are working against a Democratic landslide, particularly in regards to Israel’s role in the Iran war. In addition, Democrats in office are not immune to criticism over broad structural issues that predate Trump, including the cost of housing, health insurance, and education alongside more recent developments like the data center boom and the rising impact of AI-enabled systems.

Digging into the particulars of the USC study, while 50% of those surveyed ranked “cost of living” among their top three priorities, a relatively healthy 14% gave a top three ranking to “energy and electricity.” The category “clean air and water” also earned 14%, while “climate change” clocked in at 12% — a relatively small showing but still worth a mention in campaign materials. USC emphasizes that caring about an issue is not the same as voting on it, but the team’s findings on Claim 2 indicate that climate-carers are significantly more motivated to vote for candidates who center climate change.

“Climate supporters and opponents were sharply mismatched. Supporters rated the pull of climate on their vote at nearly 75 out of 100,” the USC team reported.

“Opponents rated it as under 38 out of 100, a gap of 37 points. Clean energy followed a similar pattern, with a 36 point gap. These findings suggest that supporters will reward climate candidates, while climate opponents will remain relatively indifferent,” they elaborated.

Notably, the researchers also found broad, non-partisan support for specific decarbonization technologies, with rooftop solar taking the lead at 69% favorable compared to just 20% unfavorable. The team also cites onshore wind, large solar farms, and heat pumps among those with wide favorability margins.

“These findings suggest that climate messaging can be grounded in clean technologies themselves, which are broadly popular with voters,” they emphasized.

Readers, if you are voting this year, drop a note in the discussion thread and share your priorities. Better yet, find your representatives in Congress and let them know what you think.

title: 9 States With The Most Solar Panels (And How They Use Them) - BGR

text:
Solar energy is a key pillar not only within the world of renewable energy, but also in the total energy mix of the world. Interest in photovoltaic panel technology continues to grow as individual home solar installations are able to reduce the strain on grids and save individual residents significant money. Countries like China are steaming ahead with a solar power surplus the U.S. could only dream of, but don't make the mistake of thinking America is sitting on its laurels and letting the sunshine go to waste.

That said, making the shift to solar isn't easy, whether you're an individual or a government entity. It requires expensive infrastructure and careful planning. At a state level, the amount of progress toward making solar a key part of the energy mix has gone better in some places than others. Sometimes it's just that a state's geography doesn't mesh well with solar, but more often than not it's the exact mix of public policy and private appetite for this rapidly developing technology that determines how fast the rollout can happen.

So, which states are doing the best job of making the move to solar? We looked up the data from the Solar Energy Industries Association (SEIA) to determine which states are generating the most total solar power as of June 2026, and then we found examples of how each state is using its solar energy.

It should be no surprise that sunny and progressive California sits atop this list. Not only does it have the right climate for solar panels, but California has a long history of environmentalism and its support for renewable energy has been nothing short of exemplary. The state has an RPS (Renewable Portfolio Standard) that requires 60% of power to be from renewable sources by 2030. State net metering (where you offset your grid use with solar) is layered on top of federal investment tax credits (ITC) making solar highly attractive to both businesses and household.

The actual numbers are staggering. California has 55,510 MW of installed capacity, and it can store over 60,000 MWh of power. That's enough power to run 16,271,789 homes according to SEIA. Net Energy Metering (NEM) has helped homeowners save money on their monthly bills and reduced California's reliance on "dirty" power sources such as coal.

There's also the Self-Generation Incentive Program (SGIP), which brings a bundle of incentives to encourage the installation of solar infrastructure and to support existing installations. The potential savings are substantial, with the expected savings over 25 years ranging from $40,000 to $80,000. California's new energy experiment, called "Project Nexus," started in 2025 and uses solar panels over canals to both harvest solar energy, and reduce water losses from evaporation. California is also home to the largest solar farm in America, so this victory is unsurprising.

It's rare for California and Texas to be right next to each other on a list, but while each state has its own distinct character and culture, they share an abundance of sunshine. It's even more jarring to see that Texas is second on the list of top solar states, because it's also the top oil-producing state in the U.S. You'll still see plenty of oil pumpjacks throughout the state, but as Texas increases its focus on renewable green energy, you'll also be seeing more solar farms get built.

With 53,568 MW of solar installed, Texas isn't far from the top spot, but its storage capacity of 29,163 MWh is only about half of what The Golden State has. This makes sense given that unlike California, most of Texas' solar generation goes towards utility-scale generation rather than residential. Less than 2% of the rooftop solar potential in the state has been exploited so far, but despite this Texas still ranks third in the U.S for residential solar generation. In late 2025 solar output overtook coal in Texas, so there's no doubt that this oil-rich state has a bright renewable future.

An interesting thing to watch about this trend involves the number of tech companies that are moving from California to Texas, and it seems a data center boom is following in the wake of this shift. For example, TotalEnergies is set to provide a full Gigawatt of solar power to Google Data centers in Texas.

Florida holds a respectable third place in the national solar race, but despite being The Sunshine State, it sits quite far behind California and Texas in terms of installed capacity with 21,968 MW. Likewise, the state's storage capacity is virtually non-existent, with just 1,476 MW of room for surplus energy. Similar to Texas, Florida's solar industry is driven more by utility-scale infrastructure than residential.

Florida is sunny, but it is also notorious for its violent weather events, which is why it needs houses that survive category 5 hurricanes. The same weather that would be ideal for renewable energy sources such as wind and solar, also make things difficult. Residential rooftop solar installations, for example, are an issue since a storm powerful enough to blow the roof itself off will obviously also destroy any solar panels attached to it. Even so, Floridians are clearly pushing for rooftop solar with around 4% of homes using solar as of 2025, but experts expect rapid growth in the coming years.

One of the most interesting applications of solar energy in Florida is the production of hydrogen. This abundant chemical is an excellent energy carrier, and Florida has unique hybrid solar farms that use a portion of the solar energy to split water into oxygen and hydrogen. That hydrogen can then later be used after the sun goes down, bypassing the cost and environmental issues of chemical battery storage. The end result is just the same water that you split in the first place.

Given that Arizona is mostly arid and semi-arid containing no fewer than four major deserts within its borders, it's perhaps no surprise that it's rated this high in the U.S. rankings for solar power infrastructure. As of 2025, however, the state has only 11,751 MW of installed solar capacity, but what is surprising is that its storage capacity, at 20,245 MWh, is practically double that figure.

Like Florida, Arizona is one of the sunniest states in the country, so it has incredible growth potential. Especially with all that desert terrain. That said, we've already seen how solar farms in a Chinese desert can alter the ecosystem. By intercepting solar energy, the soil retains more moisture and becomes more fertile. This sounds like a good thing, but any ecological change can have unforeseen consequences, which means Arizona will have to think carefully on how best to use that sunny desert land. Arizona wants to be carbon neutral by 2050, though, so the pressure to find solutions is definitely on.

Arizona is already innovating with solar and nature by placing solar panels over crops. This practice is known as agrivoltaics, which generates clean energy while shielding crops and farmers from harsh sunlight. Doing so allows farmers to use the same piece of land for two purposes simultaneously.

While North Carolina has 10,093 MW of installed solar capacity, its storage capacity of under 1,000 MWh means that not much of that solar power can be stored. Not to be deterred, NC is one of the national leaders in utility-scale solar development, and as solar grows in this state, expect to see North Carolina's rankings rise when it comes to both its solar capacity and storage capacity.

North Carolina is known for having diverse landscapes within its border, and this is also a state that has a massive agricultural industry. While solar and agriculture have been growing together, utility-scale solar projects have taken up surprisingly little agricultural land. Where there has been overlap, NC has engaged in agrivoltaics similar to what we saw in Arizona. The state that gave us Pepsi, Krispy Kreme, and unique barbecue might one day mainly be known for its clean energy.

Given the diverse landscape, it makes sense that solar projects are equally eclectic. The U.S. Army stationed at Fort Bragg boasts the largest floating solar array in the Southeast. Producing 1.1 MW of energy with a 2MWh storage system. In 2024 the EPA granted $156M to an organization called EnergizeNC. A coalition aimed at giving solar power access to as many residents as possible by expanding rooftop solar, multifamily solar, and community solar for low-income communities in particular. NC's legislation is particularly community solar friendly, which means projects like this will steadily increase both solar capacity and equitable solar access.

At 8,290 MW of installed solar capacity, Illinois manages sixth position nationally. A much more pressing issue is the lack of storage capacity in light of all that generation capacity. The state relies on coal and nuclear power for baseload, which needs to change in the long term. Right now, Illinois can only store 93MWh of renewable energy. However, if new laws that have been signed by the governor take effect, then Illinois plans to install 3GW of battery storage by 2030. Given that this capacity is effectively nothing at the moment, this would be a tremendous achievement.

Clean energy is growing at a tremendous pace, and the state is focused on expanding solar deployment wherever it can. The Illinois Solar For All program is worth mentioning here, since it aims to help "income-eligible" homeowners and even people who rent access cheaper solar power. According to the program, the average annual savings on power for families that have been assisted by the program is over $1,000.

Another highly-notable project is Illinois Shines, a state-administered project that can award incentives to a wide variety of solar projects. This means that, like North Carolina, the spread of solar generation projects are diverse. The incentives given to solar vendors through this program can be passed on as savings to end users, which means it has the potential to bring more users into the solar fold. Illinois Shines is also actively helping public schools switch to solar, which has economic and educational benefits.

Nevada hits the seventh spot with 8,244 MW of installed solar capacity and 6,331 MWh of storage capacity. This is another state with open desert regions and a sunny, dry climate, making it ideal for solar power development in the future. While it might only be in seventh place for capacity, Nevada gets 33.5% of its power from solar — putting it behind only California for this statistic. This means that a third of those bright lights Las Vegas is famous for get their power from solar.

Nevada's Renewable Portfolio Standard was established all the way back in 1997 and currently stipulates that the state must get 50% of its power from renewable sources by 2030. Given that more than a third of its power already comes from solar and there's plenty of room to grow, this is a target that it might actually, realistically hit. With a current storage capacity that is so low, Nevada might be the best place to be over the next few years if you're a battery salesman.

In a wonderful nominative coincidence, Nevada's Freedom Park received a 1,500-panel 480KW solar parking bay system in 2024. This is a great example of solar technology pulling double-duty. shading parked cars from the harsh Nevada sun, while also turning energy that would have been wasted cooking a car into energy that can, instead, cook your dinner.

The Empire State is ranked eighth for solar capacity with 8,226 MW installed, but it also has a low relative storage capacity at 1,096 MWh. Solar only makes up a modest 7.7% of the New York's total energy mix, but it is growing. The NY-Sun program is aiming to grow that number by offering both on-site and community solar access and making citizens aware of the various incentives and tax breaks afforded to those who go solar in NY.

As for New York City, the drive for rooftop solar is substantial. NY-Sun is providing $200M of funding to add a gigawatt of power generation to the state as a whole from rooftop and community solar, but the mayor's office has committed to adding 1,000MW within the city by 2030. One project that neatly encapsulates the unique New York flavor of solar power is Sunset Park. Claimed to be the first New York City community solar project that's actually owned by a cooperative and not a nonprofit or government entity. Sunset Park allows people who own or rent homes (as well as small businesses) to access solar power without actually installing any solar equipment. Subscriber-members vote how the project invests its resources, so it's truly equitable.

Virgina ranks ninth on this list with 7,841 MW of capacity, but it only has 162 MWh of storage. This state's solar journey is shaped by the Virginia Clean Economy Act (VCEA), and its growth of solar capacity has been consistent. Nearly 10% of all power in the state comes from solar and its capacity is expected to more than double over the next five years.

This sounds like a tall order, but Virginia's track record here is impressive. The state had zero solar capacity in 2015, but by 2021, it was topping 3,500 MW. That represents massive coordination and investment at every level. The Virginia Clean Economy Act of 2020 played an important role here, and this act set a 16,100 MW capacity target with solar and wind combined. Virginia is about halfway there, but given how quickly these numbers have been growing, the timeline might be much shorter than the experts predict.

The Spotsylvania Solar project, is a remarkable example of how solar energy generation can be used not only to directly provide clean energy, but also to fund environmental protection. Combining four solar projects, Spotsylvania covers 6,350 acres of land. However, 2,000 acres of that are being preserved as undeveloped land for conservation purposes. That's in stark contrast to the land destruction involved when building coal or nuclear facilities, and it's one way Virginia is showing the way for green energy potential.

In order to get accurate rankings of current solar capacity of states, we used the most current rankings from the Solar Energy Industries Association (SEIA). This is a national trade association for both the solar power generation industry and the renewable energy storage industry. It's a good place to find both official state data outlined in a clear way, and to see the various regional solar energy policies, and what policy changes SEIA is pushing for in each state.

Once we'd established the official rankings for each state from SEIA, we investigated federal and state sources of official information to see where that total solar capacity comes from and how it breaks down. Each of these states have been the most successful at building, growing, and managing their solar power industries, but they all have unique challenges, too.

Finally, we searched for notable or interesting solar projects on a state-by-state basis, that illustrate the renewable energy philosophy and creative problem solving of both government and private projects. With most states aiming for a 2050 carbon-free date, we expect all of these numbers to rise dramatically over the coming years, and solar energy to play a bigger and much more visible role in the daily lives of citizens all over the United States.

title: Healey wants 'swift action' on energy bill, but negotiators just getting started | WWLP
description:

text:
BOSTON (SHNS) – Gov. Maura Healey talked to legislative energy affordability bill negotiators Thursday and sent them a letter on Friday urging “swift action” to resolve differences in House and Senate bills that are very different.

Healey, who has spoken for more than a year about her energy agenda after filing a bill in May 2025, railed on utility companies during a State House press conference, two days after conferees tasked with hashing out the legislation met for the first time.

The governor’s office announced at 10:16 a.m. Friday that Healey would hold a press conference that afternoon, where her office distributed a letter she sent to the energy chairs and she talked about her energy affordability priorities.

“When it comes to utility companies, we’ve got to end business as usual. Utility companies are seeking rate hikes and excessive profits, while people and businesses are struggling to pay their bills,” Healey said, outlining the contents of her four-page letter to Rep. Mark Cusack and Sen. Mike Barrett.

Healey said she supports provisions to modernize procurement policies, accelerate new energy resource development and lower the cost of electricity. She said Friday that among a slate of other policies, she wants to change how utilities buy their energy, a “full audit” of utilities companies, and to end “sweetheart deals” that enable a profit bonus for being part of New England’s grid.

“We’ve talked to them a lot over the last, well, several months,” Healey told reporters when asked whether she had talked to Cusack and Barrett about the letter. “I talked to all of them as recently as yesterday. We’re going to keep talking because I think we all recognize how important it is that we get this done and that we take the actions that we can take to lower people’s energy bills.”

But Healey, who has taken heat from political opponents who say her energy policies are contributing to rising costs, isn’t the only one pitching lawmakers.

While Eversource supports an affordability focus and an all-of-the-above energy approach to address supply constraint issues, “At the same time, we must recognize that the lack of baseload supply causes the region to burn millions of gallons of oil during times of peak demand, adding billions in costs for customers across New England and significantly increasing carbon emissions to the environment,” Eversource spokesperson William Hinkle said.

“It is also important to note that increased investments in utility infrastructure will be necessary to support the commonwealth’s goals – such as bringing more solar online and strengthening demand response programs,” Hinkle continued.

The Mass Coalition for Sustainable Energy on Thursday wrote a letter to Cusack, Barrett, and other members of the committee urging them “to prioritize energy affordability” and “to refrain from adding new costs to already record-high energy bills.” The coalition’s letter opposed efforts to “create or expand incremental programs that will add costs,” sunset GSEP, “terminate the requirement that utilities must serve natural gas to customers that choose it,” and “‘securitize’ clean energy costs.”

“Should the product of this conference report fail to lower ratepayer bills or put the reliability and safety of our energy infrastructure at risk, we would urge conferees to table any energy legislation until next session,” the coalition, which includes some labor unions and business groups, wrote.

On the same afternoon that the governor was railing against utility companies, including a specific reference to Berkshire Gas, her Department of Public Utilities approved a settlement that would allow Berkshire Gas to increase its gas base distribution rates to generate approximately $18.5 million in additional revenues, down from the $28 million the company requested. The new rates are effective Saturday.

“The Department has considered the estimated bill impacts associated with the settled rate increase. The Department is mindful of the burdens associated with higher bills and recognizes that the magnitude of the proposed rate increase, even as reduced in the Settlement Agreement, is significant,” the DPU order said. “We also acknowledge that the Department must ensure that the rates we approve today are sufficient to ensure the financial viability of the Company, without which it cannot serve its customers. In doing so, the Department must balance the concerns of customers, the utilities who serve them, public officials, and other regulatory bodies, summed up in our goal of providing safe and reliable service at the lowest possible cost.”

National Grid Director of Strategic Communications for Corporate Affairs New England, Brendan Moss, said Friday that “Any final legislation should focus on measures that provide real, measurable affordability benefits for customers while preserving the investments necessary to maintain a safe and reliable energy system that drives our economy and maintaining customer choice. Approaches that simply shift costs to future customers, defer essential infrastructure work, remove customer choice, or repackage costs without reducing them will not deliver meaningful affordability.”

Massachusetts households pay some of the highest energy costs in the country, and lawmakers have pointed to billions of long-term savings that would come as the result of their energy proposals. The House passed its energy bill (H 5151) in February, proposing to cut the Mass Save program by $1 billion, and the Senate passed its own (S 3166) on July 1, proposing instead to phase out the Gas System Enhancement Program.

Asked Friday which version of the bill she’d sign, Healey said, “Let’s see what I get, and let’s see how this process goes,” noting that she’s “concerned about utility profits when it comes to the GSEP program.” Healey also said that she thinks Mass Save is “something that should be reformed” and that she has called to “cap spending” on the program, but that “it’s a program that’s been around for a while. It’s played an important role.”

Cusack said on Wednesday that “there are a lot of agreements … and significant disagreements, as we know. And I look forward to working through those with some urgency to try to get relief to our constituents, the households, and businesses before this winter.”

Barrett added, “We should do this, ideally, before a November election, so that those of us who have races can point to an achievement.”

Asked what she makes of lawmakers pushing lawmaking past July 31 and into campaign season under new joint rules, Healey said, “I don’t think about it in terms of a campaign schedule.”

As to whether she has any indication of whether lawmakers are close to an agreement on energy, Healey said, “Well, they’re meeting. The good news is the conference committee met the other day. That was for the first time, and they’ve got, you know, a lot of work ahead.”

Healey was also asked about the potentially tumultuous nature of the relationship between energy chairs, and her strategy for getting them together and getting a bill to her desk before November. Healey replied: “I don’t accept any characterizations about members of the Legislature.” She did not stop to answer a question about whether she had spoken to House Speaker Ron Mariano or Senate President Karen Spilka on Friday, or if she planned to visit them.
