text:
A nuclear cooperation pact between Washington and Riyadh could reshape how Middle Eastern nations approach low carbon energy infrastructure over the next three decades.

The agreement, finalised on 22 July by US Secretary of Energy Chris Wright and Saudi Minister of Energy Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman al-Saud, combines a peaceful nuclear cooperation framework with a bilateral safeguards arrangement.

It represents the culmination of two decades of negotiation.

Chris describes the arrangement as one that upholds the "highest standards of nuclear safety and non-proliferation".

Enrichment raises proliferation questions

The deal is expected to span approximately 30 years and could be worth tens of billions of US dollars to American firms.

Westinghouse Electric Company has been identified as a probable partner, with its CEO Dan Sumner saying the agreement is a step that "strengthens energy security" and expands opportunities for US industry.

The agreement's uranium enrichment provisions have drawn attention from energy analysts and non-proliferation specialists.

Enrichment increases the concentration of fissile material in uranium to levels required for reactor fuel or, at far higher purities, weapons.

Civilian power plants typically require uranium enriched to around 3.67%.

Weapons-grade material requires enrichment above 90%.

Reports suggest the deal could eventually permit Saudi Arabia to enrich uranium domestically at a US-built facility, pending a two-year joint study, rather than importing finished fuel as most nuclear energy nations do.

This would be a departure from established practice.

Rosemary Kelanic, Director of the Middle East programme at the Defense Priorities think tank, calls the prospect "quite shocking", noting that Washington has never previously helped a partner nation enrich uranium on its own soil.

UAE precedent sets different standard

Industry observers have compared this arrangement to the 2009 US-UAE nuclear deal.

Washington has previously labelled that agreement the "gold standard" for such pacts because Abu Dhabi agreed never to enrich or reprocess nuclear fuel.

The UAE also accepted the International Atomic Energy Agency's Additional Protocol, a stricter inspection regime used to verify peaceful use.

According to reports, the Saudi agreement could fall short of that standard.

Riyadh is not expected to accept the same level of IAEA oversight.

This difference could affect how other nations seeking nuclear power infrastructure approach fuel cycle arrangements.

For countries evaluating nuclear energy as part of decarbonisation strategies, the precedent set by enrichment permissions could influence future agreements.

The choice between importing finished fuel and developing domestic enrichment capacity has implications for supply chain resilience and programme costs.

Congressional approval faces limited opposition

The agreement now requires Congressional review, where opposition has been vocal but is unlikely to prevent implementation, according to The Guardian.

Democratic congressman John Garamendi calls it a "consequential mistake", while Senator Chris Murphy warns it could "set off a nuclear race in the region".

Republican reaction has been more muted, with representative Marlin Stutzman saying he has no "initial" concerns. Blocking the deal would require a joint resolution passed by a two-thirds majority in both chambers.

Critics are widely expected to fall short of that threshold.

The approval process could conclude within weeks.

Regional tensions complicate timing

Secretary of State Marco Rubio has dismissed proliferation concerns.

LUBBOCK, Texas, July 31, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- American Fusion Inc. (OTC: AMFN) ("American Fusion" or the "Company"), developer of the proprietary Texatron™ Fusion Engine™, announced the successful completion of the initial phase of its Texatron™ engineering and testing program at the Center for Emerging Energy Sciences within the Department of Physics & Astronomy at Texas Tech University in Lubbock, Texas.

During the week, a seven-member American Fusion scientific and engineering team worked alongside Texas Tech personnel to complete a series of engineering evaluations, subsystem demonstrations, instrumentation testing, and laboratory activities supporting the Company's ongoing Texatron™ development program. The initial phase of testing achieved several important engineering objectives and generated valuable operational and diagnostic information that will help guide subsequent phases of the Company's planned testing activities.

No measurable radiation was detected during the testing performed in this initial phase. The Company emphasized that radiation monitoring will remain an integral part of each phase of the Texatron™ testing program as development continues.

Information obtained during testing, including observations relating to system performance under high-voltage operating conditions, is expected to support additional engineering refinements and future phases of the Texatron™ testing program.

title: Christian: The 765-kV Debate Is the Price of Losing Our Way - Texas Scorecard
description:
Infrastructure growth requires more energy.
More localized natural gas generation.
Texas needs more infrastructure to strengthen grid reliability, but the 765-kV transmission line proposal is not the cure.
In response, all we’ve done is further the proliferation of intermittent power generation across our great state.
The tax credits and subsidies they imposed deliberately tilted the playing field against Texas natural gas and coal, undermining their competitiveness.
text:
Now more than ever, Texas must confront the challenge before us. Our state is growing at a historic pace, and it remains the beating heart of America’s economic, energy, and technological future.

That growth requires infrastructure.

Infrastructure growth requires more energy. More pipelines. More localized natural gas generation. More dispatchable power. More infrastructure that strengthens the reliability of our grid.

But only if that infrastructure is built the Texas way.

After nearly sixteen hours of testimony before the Texas Senate Committee on Business and Commerce this past week, where lawmakers heard from landowners, industry leaders, regulators, and Texans who will live with the consequences of these decisions, I was left with one unmistakable conclusion.

Texas needs more infrastructure to strengthen grid reliability, but the 765-kV transmission line proposal is not the cure. It is the consequence. It is the bill coming due after years of energy policies that prioritized bending the knee to climate catastrophism and “all-of-the-above” energy sycophancy while ignoring the clear and obvious shortcomings of that approach.

After Winter Storm Uri, the consequences of overreliance on intermittent energy production should be clear to every Texan. I said it then, and it bears repeating today. We invested so much in renewable energy that we let the pilot light go out on reliable power. In response, all we’ve done is further the proliferation of intermittent power generation across our great state.

Texas needs to ask itself why the Permian Basin, one of the richest natural gas regions on Earth, now requires billions of dollars in new transmission infrastructure simply to sustain its growth and maintain reliable power. The answer is clear. Years of federal subsidies, regulatory pressure, and political mandates have distorted our electricity market.

Under the banner of an “energy transition,” Washington pushed policies designed to accelerate renewable generation, not because wind and solar alone can provide the reliability required to power a growing industrial and technological economy, but because the climate cult convinced policymakers there was no other solution. The tax credits and subsidies they imposed deliberately tilted the playing field against Texas natural gas and coal, undermining their competitiveness.

But let’s now discuss the greatest sin.

Instead of the beating heart of North America’s fossil fuel industry refuting the false notion that carbon dioxide emissions were to be embraced, not feared, Texas instead welcomed climate alarmism in the name of reaping the benefits of federal subsidy. Texas actively chose, through both state policy and advocacy, to proliferate the expansion of our federal debt in the name of greed at the expense of grid reliability.

That sin has distorted our energy market and brought us here.

It should not be possible that one of the most fossil fuel-rich regions on the planet is facing a growing need to import, rather than export, electricity because the proliferation of tax credit-backed renewable power has made local, dispatchable fossil fuel generation less economically viable.

What makes my skin crawl most is that these transmission lines are doubling down on that problem.

Rather than correcting market distortions and ensuring that the region producing our nation’s energy can power itself, Texas is considering a multi-billion-dollar transmission project to accommodate the shortcomings of intermittent, unreliable energy investments, and the harm they’ve done to our natural gas and coal industries.

Enough is enough.

Ratepayers should not be asked to further subsidize this problematic plan, born from our grid’s growing reliance on renewable energy, to build the infrastructure required to compensate for its limitations.

For months, I have been one of the strongest advocates in Texas for defending data centers because I believe our state’s pro-growth, pro-business principles require us to solve the challenges growth creates—not simply hit pause on economic opportunity. That is what Texas has always done. We don’t fear growth. We build the infrastructure necessary to support it, and we should build it the Texas way—or not at all.

I have consistently argued that new demand should be met by encouraging more localized, dispatchable natural gas generation, not by socializing costs or asking Texans to subsidize workarounds for a broken market.

That is why I oppose these transmission lines.

These transmission lines aren’t a free-market solution. They’re a government correction for a government-created distortion. Instead of restoring competitive conditions so reliable generation can once again be built where it’s needed, we’re proposing another multi-billion-dollar intervention to prop up the consequences of the last one.

Texas doesn’t need another expensive workaround. It needs the courage to fix the policies that created the problem in the first place.

text:
Rivian spinoff Also will finally start delivering its first e-bikes to customers next week, after months of delays related to unspecified supply chain issues.

The company told TechCrunch on Friday that the Launch Edition of its TM-B e-bike, which retails for $4,500, has started shipping from its manufacturer to its warehouse in the U.S. Also said it expects to deliver all Launch Edition bikes between next week and September.

Also began as a skunkworks project inside Rivian in 2022, after CEO RJ Scaringe started looking into making an e-bike to complement his portfolio of electric vehicles for the outdoorsy set. The company spent a few years tinkering with the idea, and even hired Jony Ive’s design firm LoveFrom to help with an early design, as TechCrunch first reported in 2025.

In March 2025, Rivian spun out Also as its own company, with $105 million in backing from Eclipse. The startup revealed its first e-bike, the TM-B, in October of last year. It originally targeted a “spring” 2026 ship date, but supply chain headaches got in the way, and the company pushed the delivery window to July.

“The primary factor driving our updated summer timeline is current stress on global supply chains. A rapid, industry-wide spike in demand for raw materials and electronic components has impacted key parts required for the TM-B. This has temporarily delayed our planned manufacturing ramp-up and pushed our first delivery dates past our original spring window,” the company wrote in June on a support page. “Our engineering and production teams are working around the clock to minimize these constraints without cutting a single corner on safety or quality.”

Also declined to say what components, specifically, caused the delay.

Also has big plans beyond the TM-B. The startup mostly refers to itself as a “vehicle” company and has plans to make four-wheel pedal-assist cargo vehicles for Amazon. The company is working on an autonomous delivery vehicle for DoorDash, too.

But for now, Also needs to focus on delivering its first e-bikes while navigating the next set of headaches for a company shipping products like these: customer service. On Friday, the last day of July, a number of customers were venting in a thread in the r/ALSOmicromobility subreddit about the repeated delays.

“I’m really frustrated by the lack of communication and the actual miscommunication/lies from Also regarding shipment timelines,” the original poster wrote. “Why do they keep making these promises about shipping timelines just to blow right past them without any communication or actual updates? It really makes no sense.”

“Hey we’ve still got a few business hours left in July. Maybe we’ll get an email later this morning ☺️,” a different user responded.

Not everyone was so patient.

“Couldn’t wait any longer and canceled my reservation,” another wrote.

title: Nevada braces for Colorado River showdown with feds as it faces steepest cuts in history
description:
Allocating water shortages from the Colorado River has been largely left to state officials.
Other states, such as Arizona and Utah, have publicly appropriated millions to defend their allocations from the Colorado River.
“Litigation is not going to get us anywhere on this river,” said Amy Haas, executive director of the Colorado River Authority of Utah.
“This is a reflection of river diplomacy and river politicking as much as it is river policy.” Contact Alan Halaly at ahalaly@reviewjournal.com.
Follow @AlanHalaly on X. CONSUMPTIVE USE Between 2020-24, the average consumptive use in the Colorado River Basin was 13.1 million acre-feet.
text:
Nevada is likely to give up a sixth of its Colorado River allocation next year as the federal government prepares to impose its strictest limits ever on the state’s water use, according to a document released Friday.

That could be followed by even more draconian cuts: The federal government is claiming the legal authority to force the Silver State to reduce its share of the river after 2028 by between one-third and two-thirds of its current allotment — prompting swift objections from state officials.

“We’re seeing the first iteration of a plan that contemplates all of the reductions on the Colorado River being taken by a minority of the states that share the river,” said John Entsminger, general manager of the Southern Nevada Water Authority and the state’s governor-appointed Colorado River czar, in a Friday interview. “That’s not going to work for us.”

The federal government says the 1.5 million acre-foot yearly reduction proposed by the Lower Basin states of Nevada, California and Arizona won’t be enough. Now, the states may be on the hook for up to 3.6 million acre-feet of annual cuts past 2028, according to what’s been identified as the feds’ preferred path forward.

Nevada Gov. Joe Lombardo said in a statement that preferred federal route would “impose unrealistic reductions” on the state, which has led the way in stretching its tiny share of the river via water recycling and conservation.

A final environmental impact statement on the plan released Friday leaves some uncertainty about specific volumes of reductions until a record of decision is released that will certify an official plan.

“If carried forward, the plan outlined in the FEIS could have devastating economic and environmental impacts on Nevada,” Lombardo said. “Nevada has put forward reasonable compromise proposals to the other states, and I will fight against any outcome that imposes unreasonable impacts to our communities.”

Whatever plan is imposed on the states will be revisited every two years through 2036, rather than every 20 years.

Notably, the Upper Basin states of Colorado, Utah, New Mexico and Wyoming will not be forced to adopt mandatory cuts to water use, instead cutting back by a mere 200,000 acre-feet on a voluntary basis, as conditions allow.

Litigation threats shade negotiations

Friday’s document leaves an open end to years of back-and-forth between two coalitions of states that failed to agree on how to update 20-year operating guidelines for the river that expire at the close of this year.

Interior Secretary Doug Burgum praised the proposed operating rules in a statement.

“This framework provides the flexibility to respond to changing hydrologic conditions while preserving the opportunity for the Basin States to continue working toward durable, consensus-based solutions,” Burgum said.

Allocating water shortages from the Colorado River has been largely left to state officials. Federal intervention now may lead to a yearslong fight at the U.S. Supreme Court, according to state officials and experts.

For years, Nevada officials have declined to say whether the state was preparing for a lawsuit, and Entsminger on Friday would not say how much money may be set aside for a legal challenge. Other states, such as Arizona and Utah, have publicly appropriated millions to defend their allocations from the Colorado River.

“The specter of litigation has been hanging over this basin for five or six years, easily, and that certainly didn’t go away today,” Entsminger said. “While we can express our concerns with what’s been articulated thus far in the FEIS, we do need to see that record of decision before we start getting too far down the road of what our next steps are.”

In the barrage of statements that followed the release of the document Friday morning, the only other state to take issue with the reductions was Arizona, which will generally see its water rights cut before California.

The Arizona Department of Water Resources issued a statement calling proposed reductions “unacceptable” and added they “would devastate Arizona’s water users and its economy.”

DeEtte Person, a spokesperson for the Central Arizona Project that delivers Colorado River water to Arizona’s biggest cities, had a similar message.

“We believe the FEIS contains several fundamental legal flaws, fails to encourage consensus among the seven Basin states and inaccurately portrays Arizona’s rights to Colorado River water,” Person wrote in a statement.

In a virtual news conference Friday, Utah water managers didn’t rule out the possibility of a lawsuit but reiterated it wasn’t their preferred method of dealing with the inter-basin disagreements.

“Litigation is not going to get us anywhere on this river,” said Amy Haas, executive director of the Colorado River Authority of Utah. “It’s not going to get us more water. It’s not going to buy us more time.”

The Nevada picture

Southern Nevada’s collective water use, according to the water authority, came in at 198,000 acre-feet in 2025. That puts the state in a rare position in using significantly less water than its total 300,000 acre-foot allocation.

In the short term, University of Nevada, Reno professor Elizabeth Koebele said in an interview that the state is in a good position to meet the demands of the federal government. Beyond what the Lower Basin has agreed to — the 1.5 million acre-feet in reductions that the federal government is floating — it gets more tricky, she said.

“If reservoir levels drop even further, then will we need to take bigger cuts?” Koebele said. “We’re also dealing with new demands on water resources in the state and continued pressure for growth. And while we’ve sort of decoupled water use from population growth to a limit, that’s not forever.”

According to Koebele, she believes the more modest cuts that the Lower Basin has agreed to aren’t enough to stabilize the Colorado River system over the long term as water levels in Lake Mead and Lake Powell continue to fall.

“It’s something that will probably help us get through the two years of crisis, but we don’t expect the crisis to end after two years,” she said.

Kevin Moran, associate vice president of regional affairs for the Environmental Defense Fund, said his larger hope after reading the federal government’s plan is that it might get the Colorado River Basin out of crisis mode.

That’s easier said than done, he said.

“The economic, social, and political realities of water scarcity are difficult, and there’s no avoiding the fact that the Colorado River is tanking,” Moran said. “That creates a whole set of challenges that, up to now, the seven-state process hasn’t been able to address comprehensively.”

Kyle Roerink, a senior adviser to the nonprofit advocacy group Great Basin Water Network based in Nevada, said the document is another wake-up call for Congress to use the power of the purse to provide funding for drought mitigation.

He said the federal government’s willingness to revisit the guidelines every two years is a reflection of its attempt to preserve states’ rights and avoid litigation.

“How do you get accountability from all stakeholders without tipping the cart to a point where somebody would take action that could upend a potential deal?” Roerink said. “This is a reflection of river diplomacy and river politicking as much as it is river policy.”

title: Maine lobster boat builder nets first clean engine waiver - The Portland Press Herald

text:
A Maine boatyard is building the nation’s first lobster boat exempt from modern clean-air rules thanks to a waiver program designed to offer financial relief to the state lobster fleet, but that opens the door to more diesel pollution in fast-warming New England waters.

The exempted vessel taking shape in the yard at Wesmac Custom Boats in Surry is heading south to a Massachusetts buyer, but it sets a powerful example for Maine, home to the country’s largest lobster fleet.

The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency rolled out Tier 4 diesel engine restrictions in phases, starting in 2008. Under these rules, heavy trucks, trains and ships must install advanced exhaust systems that remove smog-forming gases and fine black soot before they leave the tailpipe.

For ferries or shipping vessels, finding room for the scrubber gear is easy. But lobster boats have shallow, flat bottoms and cramped engine rooms. Limited space under the deck is used to house seawater tanks that keep high-value lobsters alive on long trips.

The Wesmac Super 46 — an extra-wide, Downeast-style vessel measuring 46 feet, 9 inches long with a 17-foot, 1-inch beam — didn’t have room under its deck for a Tier 4 exhaust system unless the live lobster tanks were removed, said Wesmac President Steve Wessel.

“The Tier 4 will simply not fit in the boat,” Wessel said.

The bulky cleanup gear required by the modern diesel engine rules generates intense heat. Boat builders say trapping that heat inside a small engine room would warm the live tanks, killing the catch before the boat ever made it back to the dock.

Only lobster boats powered by engines with more than 800 horsepower must have the scrubber systems. As climate change pushes lobsters farther offshore into cooler, deeper waters, however, fishermen need higher-horsepower engines to make the longer trips safely.

Despite multiple extensions by the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, boatyards said they could not build new offshore boats that complied with the clean engine standards. In 2024, the EPA decided to offer waivers to those who could prove a T-4 engine would not work for them.

Many lobstermen have considered applying for a waiver but were discouraged with how much time and paperwork was involved in the process, Wessel said. But he said the EPA has been easy to work with and has been offering assistance at every turn.

Supporters say the waiver program protects maritime jobs. Without it, custom boatyards would lose business, and lobster fishermen would have no choice but to keep running the older, dirtier vessels rather than buying new ones, according to Mark Sanborn, the EPA’s regional administrator.

“Balancing it all out, this meets the administration’s goal of protecting the environment and human health while also being reasonable and realistic in terms of supporting industry,” said Sanborn, the former deputy commissioner of New Hampshire’s state environmental agency.

Sanborn is promoting the waiver program as a “blueprint” for other Maine boatbuilders and lobstermen who have been vocal advocates for this flexibility. The agency has launched a new website to guide applicants through the case-by-case review process.

When the waiver program was first rolled out, the EPA estimated that no more than 92 pilot, lobster or law enforcement vessels would be eligible for the exemption over the course of the program’s lifespan through 2035.

Environmental advocates, however, view the decision with alarm. The older model engines that can be allowed by the waiver release up to 80% more nitrogen oxides and almost double the amount of soot compared to new cleaner models.

Nitrogen oxides are the primary ingredient in ground-level smog, which triggers asthma and air quality warnings along the coast. Exhaust fumes settle into the ocean, adding excess nitrogen to coastal waters that can fuel toxic algae blooms and speed up ocean acidification.

Ocean acidification can make it harder for shell-building creatures like young lobsters to survive.

By using Tier 3 engines instead of Tier 4 models, the EPA calculated at the outset of the waiver program that exempted boats will miss out on cutting about 3,764 tons of nitrogen oxide and 79 tons of soot over the lifespan of the engines.

Even if all the exempted boats were based in Maine, however, they’d represent just 0.4% of the state’s smog-forming emissions and 0.1% of its soot, according to the EPA. The emissions would be released 40 miles out at sea, where the winds often blow away from the populated coastal areas.

But it wouldn’t help the fast-warming Gulf of Maine, environmental groups say. Although the warming rate has slowed, climate change is still heating up the gulf faster than most ocean bodies.

Critics say giving high-powered boats a pass on air pollution undermines Maine’s climate goals.

Clean-air groups argue that granting one waiver makes it easy for other fishermen to claim they need relief, too. If waivers become routine, engine manufacturers will have little reason to spend money designing smaller, cooler models with scrubber systems that actually fit on lobster boats.

Lobstermen are the backbone of Maine coastal communities, and it makes sense that they want stronger engines to chase lobster into cold offshore waters, said Meredith Moore, senior director of Ocean Conservancy‘s fish conservation program.

“This is a missed opportunity to provide cleaner engine alternatives, rather than lock in a new generation of boats using old, dirty engines,” Moore said. “Maine coastal businesses are already leaders in electrifying boat engines, and we should lean into that innovation.”

Moore said the T-4 waivers prove how little is being done to address the impacts on our fisheries. Until the U.S. starts managing fisheries with climate change in mind, fishermen will be pushed to the brink to keep supporting their families, she said.

The EPA insists the program will remain limited, reviewing requests one boat at a time.

Wessel said Friday he’s heard the EPA is going to roll back the T-4 rules for everyone, from heavy trucks to fishing boats. The EPA didn’t respond to questions about the future of the T-4 rule.

For now, the hull under construction in Surry — which won’t be finished until next year — represents a relief valve for a multimillion-dollar fishing industry trying to adapt to changing waters and a rollback of clean air standards put in place to protect the sea where they fish.

text:
California is introducing an instant rebate for residents getting their first electric vehicle as gas prices climb and federal EV tax credits are no longer available.

State officials are betting that lower upfront costs could make EVs more attractive to drivers frustrated by expensive trips to the pump.

What happened?

Beginning next month, the MyFirstEV program will provide eligible Californians with $3,500 off a new EV or $1,750 off a used one, the Los Angeles Times reported. The offer is for people buying or leasing their first EV.

California launched the effort after the Trump administration ended the $7,500 federal credit for new EVs in September. State officials say that change caused a short-lived slowdown, but higher gasoline prices have since helped revive demand.

Between April and June, Californians bought 86,857 new zero-emission vehicles, according to the California Energy Commission, including 75,597 EVs. Those vehicles made up 19.1% of the state's new-car market, 3.3 percentage points higher than in the first quarter.

Gil Tal, director of the Electric Vehicle Research Center with UC Davis, said rising fuel prices can quickly change buying behavior: "At $5.77 a gallon, the operating-cost math swings decisively to the EV, about $125 a month for a typical driver, and buyers acted on that price signal within weeks."

Why does it matter?

For many households, the biggest obstacle to switching from gas to electric is the upfront price. EVs often cost more upfront than comparable gas-powered cars, even if they save drivers money over time on fuel and maintenance.

The rebate could be especially important for moderate-income buyers who were interested in going electric but struggled with the initial cost. The discount is applied at the time of purchase rather than arriving later as a tax credit.

Tal warned that supply is a major issue.

He said, "We have no supply because we have no regulation that forces supply."

He added that automakers have started "backpedaling" after federal policy changes weakened pressure to keep expanding EV lineups.

Jeremy Michalek, who leads Carnegie Mellon University's Vehicle Electrification Group, said the recent sales growth does not necessarily mean attitudes changed overnight: "It's not that people started liking electric vehicles more. ... It's because electric vehicles kept getting better and cheaper."

What's being done?

Gov. Gavin Newsom signed Senate Bill 168 this month, setting aside $135 million for MyFirstEV. Thirteen automakers — Tesla, Toyota, Ford, General Motors, Honda, Hyundai, Kia, Lucid, Mitsubishi, Nissan, Rivian, Subaru, and Volvo — are expected to match that funding.

To get the rebate, Californians must be acquiring their first EV and verify that through an attestation. New models qualify only if their MSRP is $50,000 or less, while used ones must cost no more than $25,000 and be sold through a manufacturer's pre-owned program.

One exception removes those price caps for vehicles from California-based automakers, including Lucid and Rivian.

Michalek said the program could help in two ways: It may encourage more new EV production while also making used EVs attainable for buyers who were previously priced out. He added that backing used EVs also speaks to equity concerns so the benefits do not go only to higher-income households.

"While Donald Trump makes Americans pay the bill for his Iran war at the pump, California is giving families the freedom to choose a cheaper way forward by going electric," Newsom said.

For Tal, the financial argument is straightforward: "At $5.77 a gallon, the operating-cost math swings decisively to the EV."

title: Two million solar panels and 34,000 tons of American steel are going up on a ... - Autonocion.com
description:
Around 2 million First Solar panels, more than 34,000 tons of domestically made steel, over 20 miles of new 345-kilovolt transmission.
Panamint calls it the largest solar project ever built at an existing coal mining site in North America.
Big Rooter West Solar, queue ID 26INR0431, is listed at 403.2 MW.
Coal-mine solar is a small club, and two of its members answer to carmakers For scale, the biggest operating project in this category is the 186-megawatt Tilden Solar Project in southern Illinois, followed by the 111-megawatt Martin County Solar Project in eastern Kentucky.
It is a different claim from the one most of the headlines made, which is that a Texas coal mine is turning into a solar farm.
text:
The usual version of this story only runs one way. A coal plant gets a retirement date, the mine beside it stops digging, and a solar farm goes up on the ground the shovels already tore open. Minnesota just did exactly that. Illinois and Kentucky did it last year.

Robertson County, Texas is doing something else. On July 23, Panamint Capital broke ground on Big Rooter Power, a $1.7 billion solar project at its Twin Oaks power station near Bremond, roughly halfway between Dallas and Houston. Around 2 million First Solar panels, more than 34,000 tons of domestically made steel, over 20 miles of new 345-kilovolt transmission.

Panamint calls it the largest solar project ever built at an existing coal mining site in North America. The word existing is carrying that whole sentence. A fair amount of the coverage that followed swapped it out for former, which is a claim about a completely different kind of place.

The 310-megawatt lignite plant at Twin Oaks has no announced retirement date. The Calvert mine that feeds it is still producing. And the company says it is looking at expanding the mine and building a rail terminal to bring in more coal on top of that.

The coal plant is staying, and Panamint said so on the record

Two outlets checked the plant’s status directly rather than reprinting the announcement, and both came back with the same answer. Electrek reported on July 24 that no retirement had been announced. Six days later, Maria Gallucci at Canary Media got Panamint CEO Apolka Totth to say it herself.

Totth wrote by email that the company sees “no reason for an early retirement” at Twin Oaks, describing it as an economically competitive unit that keeps costs down for Texas ratepayers. She also confirmed Panamint is investigating a larger footprint for the Calvert mine and a terminal to rail coal in.

That makes this the only project of its kind in the country. Everything else in the small coal-to-solar niche sits on mines that already stopped and plants that already closed. Big Rooter is going up inside a live operation.

The 1.2 gigawatts is a direct current number, and the grid never sees it

Add the two phases from the announcement and you get 1,149 megawatts of direct current. Big Rooter West is 491 MWdc and under construction now. Big Rooter East is 658 MWdc and breaks ground in December.

ERCOT’s interconnection queue carries the other number, the one measured after the inverters. Big Rooter West Solar, queue ID 26INR0431, is listed at 403.2 MW. Big Rooter East Solar, 29INR0017, is listed at 554.7 MW. Total: 957.9 megawatts of alternating current, about 17 percent under the headline figure.

This is normal, and it is deliberate. Developers oversize the panel field relative to the inverters because it fattens the shoulders of the day, pushing the array to full output earlier in the morning and holding it later into the evening. A DC-to-AC ratio around 1.2 is unremarkable in Texas.

It just means the round number everybody printed is not the number ERCOT dispatches. The dates do not line up either. Panamint says August 2028 and August 2029. Both queue entries say May 31.

The panel count deserves the same arithmetic. Divide 1,149 megawatts by 2 million modules and you land on 574.5 watts apiece, which sits above every power bin First Solar publishes for the Series 7. Take the top of that range and the real figure is closer to 2.1 million panels. The release says approximately, and approximately is doing quiet work in there.

The switchyard is the actual asset

Twin Oaks opened in 1990 as TNP One, built for Texas-New Mexico Power. It burns Texas lignite in a fluidized bed with crushed limestone injected to knock down sulfur dioxide, which was a fairly advanced way to run a coal boiler in 1990. Sempra bought it in 2002 and gave it the current name. Panamint acquired the plant and the neighboring mine in 2023.

That mine is Calvert, operated by Walnut Creek Mining Company out of Bremond. Railroad Commission of Texas records list it under permit 27I, with 7,776 permitted acres in Robertson County. The full complex runs to about 10,000 acres, though nobody has published how much of that the solar field itself will cover.

Here is why a developer pays for a site like this one. In ERCOT, the bottleneck is not sunshine or panels or money. It is the interconnection queue, and a 345-kilovolt switchyard that has been energized and moving real power for 36 years is the rarest item on the shopping list.

Both Big Rooter requests entered the queue on the same day, March 22, 2024, aimed at the same node. Panamint is not building a solar farm near a coal plant. It is building one on top of the coal plant’s grid connection, which is the part you cannot order new.

The battery, the data center and the gas turbines are still sentences

The 10,000-acre pitch also includes 1.6 gigawatt-hours of battery storage, 790 megawatts of what Panamint calls Batch Zero data center capacity, and enough gas access to support at least 800 megawatts of thermal generation, either for the grid or for a tenant.

Some of that has hardware behind it. A third ERCOT filing, Big Rooter West Storage, sits in the queue at 201.08 megawatts with a proposed completion of December 1, 2028. The rest is described by the company itself as under development.

Local station KBTX in Bryan reported on July 30 that it had asked both Panamint and Robertson County officials whether those 790 megawatts mean an actual building on the site or somewhere nearby, and was still waiting on an answer.

The power buyer is a blank too. The announcement mentions a long-term purchase agreement with “one of country’s largest companies” and stops there. Panamint says it also expects a federal investment tax credit worth half the project cost, on the grounds that the site qualifies as an energy community and the equipment is American-made, and that it ordered transformers and breakers early enough to get ahead of last year’s rollback of clean energy credits.

The confirmed hardware is worth a look. First Solar is making the cadmium telluride modules in Ohio, Louisiana and Alabama. Nextpower supplies the NX Horizon trackers, including the Hail Pro-75 stow package, which in this part of Texas is closer to an insurance requirement than a feature, given what hail does to a panel field. SOLV Energy is handling the array, the substation and the transmission as EPC contractor.

Coal-mine solar is a small club, and two of its members answer to carmakers

For scale, the biggest operating project in this category is the 186-megawatt Tilden Solar Project in southern Illinois, followed by the 111-megawatt Martin County Solar Project in eastern Kentucky. Both switched on last year over abandoned mines. Martin County sends its output to Toyota’s Kentucky manufacturing operations.

Louisiana has the 240-megawatt Dolet Hills project going up on a former mine property. In Kentucky, BrightNight’s Starfire installation on remediated mine land signed Rivian as anchor customer back in 2023, with a 100-megawatt purchase agreement. Starfire was originally floated at roughly 800 megawatts and now tracks toward 410, with construction slated for late 2027.

So Big Rooter at 957.9 MWac would be about five times the largest thing currently running in the niche, and it will share a fence line with the coal that every other project on that list replaced.

The federal support that made mine-land solar attractive has thinned out as well. Credits for solar and wind were phased down last year, which effectively removed the brownfield bonus that helped these sites pencil out. The Nature Conservancy is still pushing ahead with 25 projects across former mine land in the Cumberland Forest, starting with a 10-megawatt array in Virginia that breaks ground this fall.

What is standing in Robertson County right now

A construction crew, two interconnection requests holding position at an energized 345-kilovolt node, and a 1990 lignite plant that will keep burning Calvert coal while the trackers go in around it.

The battery has a queue number. The gas turbines, the data center, the named power buyer and the bigger mine do not. Each of those is a plan, and plans at this scale get resized, as Rivian’s Kentucky project showed when it lost half its megawatts between announcement and construction.

Totth’s framing is that the solar will generate enough carbon-free power to cancel out the coal plant’s annual emissions profile. That is a real claim and it may well pencil out. It is a different claim from the one most of the headlines made, which is that a Texas coal mine is turning into a solar farm. What it is turning into is a solar farm and a coal mine, at the same time, on the same 10,000 acres, wired into the same switchyard.

Continued executing ABOUND’s strategy of building a diversified Energy Solutions Platform spanning commercial products, near-term technology commercialization and next-generation energy storage development.

Fully Subscribed Financing

The Company successfully completed its previously announced non-brokered private placement, which was fully subscribed. The financing resulted in gross proceeds of $299,286.96 through the issuance of 3,741,087 common shares.

The net proceeds are intended to support engineering, manufacturing, business development, working capital and general corporate purposes across the Company’s expanding technology portfolio. The successful completion of the financing strengthens ABOUND’s financial position as it continues advancing multiple commercialization initiatives across its Energy Solutions Platform.

The participation of one insider in the Private Placement constitutes a "related party transaction" within the meaning of Multilateral Instrument 61-101 – Protection of Minority Security Holders in Special Transactions ("MI 61-101"). The Company relied on the exemption from the formal valuation requirement contained in section 5.5(a) of MI 61-101 and the exemption from the minority shareholder approval requirement contained in section 5.7(1)(a) of MI 61-101, on the basis that, at the time the transaction was agreed to, neither the fair market value of the securities to be issued to, nor the fair market value of the consideration to be received from the related party exceeds 25% of the Company's market capitalization.

Completion of the H2Si™ Transaction

The previously announced License Agreement with the Vendor and Amerada R&D Ltd. has officially closed following shareholder approval. Shareholders of Amerada R&D Ltd. voted 100% in favour of the transaction, satisfying the final closing condition.

Under the agreement, ABOUND has secured exclusive commercialization and licensing rights to the H2Si™ hydrogen technology, together with a contractual pathway to acquire the underlying intellectual property upon the achievement of specified commercial milestones.

H2Si™ generates hydrogen through a controlled reaction between silicon nanoparticles and water. The process uses no hydrocarbon-based feedstocks and produces hydrogen gas and silica.

One of H2Si™’s unique advantages is its deployment flexibility. Because the technology is engineered to operate with a variety of water sources, the Company believes H2Si™ may be well suited for deployment in applications where non-potable or brackish water infrastructure is available, including certain AI data center environments. By leveraging existing site water infrastructure, H2Si™ has the potential to provide an efficient pathway for on-demand hydrogen production to support backup power, peak demand, or other distributed energy applications.

As previously announced, independent testing by the University of Saskatchewan confirmed that H2Si™ consistently produced hydrogen as the primary reaction product and demonstrated reproducible performance under laboratory testing, providing an important technical milestone as the Company advances toward commercial deployment.

The completion of the transaction expands ABOUND’s Energy Solutions Platform into hydrogen and adds a technology the Company intends to advance toward commercial deployment alongside its existing cathode manufacturing operations and longer-term energy storage development activities.

As consideration for the transaction, the Company issued 5,000,000 common shares to the Vendor at a deemed price of $0.08 per share, representing aggregate deemed consideration of $400,000. Of the consideration shares, 1,000,000 were issued to the Vendor on closing. The remaining 4,000,000 common shares were issued in the Vendor’s name and are held by an escrow agent under a pooling agreement, to be released only upon the achievement and certification that the first commercial unit (the "FCU") has attained sustained hydrogen production of approximately 1,600 kg/day and satisfied other specified performance criteria ("FCU Success"). While those shares remain escrowed, the Vendor has agreed to vote them at the direction of the Company's board of directors.

Under the License Agreement, the Company is responsible for funding the technical development and construction of the FCU, which is led by the Vendor, on a budget currently expected to be up to CAD$2.4 million. The Company expects to satisfy this commitment over time through a combination of equity financings, debt instruments and/or strategic third-party partnerships.

All securities issued pursuant to the private placement and transaction with the Vendor are subject to a four-month-and-one-day hold period until December 1, 2026. The Vendor is not a related party of the Company, and no finder's fee, commission or other compensation is payable in connection with the transaction with the Vendor or the private placement.

Following completion of the private placement and the H2Si™ transaction, the Company has 30,542,348 common shares issued and outstanding.

Expansion of Commercial ZaeroTex™ Production

ABOUND continues the commercial production of its proprietary ZaeroTex™ advanced air-cathode materials and is advancing fulfillment activities related to the largest purchase order received by the Company to date for its cathode business.

The Company has completed the move into its new manufacturing facility, which will be configured to improve production workflow, maximize manufacturing efficiency and support the continued expansion of ZaeroTex™ production. In addition to providing greater operational capacity, the new facility is expected to improve operating efficiency while reducing ongoing operating costs.

ZaeroTex™ represents ABOUND’s commercial business today. H2Si™ is being advanced toward near-term commercial deployment, while Zaeras™, the Company’s proprietary zinc-air long-duration energy storage platform, remains under development. Management believes this combination provides a balanced platform through which current and prospective commercial activities may support the continued development of next-generation energy technologies.

“These milestones represent another important step in ABOUND’s evolution,” said Keith Morlock, Chief Operating Officer and Director. “We have strengthened the business, expanded our technology portfolio and established a more efficient operating foundation. Our objective is to build a diversified Energy Solutions Platform in which continued growth from ZaeroTex™ and the commercialization of H2Si™ provide greater financial flexibility to support the development of Zaeras™ while reducing reliance on future equity financings. We remain focused on disciplined execution, strategic diversification and long-term shareholder value.”

ABOUND Energy Inc. is a clean-energy technology commercialization company focused on advancing practical, scalable energy solutions from development through commercialization. The Company is building a diversified Energy Solutions Platform across three complementary pillars:

title: Michigan high court rejects Line 5 tunnel permit - Planet Detroit
authors: Kelly House, Bridge Michigan, Kelly House, Bridge Michigan
description:
The Michigan Supreme Court on Friday ruled that the Michigan Public Service Commission erred when it granted a key permit for the Line 5 petroleum pipeline tunnel under the Straits of Mackinac.
The issue reached the state Supreme Court after the Michigan Court of Appeals sided with the state.
The justices also found that, when analyzing possible alternatives to the tunnel project — a required step in the permitting process — commissioners applied their analysis inconsistently.
Dueling lawsuits in state and federal court will settle the question of whether Enbridge can legally keep pumping oil through the Straits.
The other is on hold in state court pending the outcome of the first case.
text:
This story was originally published by Bridge Michigan, a nonprofit and nonpartisan news organization. To get regular coverage from Bridge Michigan, sign up for a free Bridge Michigan newsletter here.

The Michigan Supreme Court on Friday ruled that the Michigan Public Service Commission erred when it granted a key permit for the Line 5 petroleum pipeline tunnel under the Straits of Mackinac.

Among other findings in its 58-page ruling, the majority found the commission’s permit review was overly narrow, failed to consider whether the tunnel project would harm public rights to the Great Lakes, and failed to study whether Line 5 would shut down if the tunnel isn’t built.

“To accurately assess the environmental consequences of the Replacement Project, the PSC should have determined whether the project would be the proximate cause of Line 5’s continued operation and its alleged attendant harms,” stated a majority opinion written by Justice Elizabeth Welch.

The 6-1 decision sends the matter back to the commission with an order to “fully assess the Replacement Project’s potential harms.”

Justice Brian Zahra agreed that commissioners failed to consider impacts on public use rights in the Great Lakes, but disagreed with the rest of the majority opinion.

Friday’s ruling represents a victory for Line 5 foes who have argued the tunnel would harm the environment by locking in decades of continued fossil fuel transports along a 73-year-old pipeline that would otherwise soon shut down.

And it further clouds the fate of the proposed tunnel project, which has been in limbo since it was first proposed eight years ago in response to growing concern that Line 5 could cause a catastrophic oil spill in the Great Lakes.

“Today is a reminder that when people stand together with courage and conviction, change is possible,” Bay Mills Indian Community President Whitney Gravelle said in a written statement.

Gravelle’s tribe challenged the permit along with the Little Traverse Bay Bands of Odawa Indians, Grand Traverse Band of Ottawa and Chippewa Indians, and Nottawaseppi Huron Band of the Potawatomi.

“For years, Tribal Nations, communities, and thousands of people across the country have raised their voices to protect the Great Lakes,” Gravelle said. “This decision gives us another opportunity to honor our treaty rights, protect our waters, and consider the generations who will inherit this place.”

Enbridge spokesperson Ryan Duffy expressed disappointment with the decision and said the company is assessing its legal options.

“One thing remains unchanged, we are fully committed to the safe and responsible operation of Line 5, incorporating enhanced safety measures in the Straits and continuing to safeguard Michigan’s natural resources now and for future generations,” Duffy said in a statement to Bridge Michigan.

The ruling stems from the Public Service Commission’s December 2023 approval of a key permit for the proposed tunnel, which would reroute a 4-mile segment of the 645-mile pipeline that currently sits exposed on the lakebottom as it transports petroleum products from Superior, Wisconsin to Sarnia, Ontario.

A coalition of four Michigan tribal nations, the Environmental Law & Policy Center, Michigan Climate Action Network and Traverse City-based environmental group FLOW (For Love of Water) challenged the approval, arguing the commission’s analysis was flawed and the pipeline should be shut down rather than merely rerouted.

The issue reached the state Supreme Court after the Michigan Court of Appeals sided with the state.

In March arguments before the high court, an attorney for environmental groups challenging the permit argued the decision had been based on “a lopsided analysis that needs to be corrected.”

Enbridge lawyers argued the commission had correctly determined that building the tunnel is the best way to avoid a spill — a conclusion that rested in part on the belief that Enbridge had the legal right to keep operating Line 5.

In their ruling Friday, the court’s majority rejected that logic.

“Line 5’s continued operation, with and without the Replacement project, was a factual question, not just a legal one,” they wrote.

The justices also found that, when analyzing possible alternatives to the tunnel project — a required step in the permitting process — commissioners applied their analysis inconsistently.

For example, they took a narrow view of the oil spill risks caused by transporting Line 5’s products, considering the possibility of spills only in the Straits rather than along the length of the pipeline (which has repeatedly caused inland spills). They then took a broad view of spill risks from tunnel alternatives such as rail transport, assessing risks along the entire length of the hypothetical rail route.

Such inconsistencies amounted to “errors that did not allow for a reasoned choice among the alternatives,” Welch wrote.

Finally, the majority concluded, the commission failed to consider “whether the Replacement Project would pollute, impair, or destroy public trust resources.”

Michigan’s public trust doctrine says the state holds resources like the Great Lakes and bottomlands in trust for the people.

David Scott, an attorney who represented the Environment Law & Policy Center in the case, said the ruling brings “important precedent and clarity” about how state agencies must uphold Michigan’s environmental laws.

“I think this is the most important opinion from the Michigan Supreme Court under (the Michigan Environmental Protection Act) in probably decades,” Scott said.

Friday’s state Supreme Court decision further clouds the fate of a tunnel originally pitched in 2018 as a four-year, $500 million project that would come online by 2024.

The Michigan Department of Environment, Great Lakes and Energy recently granted one of the final permits Enbridge needs for the project, but the Bay Mills Indian Community has vowed to appeal the decision.

Enbridge is also awaiting a federal permit that the US Army Corps of Engineers appears poised to grant.

Meanwhile, the existing pipeline continues to transport oil across Michigan and into Canada through the open water of the Straits in defiance of a 2020 shutdown order from Gov. Gretchen Whitmer.

Dueling lawsuits in state and federal court will settle the question of whether Enbridge can legally keep pumping oil through the Straits. One case is on appeal after a federal District Court judge ruled in December that federal pipeline safety law leaves Michigan no authority to order a shutdown. The other is on hold in state court pending the outcome of the first case.

A 2017 state-commissioned report found Line 5 has a 1-in-60 chance of breaking by 2053, while reports have offered varying estimates of how far oil might spread, from about 20 miles to several hundreds of miles.

text:
Advocates for an increase in mandated distances between Pennsylvania communities and natural gas infrastructure said their call has become more urgent with an expected surge in fracking to fuel the state’s data center buildout.

The Environmental Integrity Project, Clean Air Council and their allies urged Pennsylvania towns and lawmakers to support a plan to widen most setbacks by more than 2,500 feet to protect public health, which they say is endangered by a current rule allowing energy companies to build well pads, compressor stations and pipelines as close as 500 feet from homes, schools and hospitals.

The request was first made in a petition to the state’s Environmental Quality Board in 2024. In December the board passed it along to the Department of Environmental Protection, which is expected to conclude an analysis of the proposal by year’s end. Meanwhile, natural gas production is expected to increase to help supply electricity to energy-hungry data centers, dozens of which are now planned for Pennsylvania.

“The majority of the data-center buildout will be powered by fracked gas,” said Matt Kelso, manager of data and technology at FracTracker Alliance, a nonprofit that maps, analyzes and shares data on the oil, gas and petrochemical industries, during a webinar on Wednesday. “It will require not just the wells but pipelines, trucking, water usage, injection wells. This will allow the industry to pump the gas from where it is, safely locked in the ground, to the data centers or to the power plants that provide their electricity.”

According to Data Center Proposal Tracker, an independent website, 47 data centers are proposed or in either pre-construction or construction phases in Pennsylvania. Another 21 are on the drawing board and haven’t applied for government approvals yet.

The petition calls on the Department of Environmental Protection to increase the distance between gas infrastructure and homes to at least 1 kilometer (3,281 feet), and to at least 1 mile (5,280 feet) for buildings such as schools or hospitals with “vulnerable” populations. A new rule would also increase the buffer between gas plants and a body of surface water to at least 750 feet.

The American Petroleum Institute of Pennsylvania told the Environmental Quality Board that it “strongly” opposed the plan, saying it would impose onerous restrictions on the industry. The petition exceeds the authority of the panel because changes in well locations cannot be achieved through regulation, said the chapter’s executive director, Stephanie Catarino Wissman, in a December letter to the board.

“The petition’s proposed setbacks would function as a de facto ban on unconventional natural gas development in Pennsylvania by confining operations to extremely limited areas,” she wrote, contending that residents are already protected by “stringent” regulation of natural gas development.

The petition includes 42 peer-reviewed studies showing that people living near gas infrastructure are more likely to get sick, said Lisa Hallowell, an attorney for the Environmental Integrity Project (EIP). One study showed that children living within a mile of a gas well were five to seven times more likely to suffer from lymphoma, a type of blood cancer, than those who had no wells within five miles of their homes, she noted.

Hallowell denied that the proposed rule change would effectively ban fracking. She said it would not relocate existing gas plants and would only apply to new unconventional oil and gas wells.

“Don’t believe the false narrative that protective buffers would ban fracking,” she said.“Requiring increased buffers is well within their capabilities, and will not infringe their abilities to reach the gas they seek to extract.”

Donate Now

The American Petroleum Institute of Pennsylvania said that extending the current 500-foot setback to 3,281 feet would block production in an area 43 times larger than the current rule, while the area off-limits to gas production would be 112 times larger if the setback area is increased to 5,280 feet for buildings housing vulnerable populations.

“Such subjective and sweeping changes would also impede Pennsylvanians’ ability to responsibly develop their private mineral rights—effectively condemning property without just compensation,” the group’s letter said.

Lisa Graves-Marcucci, a community advocate at EIP, said the proposed setbacks were inspired by a Pennsylvania grand jury report in 2020 that found communities had been harmed by fracking. That report proposed setbacks of at least 2,500 feet.

The report was led by then Attorney General Josh Shapiro, who is now governor. Shapiro, a Democrat, has courted the data center industry by offering to speed permitting on the condition that data centers bring their own power rather than taking it from the grid.

Graves-Marcucci said towns have a legal right under the state’s municipal planning code to increase setback distances above the state minimum of 500 feet. But she wasn’t sure that all local officials were aware of that right and said EIP and other advocates are hoping to educate them.

She urged activists to join a rally at the state capitol in Harrisburg on Oct. 7 to call on lawmakers and the governor to support bigger setbacks.

Cecil Township, in heavily fracked Washington County, increased its minimum setback distance to 2,500 feet in 2024. That prompted a bill by its Republican state senator, Camera Bartolotta, that would reduce or eliminate revenue from the state’s impact fee on fracking allocated to any town that followed its lead.

Activists said Pennsylvania, which produces the second-largest amount of natural gas of any U.S. state after Texas, has attracted many data center proposals because one of the world’s biggest gas fields underlies about two-thirds of the state.

The state’s rich natural resources, starting with oil and coal, have attracted industries that pay little attention to the communities in which they operate, argued Lauren Posey, an advocate with Protect PT, an environmental group in Westmoreland County, east of Pittsburgh.

That southwest Pennsylvania region “has long functioned as an industrial hub for all sorts of industries, and a public health sacrifice zone,” Posey said during Wednesday’s webinar. “Now it’s easy to see this history repeating itself as our region is being targeted for large-scale data center development, in large part because we’re an energy-producing state, and we already have these industries and this infrastructure in place.”

title: Westlake's massive planned data center sparks concerns in Keller
description:
A spokesperson for Westlake said the data center buildings would be 1.1 million square feet from the property line of the project site.
The development sits along the Westlake-Keller border, placing some homes just feet from the project site.
According to the town's informational page, the data center would be required to comply with local noise ordinances limiting sound levels to between 49 and 56 decibels.
The town also referenced comments made by Ross Perot Jr., chairman of Hillwood, the company that owns the property where the data center is planned.
“If you're an AI data center developer, you must be very responsible, and you must take great care of the local community,” Perot said during a recent CNBC interview.
text:
A planned data center development in Westlake is drawing concern from residents just across the city line in Keller, where neighbors say they were caught off guard by the project and are worried about its potential impact on their community.

According to the site plan submitted to Westlake's Planning and Zoning Commission, the Circle T Data Center project would encompass about 3.83 million square feet of commercial space on 87.96 acres near Highway 377 and Westport Parkway.

A spokesperson for Westlake said the data center buildings would be 1.1 million square feet from the property line of the project site.

The development sits along the Westlake-Keller border, placing some homes just feet from the project site.

Keller resident Kevin Myers can see it through a hole in his fence.

“If you look right here, it's basically where that barbed wire fence is,” Myers said, pointing to the property line separating his neighborhood from the proposed development.

Myers said he first learned about the project through a social media post shared by the Town of Westlake on Wednesday.

Local

The latest news from around North Texas.

The City of Keller later posted on its social media page, saying that neither the mayor nor city council members were aware of the project before it was publicly announced.

"My City Council colleagues and I were unfortunately surprised by the news as well," Mayor Ross McMullin posted on the city's official Facebook page.

In comments, Westlake told neighbors city leaders spoke with Keller about the data center a year ago, to which McMullin responded, "Even if they met with other city leaders a year ago, I wasn’t part of it and would have appreciated the opportunity to meet with Westlake officials to discuss the project before it was announced so as to understand the actual impact to our residents."

City leaders from Westlake and Keller said they were unavailable for interviews with NBC 5 on Friday, as the cities' offices are closed on Fridays.

“Our concern is, one, the noise. Two, what health impacts it may have on people in this neighborhood, because this neighborhood's an older crowd, predominantly 50 and up," Myers said. “And then three, what everybody's really worried about seems to be the number one topic, how it's going to negatively affect or impact our property values.”

Westlake's informational webpage about the development addresses some of those concerns.

A spokesperson also emailed NBC 5 a statement, saying, "Town staff has been working with the developer to ensure that the site has as little impact as possible on the adjacent Keller residents. The project is meeting all safety standards and will meet the town’s ordinance for noise generation."

The spokesperson added that "a landscaped berm" will be installed along Highway 377 and a landscape buffer of at least 75 feet along the southern property line.

"The developer is also adding mature vegetation to the berm and surrounding area to further screen the site and increase sound dampening," the spokesperson said, stating that the developer will also increase the setback required by the town "to further add to the screening effect of the vegetation and berm. The closest Keller residence is 506 ft from the building line."

According to the town's informational page, the data center would be required to comply with local noise ordinances limiting sound levels to between 49 and 56 decibels. Westlake also states that data centers are highly regulated facilities subject to environmental and safety standards, and that existing town ordinances are designed to address projects of this scale.

The town also referenced comments made by Ross Perot Jr., chairman of Hillwood, the company that owns the property where the data center is planned.

“If you're an AI data center developer, you must be very responsible, and you must take great care of the local community,” Perot said during a recent CNBC interview.

But Myers and others in Keller feel they should have been included in discussions sooner.

“They didn't share that info or try to work and be good neighbors here in Keller, especially in this neighborhood,” he said.

Myers said he has written to Perot about his concerns, while Keller's mayor said in a Facebook comment that he plans to meet with Westlake officials next week.

“We're using every avenue to see if we can get this thing farther away,” Myers said.

The City of Keller is encouraging residents to attend Westlake's upcoming Planning and Zoning Commission meeting, where officials are expected to discuss and potentially approve site plans for the project.

The meeting is set for Tuesday, Aug. 4, 2026, at 5 p.m., in the Council Chamber, 1500 Solana Blvd, Building 7, Suite 7100.

text:
A battery materials manufacturer will pay nearly $7.5 million to resolve allegations that it submitted inflated reimbursement claims to the U.S. Department of Energy for construction materials, labor and more to build a plant in Kentucky.

Ascend Elements — the company that planned in 2022 to invest $1 billion in Hopkinsville for a battery recycling plant — has agreed to pay the federal government to resolve claims that between September 2023 and February 2025, the company “sought and received DOE reimbursement for goods and services that included inflated labor hours, excessive tool purchases, unnecessary equipment rentals and other wasteful or unnecessary expenses related to its industrial-scale battery precursor production project,” according to the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Western District of Kentucky.

The Department of Energy paid more than $5.3 million tied to the conduct, prosecutors said. Ascend “voluntarily divulged the issues to the government” and received credit for cooperating with the self-disclosure process. The company also cooperated with an investigation and “assisting the United States in understanding the full scope of the conduct.”

Representatives from Ascend Elements did not respond to request for comment prior to publication.

“This settlement reflects the Department of Justice’s commitment to ensuring that federal funds supporting critical energy and infrastructure projects are safeguarded from misuse,” Kyle Bumgarner, U.s. Attorney for the Western District of Kentucky, said in a statement. “Companies that receive taxpayer dollars must be held to the highest standards, and today’s recovery demonstrates that voluntary self-disclosure and cooperation will be met with appropriate credit, while still ensuring accountability.”

Ascend recently filed for bankruptcy

Earlier this year, the company voluntarily filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in order to restructure its finances without stopping work. The construction team working on the facility, Turner-Kokosing Industrial Joint Venture, acquired the under-construction Apex 1 recycling plant last month for $31.7 million in an auction.

Construction at the plant has been repeatedly delayed throughout a series of complaints from contractors — the joint venture included — over unpaid work. Construction also has been affected by shifting market conditions. Late last year, the Department of Energy pulled remaining federal funding for the Ascend Elements project.

The Ascend Elements project was intended to be the company’s largest U.S. electric vehicle battery recycling and materials manufacturing facility, the first plant of which would have the capability to supply up to 250,000 EVs annually with materials.

When the first phase of investments and new jobs were announced in 2022, Ascend Elements said its facility would help supply companies it already had relationships with, including SK Battery America, part of the same company that partnered with Ford Motor Co. on a now-dissolved plan to build EV batteries just outside Elizabethtown.

Ascend Elements previously anticipated its investment would surpass $1 billion and create 400 full-time jobs, though some of the grants it was relying on have been pulled and the facility it was building has changed ownership.

Turner Construction and Kokosing Industrial, the two companies part of the joint venture that bought the site, are construction contractors. While Christian County economic development officials told local news outlets the project will be completed, long-term plans for the facility are still to be determined.

In a statement, a Turner spokesperson characterized the site purchase as the “right next step” for trade contractors and a “responsible path forward” that protects the joint venture and various workers who contributed to constructing the facility, which is approximately 65% complete.

“We’re looking forward to working with the City of Hopkinsville, the Commonwealth of Kentucky, and the Department of Energy to bring this project to completion,” the spokesperson said. “This community invested in this vision. So did we. We’re not walking away from it.”

Ascend’s bankruptcy filing and settlement is the latest in a saga of companies across the country, especially in Kentucky, scrambling to decide what to do after they invested in clean energy projects that former President Joe Biden’s administration incentivized, but President Donald Trump’s administration does not.

When the company filed for bankruptcy earlier this spring, Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear’s office, which opposed the termination of federal grants for the state’s energy-related projects, said it had been in contact with Ascend and belived the step would not negatively impact progress being made in Hopkinsville at Apex 1.

Former Ascend Elements president and CEO Linh Austin — who left the job this month, according to his LinkedIn profile — said following the company’s bankruptcy filing, the restructuring process would give the company the chance to clarify its mission. He said the company was still focused on contributing to the battery supply chain.

Austin, who was in his leadership role for less than two years starting last March, previously acknowledged the company “had a long history of fiscal and operational mismanagement, and that its future was very much in question.”

Terms for incentives and tax credits for the project as it was being completed by Ascend were performance-based. In September 2022, the Kentucky Economic Development Finance Authority approved the company for up to $2 million through its Enterprise Initiative Act, allowing the company to recoup sales and use tax on construction costs.

Last fall, the authority approved a $13.5 million incentive from the Kentucky Business Investment program, based on project costs of almost $870 million and projections the facility would create 250 new jobs with an average hourly wage of $27.89, according to its financial incentive database.

“The state’s only direct cash support was for site infrastructure — not the company — making it more marketable if there were a need for a future investor,” the governor’s office previously said.
