text:
The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency is proposing regulatory amendments to certain compliance provisions and test procedures related to model year (MY) 2027 and later heavy-duty highway engines. These amendments would include changes to the regulatory useful life periods and the emission-related warranty periods. The EPA also proposes to add clarity to certain regulatory compliance provisions and correct errors in the regulations to support the MYs 2027 and later program for heavy-duty highway engines and vehicles.

Cyrus Western, regional administrator of the Environmental Protection Agency said the recent proposed rule to eliminate Diesel Exhaust Fluid deratements entirely will translate to $12 billion saved by American truckers. He said reversing the Biden-era compliance requirements that are tied to DEF system failures that cause sudden losses of speed is a commonsense solution.

EPA is proposing to completely remove deratements and vehicle speed restrictions for newly manufactured highway engines and vehicles and new non-road engines and equipment, including those used in agriculture. Instead of trucks and tractors lurching to a halt when DEF systems fail, under EPA’s proposal, operators would receive visible and/or audible alerts that allow them to continue operating until they can safely address the problem. EPA is also taking public comment on whether guidance should be developed to allow manufacturers to implement this change for in-use on road and non-road engines and equipment.

SAVING MONEY AND FRUSTRATION

If finalized, the savings could reach up to $6,000 per vehicle on new truck purchases, on top of the increased productivity operators are currently losing when deratements cause sudden speed loss on the road. In addition to savings, he said there have been serious issues stemming from deratements.

“There have been horror stories; it’s not just people who have been inconvenienced,” he said. “There are important functions that haven’t been happening properly. For example, we’ve heard stories of fire trucks that run on a diesel engine with DEF that went into limp mode or got derated because of a faulty code so rather than being able to rush to the scene of a fire, they’re only able to go 5 miles per hour.”

He said similar stories have circulated about ambulances, school buses, and vehicles used in agriculture, making the elimination of the requirements something that helps people do the jobs that make society function.

Troy Lake has been one of the faces of the fight over DEF systems. Lake is a 64-year-old diesel mechanic from Wyoming who spent seven months in federal prison for deleting emissions systems on engines plagued with system failures. Pardoned by President Trump in 2025, Lake’s shop was raided in 2018. He told Cowboy State Daily in a 2025 interview that a more logical solution is needed for expensive emissions repairs that won’t put people out of work. EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin, Region 8 Administrator Western, and U.S. Sen. Cynthia Lummis, R-Wyo., all worked to secure a pardon for Lake.

“The previous administration and the left in general have weaponized the Clean Air Act to beat up on and go after average, blue collar Americans who are just trying to show up for their job and work hard. We saw these folks who were beat up on using the full force and authority of the federal government and that’s not acceptable. That’s not what the Clean Air Act is for. That’s something the administration and the president immediately recognized and took corrective action to right those wrongs and to ensure that federal authority is being used in a fair and reasonable way.”

He said under the Biden administration, the EPA experienced mission drift, taking the agency away from its mission of ensuring Americans all have clean air, clean water, and a clean environment.

The comment period is currently open

“The rules and regs process have lots of small details to sort through, it’s very litigious,” he said. “But, if we follow it well, what we’re doing is we are making really good, well-crafted rules that have followed the process on the books. One of the top ways that some of these agency laws get tossed out by a judge is they review the administrative record and they review some of the petitions that are getting filed in court against these rules.”

He said to ensure the rule isn’t easily tossed out is to follow the administrative procedures act to the letter. He can’t predict what a future administration will do, but said they are able to exercise control over following the rules.

“We saw the Biden administration on certain rules and regulations take a pretty hasty and sloppy approach and we want to do the exact opposite,” he said. “We want to make sure we’re doing things by the book.”

Submit your comments, identified by Docket ID No. EPA-HQ-OAR-2026-0728, at http://www.regulations.gov . The EPA will hold virtual public hearings on July 29, 2026, starting at 9 a.m. ET and on July 30, 2026, starting at 10 a.m. ET. If there is sufficient interest, an additional day of hearings will be held on the subsequent day. Comments must be received on or before Aug. 29, 2026.

Western said the agency will review the comments and if warranted, adjust or make clarifications to the rule.

Read the full script here:

Today’s show is sponsored by the Electric Vehicle Association. Join up to support the electrification of transport today. And by EnergySage — plan your own energy independence and insulate yourself from rising energy costs. And by you: stick around to find out how to keep us 100% independent. Welcome back to another episode of TEN, Transport Evolved News. Thanks for joining me. I hope you’re well and with someone you care about, who cares for you.

We start today’s show with the official launch of the new Mercedes-Benz GLA, the smallest electric Mercedes-Benz in its refreshed lineup. Offered in three configurations — the GLA 200 Electric, GLA 250+ Electric, and GLA 350 4MATIC Electric — the entry-level GLA is powered by a 165-kilowatt rear-wheel drive motor and 58-kilowatt-hour LFP battery, capable of charge rates of up to 200 kilowatts. At the other end, the GLA 350 4MATIC puts down 260 kilowatts on all-wheel drive, with up to 320 kilowatts DC fast charging from its 85-kilowatt-hour NMC battery. All models share an 800-volt architecture, so even the entry-level charges fast, and all offer towing capability. Benz claims a WLTC range of between 394 kilometers (243 miles) and 657 kilometers (408 miles), depending on spec. Prices start from just under €48,600, putting it in tight competition against the BMW iX2.

Talking of BMW, it’s been busy this week in the EV world as well, announcing its long-wheelbase version of the X5 family of vehicles, including its iX5 EV for the Chinese market. You might think the iX5 long-wheelbase just gets a few extra millimeters of length over the standard variant and [unclear: “be it”], but BMW has pushed the boat out, adding a massive 8K entertainment screen for the rear-seat passengers alongside power, fully reclinable rear seats. It also promises a range on the Chinese test cycle of 1,000 kilometers, just over 620 miles. As a Chinese-only market vehicle, most folk won’t get to experience the extra luxury, but over in the U.S., the standard iX5 is soon due to enter production, and this week BMW gave a first look at its Plant Woodruff facility in South Carolina, which will begin series production of that vehicle’s monster-sized battery pack — larger than some electric pickup trucks — from December. The iX5 effectively replaces the outgoing iX in BMW’s stable, and the price? It’s going to be expensive.

There’s been a long-standing trend in the auto industry where automakers promise semi-autonomous functionality only to soften those promises after sale. Volvo has just become the latest to do that, although for reasons outside of its control. It’s dropping Lidar for good on its flagship EX90 SUV and ES90 sedan, after planned advanced driver assistance features built around the sensor never materialized. But this isn’t really Volvo’s failure — it’s the fault of its former Lidar supplier, Luminar. Volvo terminated its Lidar supply contract back in November, citing supply chain risk and Luminar’s failure to meet its obligations, and a week later, Luminar filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy. Rather than leave owners with dead hardware and no explanation, Volvo is compensating them with cash payouts and credit packages, varying market by market. And before Tesla fans start crowing about a win for vision-only systems — don’t. Even without Lidar, the EX90 still runs five radars, a dozen cameras, and sixteen ultrasonic sensors, and so far Volvo’s semi-autonomous systems are proving robust with the sensor fusion suite it still has.

Regulars to the channel will know we love keeping tabs on the growth in renewable energy around the world, and this week’s just-released figures from the U.S. EIA, reviewed by the SUN DAY Campaign, show significant growth. The U.S. generated 10.1% more renewable energy across its electrical grid during the first five months of the year compared to the previous year, with utility-scale solar growing 21.6% year-over-year, small-scale solar up 12.8%, hydropower up 10.8%, and wind up 4.8%. Moreover, the total output of wind and solar during the first five months of 2026 was 57% greater than the total output of the U.S.’s remaining coal plants, and 26% more than nuclear power plants. And in case you’re curious just how much of the grid is powered by renewables, the total tally — including biomass and geothermal — was 30.3% of total U.S. grid generation. Add in nuclear, and non-fossil fuel is the dominant force. By spring 2027, renewable capacity will surpass natural gas, with battery storage predicted to increase 48% over current levels by June 2027.

Retractable door handles, be they electronically or mechanically operated, are becoming common in the EV world, as they help reduce aerodynamic drag and improve efficiency. But as several well-known cases around the world have demonstrated, involving many brands of car, they can sometimes prove dangerous in the event of an accident, failing to properly allow occupants to exit or hampering rescue efforts. We’ve already seen the PRC enact a ban on flush door handles, and now the U.S. NHTSA is starting the process of implementing new safety rules regarding the design, operation, and testing of flush-fit door handles. While the U.S. federal government recently denied a petition to investigate Tesla’s Model 3 door handles as a specific safety defect, it committed to a broader rule-making process aimed at mandating a robust, obvious door egress system across all vehicles. At this time, I doubt we’ll see an outright ban, but I do expect a standard to be developed covering emergency exit use.

As we just dealt with a few U.S.-centric stories, let’s stay there a little longer — namely the world of legislative… nonsense. In a week where the U.S. saw more attempts to enforce the President’s will by any means necessary, a new bipartisan bill was introduced on Capitol Hill that would ban any automaker whose shareholders are more than 15% Chinese entities, effectively banning Mercedes-Benz, which has about 20% Chinese shareholders. But it’s okay, because in deep-red Florida, where legislators are happy to dump EVs, the state is diverting nearly $200 million in federal money — originally earmarked under the Biden administration for EV charging — into 32 flying car pads at $5.6 million a pop, for a technology that isn’t even commercially available yet. Florida’s even offering to cover the required matching funds itself, something states have otherwise left private companies to pay for their EV setups. As one clean energy advocate put it, the money is being hijacked from what would benefit everyday drivers and handed instead to the ultra-wealthy for emergent technology only they will be able to afford. And on top of that, the federal government just used an old solar farm environmental review process to wave through a new AI data center near the Hoover Dam in Nevada — not adding a data center next to new solar, but swapping it out entirely for an already-approved solar and battery project. Because who needs the natural world and renewable energy when you’ve got Skynet? Apparently.

BMW’s newest EV lineup, all built on the Neue Klasse platform, are proving extremely popular with buyers thanks to their 800-volt system architecture, efficient drivetrain, and long range. Demand is, in fact, so high right now that BMW has added a second shift at its Hungarian plant to ramp up iX3 production, with orders on track to hit 100,000. And in a separate confirmation this week, BMW says iX3 production will also soon kick off at its Mexico plant for the Americas market, starting next year. And with the iX3, i3, and iX5 all coming to market, BMW’s previous models, including the iX and i4, are on their way out. But according to BMWblog, the i4 nameplate will effectively live on — not in a new electric sedan, but in the form of a new drop-top cabriolet expected around 2028, and closely related to the i3’s Neue Klasse platform. Details are pretty sparse right now, but cabriolets have been an important part of BMW’s stable over the years, and the idea that we could be about to get a proper performance drop-top with BMW Neue Klasse performance chops fills me with a significant amount of excitement. What about you?

On last week’s show, I gave you the disappointing yet completely expected news that Honda was discontinuing its GM-built Prologue EV at the end of the 2026 model year — the latest in a massive line of North American market EVs to get the axe since President Trump returned to office. Honda is playing the now-expected game of blaming its EV decisions on customers, as EV sales soar everywhere except the U.S. And this week, as Business Insider’s Ben Shimkus noted, Honda has wasted no time in recommending people switch to a hybrid for their next car. At the bottom of all of Honda’s automotive statements throughout July, a section entitled “Consider what’s next,” meant to promote Honda’s newest vehicles, simply tells customers to consider a hybrid for their next new Honda. Given that many Honda customers went beyond a hybrid and went fully electric, that statement is already raising eyebrows among EV fans and existing Honda drivers. I’m guessing Honda can look forward to losing those customers in the not-too-distant future.

The claims being peddled by the auto industry in North America right now — namely that nobody wants to buy an EV — have been laughable at best and patently false at worst. And while the U.S. is stuck in a hell of its own making, the rest of the world is moving on. Sales data published this week for Q2 from the International Energy Agency shows that plug-in vehicle sales — EVs and plug-in hybrids — soared in the quarter, jumping 35% from Q1 and setting new records in 50 countries, even as global car sales fell 5%. Australia, Brazil, India, Korea, and Vietnam saw sales roughly double compared to last year, with other markets hitting record market shares. China’s EV sales are set to stagnate for the first time this decade, though — stagnate still means over 60% of new cars sold there are electric. Dramatic U.S. policy changes — axed tax credits, weakened fuel rules, and states like their own in Oregon piling on new EV mileage fees — have crushed sales, and the IEA wastes no time calling out the real cause. It’s not buyers. Overall, EV sales are predicted to hit 29% of total car sales worldwide this year, one point higher than originally projected back in May.

Let’s finish this segment with some more news worth celebrating: namely, that whatever you might be seeing on YouTube or Facebook — and there’s a lot of AI-generated propaganda there these days — EV owners are overwhelmingly happy with driving electric and don’t want to go back to ICE. The third annual study into EV owners this week by CDK Global shows that 90% of the 552 owners questioned said they plan to buy another EV when it comes time to replace their existing car, up 8% from the same period last year. Moreover, an astonishing 94% of respondents under the age of sixty said they’d buy another EV. Interestingly, too, 84% said they’d purchased new, 73% say they always own at least one EV, and more people purchased their EV than in prior years. 84% of those questioned said they’ll have at-home charging, 17% said doing so was a hassle, and 38% of non-Tesla owners said they purchased their EV for environmental reasons, while only 25% of Tesla owners said the same. As for happiness, 94% said they were happy with their purchase, with 79% saying their EV was the best car they had driven. That last fact ties in nicely with J.D. Power’s latest just-released APEAL study, which gauges owners’ emotional attachment to their vehicles. The headline: EV owners are on average way happier with their purchase than diesel, gasoline, and hybrid owners, with EV owners scoring an average of 910 versus 850 for other fuel types, on a scale of 1,000.

Our recall reminders are coming next, but first a message from our most important channel sponsors: you. As one of the oldest and most independent YouTube channels in the space, we’ve spent over 15 years distilling cleaner, greener, safer, smarter, and more equitable transportation and energy into the information you need to make informed choices. We don’t believe in paywalls, and we don’t give companies editorial control — that means no paid partnerships, no sponsorships from companies we cover or whose products we don’t genuinely believe in. So especially in an age of AI slop gobbling up ad revenue, our primary income is you. We are a full-time staff of myself, and I don’t pay myself. But the costs of staying independent aren’t small — payroll, health insurance, and of course bills. And you can help us remain independent and cover them all from $1.50 a month on Patreon, or YouTube, via Ko-fi, or a one-off donation through our P.O. box, or buying something from our swag store. Right now, your help would mean more than ever. My wife, whose salary covered our household bills, lost her job back in June to corporate reshuffling. She’s interviewing with some good leads right now, but we’ve only got a few months of buffer before some tough decisions about this channel and our future will need to be made. If you can help, the team and I would really appreciate it. Thanks.

And now it’s time for our recall reminders. As usual, you’ll find links to all of the recalls in our show notes. International is recalling its EVSB and CECB electric school buses due to faulty body panel joint attachments; fleet operators will be notified of the recall process in due course. All-electric Vision school buses and Vision transit buses, both made by Blue Bird, are also being recalled due to a potential brake fluid leak that could cause a loss of braking function in affected models. And Hyundai is recalling around 40,000 Inster EVs globally to address a potential fire risk caused by an internal defect in the central three-way valve of an affected car’s thermal management system. And those were your recall reminders.

Now it’s time for our news shorts, and as usual you’ll find full links on our website at transportevolved.com.

Volvo has trademarked the EX50 EV nameplate for use on a future vehicle. The trademark was filed in Europe in the middle of July, the same week that rumors surfaced that it’s looking to bring a new electric sedan and wagon to market.

Saudi Prince Alwaleed has publicly disclosed this week that he has a 5% stake in Lucid; the news caused stock to soar by 25%, boosting Lucid just weeks after unconfirmed rumors caused instability.

Kia has confirmed that its flagship model vehicles, including its electric vehicle family, will get sibling-brand Hyundai’s pleOS in-car infotainment operating system from next year, with other models to follow after.

Tesla, despite making its own solar cells, just signed deals to buy 640 megawatts of solar and 360 megawatts of battery storage in Texas and Arizona, mainly to power its massive AI and robotics push.

Factorial Energy has announced a new strategic alliance with SK On that will see the two firms work together to assess how they could use SK On’s production tech to mass-produce solid-state battery cells.

Mitsubishi has confirmed this week that the new Eclipse EV, a rebadged Nissan Leaf, will launch with a dual-charge port in North America — a NACS port on one side and a J1772 on the other for low-speed charging.

Lawmakers in Massachusetts are working on a new framework for e-bikes and scooters that would redefine legal classifications and what can and can’t be used where, rather than outright ban them.

Kia has officially opened the pre-order process in Mexico for the EV3; Kia plans on producing the EV3 locally for the Mexican market, with eventual expansion into the U.S. and Canadian markets.

META has continued its descent into enshittification, ending its global renewable energy pledge the very same week it confirmed funding for ten new gas power plants to keep its mega-server farms running.

The Leapmotor A05 electric hatchback is now officially offering up to 317 miles, or 510 kilometers, of range for an equivalent price of $7,400.; it even has optional Lidar.

Transit operator GZM in Poland was celebrating the commissioning of 31 new electric buses this week across its fleets in southern Poland; the buses will operate in 4 different cities.

Laos has halted the importation of both gasoline- and diesel-powered vehicles into the nation until the end of the year, as part of a government-sponsored attempt to accelerate EV adoption.

The Volkswagen ID Polo’s entry-level variant, the ID Polo Trend, is now officially on sale in Europe. It’s priced from €24,995 and comes with a 37-kilowatt-hour LFP battery pack for 323 kilometers of range.

BYD has confirmed pricing for its new flagship Denza Z9 GT sedan in the UK, promising hypercar-like acceleration will be available from £105,000 for the battery-electric variant.

The Auto Plus EV subsidy program has been given official approval to begin operation in Spain; it offers tiered incentives for private buyers and businesses alike for new or used EVs, with businesses using leasing or renting required to hold the vehicle for at least three years.

A research program made up of multiple academic institutions in Germany has shown for the first time that lithium metal cells lose lithium to their copper current collectors as they age; the discovery will help improve battery longevity.

Aurora has deployed its second-generation autonomous trucks in the U.S. and plans to deploy the new fleet across its commercial network, spanning ten existing driverless routes throughout the Sunbelt — but frustratingly, they’re not electric, they’re diesel.

Thailand is considering a new EV incentive program to accelerate the adoption of EVs; the subsidy program will be worth around 24 billion.

Transport Scotland has announced a new funding program worth just shy of £2 million to help small and medium-sized haulage firms plan their transition to zero-emission HGVs and build the skills needed to support them.

BMW has confirmed that some iX1 and iX2 variants now qualify for the UK’s full electric car grant; this effectively knocks £3,750 off the sticker price, meaning the two are available from £33,315 on the road.

Hyundai and Kia have announced a new product called All-Day Energy; it combines previous charging products into one service, covering smart charging, V2G, and V2H functions.

The government of Australia has announced a new AU$30 million funding program to support 14 smart grid programs, including 2 focused on EV V2X technology.

The Schwarz Group in Germany has told employees eligible for its company car program that EVs are temporarily off the list for new orders in Germany, citing concerns over low residual values.

The African Development Bank has approved a loan worth €100 million to Gotion Power Morocco that will enable it to produce an integrated cathode-to-cell LFP battery.

The Volvo ES90 has gone on sale in South Korea; with a starting price of ₩72.94 million, the flagship sedan will compete against other higher-end markets like the Genesis G80.

Tesla has quietly settled with 3 out of 5 named plaintiffs alleging its Fremont production facility was a hotbed of racism; up to 580 other unnamed plaintiffs are still suing the firm.

BYD had a busy week this week, officially opening sales in Japan for its first all-electric kei car, the Racco. At the same time, it teased pictures of its new Seal 06, while its Great Han is now being prepared for its official launch later this month.

The London Ambulance Service has officially expanded its all-electric fleet with 37 new electric ambulances and 40 new fast-response EVs; its fleet now includes more than 120 EVs.

Porsche has confirmed that it will be laying off more staff at its facilities as budgetary concerns bite. The brand hasn’t officially cancelled the Taycan, but the model’s demise is now looking increasingly likely.

Stellantis has sold its Free2move car-sharing business to German firm Mutares, closing by year-end; Mutares plans to keep expanding the fleet’s EVs across Europe and the USA.

Volkswagen is reportedly in advanced talks to give Chinese battery maker Gotion a majority stake in PowerCo’s Sagunto Spanish facility via a joint venture; PowerCo denies plans to cede control.

ESG Solar has opened a megawatt truck-charging park near Kassel, Germany, combining MCS charging with on-site solar and battery storage — it’s one of Germany’s first public MCS sites.

Thanks to a deal with contract manufacturer Steyr Automotive, Chinese brand SuperPanther has begun European series production of its eTopas 600 electric tractor unit, avoiding tariffs.

SMART has confirmed that its #1 electric SUV is getting a major facelift and battery upgrade for the new model year in China; the model will gain an 800-volt system architecture and charge at up to 6C.

ACEA data shows electric truck registrations rose 47.7% in the EU during H1 2026, while electric bus registrations grew 56.8%, now making up 27.7% of all bus sales.

Chinese firm Hongqi has unveiled a new ultra-fast charging battery that it says can offer up to 12C charging rates; this translates to a 10-70% charge time of under 4 minutes.

FREE NOW by Lyft and Baidu-owned Apollo Go have launched a new robotaxi trial program in the UK; the trials are the first step in implementing a commercial partnership in the city.

And finally, for the shorts: Tesla is asking a federal judge to intervene in an ongoing standoff over Cybertruck production tooling. It alleges its supplier is preventing it from accessing dies that it had handed over for production.

And those are your news shorts — there will be more next week. Our final two stories are coming right up, but first, a quick word about long-time video sponsor EnergySage. It’s a great way to get trustworthy, verified solar experts, whether that’s for solar panels, getting a heat pump installed, or, for those of you who rent, joining a community solar program. It was EnergySage I used when we put solar panels on the roof of our home five years ago, and our panels are still churning out electrons every day, so it’s well worth it as the cost of utility-provided power keeps rising. And while US federal incentives for solar aren’t around anymore, it’s worth using EnergySage’s network of local experts to help navigate the regional and state incentives that may still exist in your area, as well as finding local financial institutions that very often have special deals for solar panel loans, allowing for a low, manageable monthly payment. And of course, if you choose to use an EnergySage-provided installer for your project, we’ll also get a small referral fee, so you’ll be helping us out, too.

And now it’s time for our final two stories. You might not know this, but mining companies are quickly becoming one of the most important consumers of electric vehicles — not vehicles you can drive on the road, but massive battery-powered plant machinery and dump trucks. The finances for it make total sense, since mining trucks can use the added weight of being fully loaded to recharge their battery packs for their empty return trips, and their lack of tailpipes makes them safe for use in enclosed spaces. And since most heavy plant haulers are diesel-electric already, using generators to power on-board motors that drive the wheels, replacing diesel with a battery pack makes total sense. This week, the CEO of massive Australian mining company Fortescue got to test out the brand’s latest purchase — an all-electric, custom-built, 150-ton mining truck. The look on his face in the video he shared to LinkedIn is somewhere between a little kid getting to drive for the first time and the smile of someone who’s just realised how much money he’s going to save.

And finally, like them or loathe them, autonomous robotaxis are quickly becoming a common sight in many cities around the world. And while some people, including myself, are wary of their operational capabilities, given how many documented violations we’ve seen robotaxis commit on open roads, new data this week from the IIHS says that Waymo’s vehicles are crashing 68% less frequently than the average human driver. The IIHS made this conclusion after examining federally-mandated robotaxi crash data. And while that’s amazing news, less exciting for Waymo is the news that its self-driving cars keep racking up parking tickets in Austin, Texas, where it operates a fleet of robotaxis. Apparently, while Waymo’s driving skills are improving, they still can’t identify where they can and cannot park.

text:
It began with an unexpected LinkedIn message. A well-wisher, keen to see Tamil Nadu strengthen its industrial base, reached out to TRB Rajaa, the state’s industry minister at the time, with an urgent warning, “I know you’ve been talking to VinFast, but they’re now on the verge of choosing another state.”

Until then, Tamil Nadu had been engaging with the Vietnamese electric-vehicle (EV) maker for months. But the message revealed something far more significant: negotiations had entered their final stages and a rival state was close to sealing the deal.

Rajaa did not wait. As soon as word reached Chennai that the deal was slipping away, he boarded the next available flight to Vietnam. “The day before I reached, they had almost finalised the investment with another state,” recalls Rajaa. “Their representatives had met that state’s leadership the previous night and had virtually concluded the negotiations.”

4 July 2026

Get the latest issue of Outlook Business

Over the next three days, Tamil Nadu intensified its engagement with VinFast and worked across departments to resolve key issues, including land availability and the state’s final offer.

The effort ultimately paid off. In 2024, VinFast invested ₹16,000cr in Tuticorin, one of India’s biggest EV manufacturing commitments.

“The real differentiator was the ecosystem. We already have a mature automobile manufacturing base supported by a strong network of MSMEs [micro, small and medium enterprises],” says Rajaa. “Large manufacturers weren’t operating in isolation—they were backed by a deep supplier ecosystem.”

The Great EV Land Grab

The VinFast episode is an illustration of how cut-throat the contest for EV manufacturing has become.

According to a report by industry platform India Energy Storage Alliance (IESA), India’s EV market could expand twelvefold, reaching annual sales of 30.4mn units by 2032 under the high-growth National EV (NEV) scenario, driven by stronger policy support, greater localisation of manufacturing and a wider charging-infrastructure network.

The automobile industry already contributes around 7% of India’s GDP and supports over 30mn jobs; the electric transition threatens to redistribute that pie among states willing to fight for it.

The inter-state rivalry is further intensified by the absence of a national-level policy or body to manage the EV sector

When Ola Electric began scouting for land for its ambitious EV hub, Uttar Pradesh, Maharashtra, Gujarat, Karnataka, Telangana and Tamil Nadu pitched to host the project.

Tamil Nadu emerged victorious due to its strong automotive ecosystem. In 2023, Ola committed ₹7,614cr for manufacturing electric cars, two-wheelers and lithium-cell gigafactories.

The inter-state competition is further intensified by the absence of a national-level policy or body to manage the EV sector. “A dedicated policy, or at least a well-defined national target, is essential to guide investments, shape programmes and provide certainty to the industry,” says Amit Bhatt, managing director for India at the International Council on Clean Transportation (ICCT), a non-profit research organisation.

In this vacuum, states have become the de facto architects of India’s EV shift; and they are building to very different blueprints.

Different Strokes

Broadly, Indian states have followed two distinct EV policy models, with a third now beginning to emerge. The first is the manufacturing and investment-led model, adopted by Tamil Nadu, Gujarat, Maharashtra, Telangana and Karnataka.

Tamil Nadu’s EV Policy 2023 aims to make the state Southeast Asia’s preferred EV hub, targeting ₹50,000cr in investments and 1.5 lakh new jobs. Instead of offering a single incentive, the policy allows companies to choose benefits that best suit their investment plans.

Eligible manufacturers can avail 100% state goods and services tax (SGST) reimbursement for up to 15 years, turnover-linked or capital subsidies and special capital subsidies of up to 20% for advanced chemistry cell (ACC) battery manufacturing.

The policy also treats R&D expenditure, technology transfer and intellectual property-related investments as eligible costs, encouraging companies to build a complete EV ecosystem in the state.

Gujarat has positioned itself as a battery and supply-chain hub through its Industrial Policy 2020 that classifies EVs and their components as a Sunrise Thrust Sector. Projects get higher capital subsidies of 12%, 10% or 6% of eligible fixed-capital investment (excluding land), depending on the location. The policy also replaced SGST-linked incentives with an investment-linked capital subsidy and removed the overall cap on incentive amounts.

“Tamil Nadu and Gujarat lead EV manufacturing, backed by strong policies that continue to attract EV and battery investments,” says Jaydeep Mukherjee, professor at Great Lakes Institute of Management, Chennai.

Some states such as Odisha have also adopted a consumer adoption-led model. Here the priority is not factories but buyers: purchase incentives, tax waivers and charging infrastructure designed to put EVs on the road.

For instance, Odisha offers subsi-dies of up to ₹20,000 for electric two-wheelers (e2W), ₹30,000 for electric three-wheelers (e3W) and up to ₹1.5 lakh for electric four-wheelers (e4W), alongside 100% exemption on road tax and registration fees for eligible battery-operated vehicles.

Similarly, Telangana offers full exemption on road tax and registration fees for all battery EVs, including e2W, e4W and commercial vehicles.

Telangana also provides exclusive discounts of 10–20% on EV purchases for over 5 lakh state government employees. In addition, commercial EVs such as taxis, auto-rickshaws and goods carriers are eligible for the same tax waivers, while existing auto-rickshaws can receive a 15% retrofitment incentive of up to ₹15,000 to convert to electric.

Two Theories of Change

However, these two EV strategies rest on very different theories of how a transition happens. The manufacturing-led states are, in effect, betting on supply: build the factories; jobs, supplier networks and the local market will follow.

Within this, for states with established automotive clusters, the electric transition is less an environmental project than an industrial-survival one: if the internal combustion engine (ICE) is on its way out, the states that host its supply chains must capture the technology that replaces it or watch decades of industrial capital depreciate. They are keen to build up the entire EV ecosystem, including manufacturers, component suppliers, testing facilities and skilled talent.

A state like Odisha, without a legacy automotive base, is unlikely to outbid Tamil Nadu for a gigafactory; its subsidies are better understood as a clean-air and fuel-import-substitution play than a jobs strategy

“This industrial clustering strengthens the supply chain, improves operational efficiency and makes the state a more attractive destination for EV investments,” says Charith Konda, energy specialist, India Mobility and New Energy at the Institute for Energy Economics and Financial Analysis.

The adoption-led states are betting on demand. Their reasoning is that if enough people buy EVs, companies will naturally invest in dealerships, charging networks, service centres and perhaps, eventually, manufacturing. But that last link in the chain is far from automatic, and for some states it may not even be the point.

A state like Odisha, without a legacy automotive base, is unlikely to outbid Tamil Nadu for a gigafactory; its subsidies are better understood as a clean-air and fuel-import-substitution play than a jobs strategy.

“Companies typically base their investment decisions on a combination of factors, including logistics and connectivity such as proximity to ports in Tamil Nadu, the availability of a strong supplier ecosystem like the Mumbai–Pune automotive cluster, state policy support and incentives, infrastructure and access to skilled talent,” says ICCT’s Bhatt.

Delhi: The Third Way

Then there is Delhi, which fits neither template; and may be pioneering a third.

On June 29, the Delhi government approved a new EV Policy with an outlay of ₹15,000cr, running until March 2030. Like the adoption-led states, it offers carrots: a 100% road tax and registration fee waiver for electric cars priced up to ₹30 lakh, among other incentives. But its distinguishing feature is the stick.

New petrol and CNG three-wheelers and N1 trucks will be barred from registration from January 1, 2027, and petrol two-wheelers from April 1, 2028.

Instead of relying on incentives alone, Delhi is using regulation to force the transition—the approach that has driven mass adoption in Europe and China, where hard deadlines have been set for ICE vehicles. Such mandates send an unambiguous market signal: manufacturers that do not sell EVs will simply cede the market to rivals that do.

“Two-wheelers account for nearly two-thirds of Delhi’s registered vehicles, making them central to reducing vehicular emissions,” says Delhi chief minister Rekha Gupta in an interview with Outlook Business.

“Our policy provides a phased transition until 2028, giving consumers and industry adequate time to adopt affordable and reliable electric alternatives.”

Delhi can afford this approach. It has no automotive manufacturing base to protect, an air-quality emergency that gives regulation political cover and—at 8.4% electric-car penetration—a market already warmer than most.

Delhi’s first EV policy, launched in 2020, relied primarily on fiscal and non-fiscal incentives such as purchase subsidies, tax waivers and charging infrastructure to encourage consumers to switch to EVs.

While this approach helped kick-start EV adoption, it fell short of driving mass-scale transition. The policy had set a target of 25% EV sales by 2024, but it currently stands at around 11–12%.

The limitations of a subsidy-led approach are becoming evident: governments cannot indefinitely subsidise every vehicle, and such policies place the responsibility for adoption largely on consumers.

The new policy seeks to address this by shifting part of the responsibility to manufacturers, restricting the registration of certain new ICE vehicles and pushing automakers to expand their EV offerings and compete more aggressively in the electric-mobility market.

But the model carries its own risks. The bans will bite only if the charging network scales in time. Delhi is aiming to instal 32,000 public EV charging points across the city from 9,000 now. And Delhi does not exist in isolation: a buyer facing a two-wheeler ban in the capital can register the same petrol vehicle in Gurgaon, Noida or Ghaziabad.

“It is a potential loophole. The long-term solution is to extend similar policies across the entire NCR,” says Bhatt. Delhi could also deter this by imposing environmental charges on vehicles registered outside the city, adds Bhatt.

“Our strategy is centred on expan-ding a differentiated EV portfolio that addresses diverse consumer needs, while simultaneously investing in scalable manufacturing, a resilient supplier ecosystem and advanced battery technologies,” says Bharath Rao, co-founder and chief executive, Emobi, an e2W start-up.

The Scoreboard

So, how have the two bets paid off? The data suggests a paradox: the states that make EVs are not necessarily the states that buy them. According to vehicle registration data for 2025–26 from the Vahan dashboard, Telangana leads electric-car penetration at 11.6%, having registered 19,810 electric cars out of 1.71 lakh PV sales.

Delhi follows (16,986 out of 2.01 lakh). Maharashtra, despite recording the highest absolute electric-car sales at 34,066 units, has only 5.8% penetration because of its large overall market. Odisha also recorded 5.8% (5,307 out of 92,245); and Tamil Nadu, the country’s self-declared EV manufacturing champion, stood at just 5.2% (17,220 out of 3.34 lakh).

Tamil Nadu has already attracted more than ₹40,000cr in EV manufacturing investments and has built a comprehensive EV ecosystem spanning vehicle manufacturing, batteries, components, charging infrastructure and R&D.

In comparison, Gujarat has attracted an estimated ₹25,000–30,000cr in EV-related investments by leveraging its established auto-mobile manufacturing base, ports and supplier network to draw major players such as Tata Motors, Maruti Suzuki, MG Motor and battery manufacturers, making it another key EV manufacturing hub.

The pattern that emerges is revealing. Manufacturing-led policies appear to deliver on their own terms, investment and industrial activity, without necessarily electrifying the home market. Adoption-led policies lift penetration but create markets that may well be served by factories in other states. Each model, in other words, succeeds at its own objective and largely fails at the other’s.

“EV adoption is driven by consumer awareness and charging infrastructure,” says Mukherjee, adding that states with stronger charging networks have so far shown higher adoption.

According to government data, Karnataka leads the country with 6,096 operational public EV charging stations, followed by Maharashtra (4,166), Uttar Pradesh (2,316) and Delhi (1,957) as of March 1, 2026. Tamil Nadu follows closely with 1,780 charging stations.

Infrastructure, indeed, remains the binding constraint for the adoption model everywhere. India has installed 27,737 public EV charging stations as of March 2026, of which 22,753 are operational. In comparison, India added 22.7 lakh new EVs in 2025 alone.

E-Laboratories

India’s EV shift does not require every state to run the same experiment, and there is a case that the variety is precisely the point. Manufacturing states are testing whether supply-side industrial policy can build globally competitive clusters. Adoption states are testing how far subsidies can move consumers. Delhi is testing whether mandates can do what money cannot.

But experiments need someone to read the results. The missing layer remains a coherent national framework: long-term adoption targets, a predictable roadmap for the phase-out of purchase incentives, uniform charging standards and Centre-state coordination that prevents the transition from fragmenting into 30 incompatible regimes.

“Countries that have achieved large-scale EV adoption typically have clear national EV targets and defined timelines for phasing out ICE vehicles,” says Bhatt. Until then, India’s EV story will continue to be written the way it began: state by state, bet by bet and occasionally on an urgent flight to Hanoi.

text:
Summary: Banco Sabadell México and Santander México are expanding financing initiatives across two strategic pillars of Mexico's economy: Sabadell is targeting up to US$7.4 billion in renewable energy, transmission and mixed-investment infrastructure projects to support the country's goal of generating 38.5% of electricity from clean sources by 2030, while Santander has partnered with CAINTRA to channel MX$100 million in preferential credit to SMEs in Nuevo Leon amid projected 4% industrial growth in 2026. The parallel moves signal growing confidence among Mexican financial institutions in both the energy transition and the industrial manufacturing sector as durable areas of long-term capital deployment.

Mexican banks are stepping up financing efforts across two pillars of the country's economy, with Banco Sabadell México targeting energy infrastructure projects worth up to US$7.4 billion and Santander México partnering with industry group CAINTRA to unlock MX$100 million (US$5.3 million) in credit for small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) in Nuevo Leon.

The two initiatives, announced separately, reflect a broader push by financial institutions to capitalize on Mexico's economic momentum in both the renewable energy sector and its industrial manufacturing base.

Banco Sabadell Targets Renewable Energy and Transmission

Banco Sabadell México said it will reinforce its strategy to finance energy infrastructure projects, with an emphasis on renewable energy, electricity transmission and mixed-investment schemes, as part of an effort to strengthen the national electric system and accelerate the transition to a cleaner energy matrix.

The bank said it aims to position itself as a financial partner for developers and investors throughout all stages of project execution, from construction to operational stabilization. Its strategy includes financing for wind farms, photovoltaic installations, transmission lines and priority initiatives backed by the federal government.

The push comes as Mexico's energy sector undergoes a reactivation supported by a co-investment scheme in which the state retains a 54% majority stake while private companies can contribute up to 46% of capital with preferential rights. In June 2026, Mexico awarded 38 renewable energy projects that will add 8,000 megawatts of new capacity, backed by an estimated US$7.4 billion in investment.

"Our vision is to be a key player in Mexico's transformation toward a sustainable future, contributing the expertise needed to reach the national goal of generating 38.5% of electricity from clean sources by 2030," said Gustavo Martínez, Deputy General Director of CIB at Banco Sabadell México.

Carlos Herrerías, the bank's Director of Energy and Infrastructure, said Banco Sabadell also plans to participate in projects to expand transmission infrastructure, which he described as essential to integrating new renewable capacity into the national grid. "We are committed to financing large energy projects, especially priority projects, mixed-investment schemes and the expansion of transmission infrastructure," Herrerías said.

The bank said meeting Mexico's clean-generation targets will require coordinated participation between the public and private sectors, along with financial mechanisms capable of mobilizing capital toward long-term infrastructure projects.

Santander, CAINTRA Launch SME Credit Program in Nuevo Leon

Separately, Santander México and the Chamber of the Transformation Industry of Nuevo Leon (CAINTRA) launched an alliance to channel MX$100 million in credit to SMEs in the state, alongside 5,000 training scholarships aimed at strengthening business capabilities and competitiveness.

The agreement is designed to expand financing options for CAINTRA-affiliated companies and support their professionalization and long-term growth. It comes as Nuevo Leon's industrial sector shows signs of recovery, with CAINTRA projecting 4% growth in 2026 and the creation of up to 27,000 jobs, reported MBN.

Under the deal, Santander will offer CAINTRA members preferential credit conditions through products such as Crédito Simple and Crédito Ágil, with both fixed- and variable-rate options, plus opening-fee benefits on the first loans formalized under the alliance. Participating companies will also gain access to Santander's broader portfolio of business solutions, including digital tools, corporate benefits and international expansion support.

Marcos Abal Soneira, Santander México's Executive Director of SMEs, said Nuevo Leon's role as an industrial, manufacturing and export hub means local SMEs require agile financial solutions to sustain job creation and development.

“Nuevo Leon has a strategic role as an industrial, manufacturing and export hub for the country, and its SMEs require agile financial solutions that allow them to continue generating jobs and development. For this reason, we will open the credit tap and provide non-financial benefits to give them the support they need in partnership with CAINTRA,” Abal said.

Jorge Santos Reyna, president of CAINTRA Nuevo Leon, said the agreement aims to help member companies build stronger credit histories and access more competitive financing conditions.

“The objective of this agreement is clear: to establish a collaboration that allows companies affiliated with CAINTRA to access a more competitive financial offering designed to support their operational, investment and development needs,” Santos said.

A Broader Push to Mobilize Capital

Together, the two initiatives illustrate how Mexican banks are moving to mobilize capital across distinct but complementary fronts: large-scale renewable energy infrastructure needed to meet national clean-power targets, and smaller-scale industrial financing aimed at sustaining SME growth in one of the country's key manufacturing regions. Both efforts point to financial institutions positioning themselves as long-term partners in sectors seen as central to Mexico's competitiveness and economic development.

text:
State regulators hosted a public hearing for Amazon’s proposed large data center project in Richmond County on Thursday. The state Division of Air Quality had requested public feedback on two air quality permits that would allow Amazon and Duke Energy to operate approximately 650 diesel generators to provide emergency power at the site.

Over 200 people attended the public hearing, with 36 offering testimony. A major concern raised by Richmond County residents is that state regulators are issuing two separate permits: one for Amazon’s nearly 600 backup diesel generators and one for Duke’s nearly 60 temporary generators.

“All of the generators that the Division of Air Quality has allowed Amazon and Duke to split into separate permit applications must be treated as one major source of air pollution,” said Shaun Ingram, co-founder of the Richmond County Coalition for Justice and Black Empowerment.

Caroline Cress, a senior attorney with the Southern Environmental Law Center, said that by separating out the leased generators, the companies avoid more stringent modeling requirements for pollutants such as fine particulate matter.

“Because the bridge power project is included with Duke's permit rather than Amazon's, it is subject to a much lower annual emission limit,” said Russell Braswell, an engineer with the state Division of Air Quality.

Without nearby sensors, Cress said it’s impossible to know how the new data center will affect local air quality.

“The only way to get a sense of that is to do the modeling, which they're specifically getting out of,” Cress said.

Shawn Taylor, a spokesperson from the state Division of Air Quality, wrote that the diesel generators did not meet North Carolina’s requirements for a single permit, despite meeting two of the three criteria. They’re located on a contiguous or adjacent property and belong to the same “industrial grouping.” However, because Duke Energy will operate some of them, Taylor said state regulators could not combine the roughly 650 generators into a single permit.

DAQ maintains a statewide network of air quality monitors to ensure that the state meets Environmental Protection Agency requirements. More populous areas receive more sensors, and Taylor wrote that “the majority are sited in or near communities we classify as potentially underserved.”

“Our data shows that all of North Carolina has maintained compliance with all federal air quality standards for more than a decade,” Taylor said.

The nearest sensor is a PurpleAir monitor north of Rockingham, about 9.5 miles from Amazon’s construction site. The closest sensor that the state owns and operates is two counties over, about 45 miles away in Monroe. But many residents live much closer to the site.

“The campus is literally in our backyard,” Nellie Dumas said, whose family owns property in the vicinity of the tech campus. She mentioned concerns about air and water quality, though she said the smell has improved since Amazon purchased the land.

“We are not opposed to progress,” said Reverend G. Rebecca Warren, who serves as a pastor for Wayman Chapel A.M.E. Zion Church, about a mile away from the construction site. “However, we believe progress should never come at the expense of the health, safety, and quality of life of the people who already call this community home.”

Warren said that while she understands the generators wouldn’t run unless there was a blackout or routine testing, she would still like to see more community engagement from the state and Amazon. In her testimony, she proposed conditions such as limiting generator testing during the church’s worship services and activities.

Today is the final day to submit public comments on the state’s draft permits. You can email comments to daq.publiccomments@deq.nc.gov with the subject line “Amazon.25A and DukeRichmond.26C.”

“We appreciate the public comments we received on this topic and are reviewing,” DAQ spokesperson Shawn Taylor said.

text:
Republican U.S. Senate candidate Ken Paxton unveiled a new economic agenda on Friday, his first detailed policy proposal of the high-stakes campaign.

The main pillars of the plan all involve granting new tax breaks for healthcare expenses, housing down payments and family benefits as affordability dominates voters’ concerns, and as some polls show Paxton lagging behind his Democratic opponent James Talarico.

“Washington has made it harder than ever to get ahead, and the American Dream is slipping away as the cost of everything from housing to healthcare rises,” Paxton said in a release. “My agenda is very simple: I believe every Texan should be able to buy a home, raise a family, and live a healthy life without struggling to make ends meet.”

description:
In this How Oregon Works interview, Worksystems, the Portland-metro workforce development board, brings together leaders from Earth Advantage, Constructing Hope, and The Heat Pump Store to discuss the Home Energy Retrofit Occupations Academy (HERO Academy), an innovative workforce training partnership.
To meet that need, Earth Advantage developed the HERO Academy, a paid, 15-week training program that prepares pre-apprenticeship graduates for high-demand jobs installing residential energy-efficient heat pump and water heating systems.

text:
In this How Oregon Works interview, Worksystems, the Portland-metro workforce development board, brings together leaders from Earth Advantage, Constructing Hope, and The Heat Pump Store to discuss the Home Energy Retrofit Occupations Academy (HERO Academy), an innovative workforce training partnership. Hosted by Daryl Lambert, Worksystems' Clean Energy Sector Lead, the conversation explores how collaboration between employers, training providers, and the public workforce system is helping meet the demand for skilled workers while creating pathways to quality jobs.

As Portland and the broader region continues investing in energy-efficient building upgrades and home retrofits, employers face increasing demand for workers with specialized skills. To meet that need, Earth Advantage developed the HERO Academy, a paid, 15-week training program that prepares pre-apprenticeship graduates for high-demand jobs installing residential energy-efficient heat pump and water heating systems.

The HERO Academy is a model for how workforce programs can be intentionally designed to align with existing efforts rather than duplicate them. Earth Advantage recognized early on the opportunity to build on infrastructure that was already in place, partnering with Worksystems and pre-apprenticeship programs like Constructing Hope.

Pre-apprenticeship programs prepare people for careers in the skilled trades by providing hands-on training, industry-recognized certifications, and support services that help participants successfully enter registered apprenticeship programs and construction jobs. They are designed to build both technical and workplace skills while helping participants overcome barriers to employment and long-term career success.

At Worksystems, our role is to help demystify how the public workforce system functions, and where there are opportunities to connect HERO Academy into it. That means integrating existing programs like clean energy career coaching so participants have access to the full range of public resources available to them. This includes on-the-job training opportunities, which the Heat Pump Store used to continue training their HERO Academy participants following the initial program. When there’s a gap in skills, these hire-first opportunities allow employers to onboard people who show strong potential but need some additional hands-on training to meet all of the job requirements.

The collaboration and bridging of resources is what makes this program so special. The HERO Academy illustrates what is possible when existing workforce development programs are integrated into innovative clean energy training programs: stronger talent pipelines, expanded access to opportunity, and partnerships that help both businesses and workers thrive.

description:
Oregon should consider nuclear option Oregon is in an electron crunch.
Enter the next phase of the energy economy and the emerging fusion energy ecosystem.
Nuclear fusion energy fuses atoms in a process to create energy, as opposed to nuclear fission which splits atoms and creates radioactive waste that needs to be stored indefinitely.
A huge ecosystem is being built to support fusion energy production.
Fossil fuels receive them with the lowest estimates at $20 billion a year.
text:
Oregon should consider nuclear option

Oregon is in an electron crunch. Obviously, data centers are big part of that. But electrification is driving demand too. The conversations around getting rid of natural gas appliances and replacing them with electric ones will drive this demand. Ironically, it may drive electrical consumption towards natural gas-produced electricity.

With the disincentiving of solar and wind by the current administration (as well as the challenges of interconnection and transmission) and an understandable move away from fossil fuels, Oregon needs other options.

Additionally, our local tourism economy is under threat from low and no-snow winters and smoke and wildfires in the summers. Now is the time to consider the future of what we want our economy to be.

Enter the next phase of the energy economy and the emerging fusion energy ecosystem.

Nuclear fusion energy fuses atoms in a process to create energy, as opposed to nuclear fission which splits atoms and creates radioactive waste that needs to be stored indefinitely. A huge ecosystem is being built to support fusion energy production. One fusion company is building a power plant in Washington State and aims to have electrons on the grid in 2029.

If we are proactive in our economic outreach and creating regulatory frameworks, Oregon has an opportunity to benefit from not just the energy produced by fusion, but the jobs in manufacturing and the emerging fusion supply chain.

In terms of costs, most if not all energy sources are heavily subsidized. Fossil fuels receive them with the lowest estimates at $20 billion a year. The highest estimates suggest $760 billion! The eventual cost of fusion will be heavily dependent on tax breaks and subsidies like other energy sources.

The joke has always been that fusion is years away. Realistically, it’s probably 10 years away, which means now is the time to lay the groundwork to bring clean energy and jobs to Oregon. Central Oregon has a chance to be a leader if we take action.

The solar plant borrowed that connection to let 710 megawatts of solar go through.
A live connection with real capacity behind it is close to priceless, and a retiring coal plant has exactly that.
A coal plant that lives on While all of this has happened, the Sherburne County Generating Station kept burning coal, since it is not done yet.
So for the next few years, the same substation will be moving coal power and solar power at once.
text:
America is retiring coal plants slowly and steadily. The boilers are cut up for scrap, the smokestacks get dropped on camera and the land tends to sit in permitting limbo for a decade. But in Becker, Minnesota, the state's biggest coal plant is being used, not for all this hardware but for a plug. On July 21, Xcel Energy announced it had completed the third phase of Sherco Solar, pushing the site to 710 megawatts generated by 1.7 million panels. This makes it the largest solar facility in Minnesota and one of the biggest in the Upper Midwest, by the utility's own careful scoping. But this is not the most interesting part. What is making headlines is the fact that Sherco Solar feeds the grid through the transmission infrastructure and interconnection rights of the Sherburne County Generating Station, the coal giant next door that has been pushing power into the same wires since 1976. The solar plant borrowed that connection to let 710 megawatts of solar go through.

The plug that matters

Any new power plant that wants onto the US transmission grid has to join an interconnection queue, where grid operators study what upgrades the system needs before anything gets energised. According to Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory’s latest count, published July 1, some 2,061 gigawatts of proposed generation and storage are sitting in those queues. That is more capacity than every power plant currently operating in the country, combined. But Sherco Solar almost sidestepped this entire process. The Midcontinent Independent System Operator, which runs the grid across the middle of the country, gives the owner of a retiring plant three years to reuse its interconnection rights for a replacement resource. Those rights cannot be sold to anyone else, so they are strictly use it or lose it. Xcel used it. The nonprofit RMI estimates this generator replacement route can cut connection time from the five-year average to under one year. Rob Gramlich, CEO of the consulting firm Grid Strategies, put it more bluntly when CNN visited the site in 2024, saying “somebody just has this Disney pass to skip the line.” Transmission is a scarce asset underneath all this. There is seldom a spare line sitting around anywhere on a modern grid, which is why Tasmania is currently rebuilding 287 towers on a corridor it is not allowed to switch off. A live connection with real capacity behind it is close to priceless, and a retiring coal plant has exactly that.

1.7 million panels

Sherco Solar feeds the grid through the transmission infrastructure and interconnection rights of the Sherburne County Generating Station

The build of the plant also moved quickly. First power flowed in late October 2024 at more than 220 megawatts, a second phase followed through 2025, and the 250-megawatt third phase wrapped this month. All done, the site now spreads across thousands of acres of farm country around Becker and Clear Lake, and it produces enough electricity for roughly 150,000 homes on Xcel’s Upper Midwest system. The company is playing even smarter. Xcel is handling groundskeeping with the help of sheep, which gaze beneath the arrays so no one has to mow 1.7 million panels' worth of grass. There is a Great Pyrenees named Ozzy on the payroll to guard them. Every module is also on a 25-to-30 year clock, which is its own looming industrial story.

A coal plant that lives on

While all of this has happened, the Sherburne County Generating Station kept burning coal, since it is not done yet. Units 1 and 2 came online in 1976 and 1977 as a matched pair designed to run together, Unit 3 followed in 1987, and together they gave the plant a nameplate capacity of 2,238 megawatts. In its prime, it burned about 30,000 tons of coal a day, delivered three trainloads at a time and was emptied by a rotary dumper that flips a full rail car upside down every three minutes. Each boiler stands more than 200 feet tall, higher than the dome of the Minnesota State Capitol. The 680-megawatt Unit 2 shut down for good on New Year’s Eve 2023. Unit 1 is scheduled to follow before the end of this year, and the final unit runs until 2030. So for the next few years, the same substation will be moving coal power and solar power at once. But retirement does not mean the coal plant dies completely. One of the retiring units is being converted into a synchronous condenser, a spinning mass that steadies grid voltage without burning anything. Part of the coal plant will keep clocking in to smooth out the solar farm that replaced it. Moreover, the site is also getting a battery. Form Energy is building an iron-air system there rated at 10 megawatts and 1,000 megawatt hours, which works out to 100 hours of storage against the four hours a typical lithium-ion battery manages.

A solar-powered future

Xcel has more plans. A proposed fourth phase would add 200 megawatts by 2029, lifting the site to 910 megawatts, enough for more than 190,000 homes. The company pegs the expansion at roughly 300 union construction jobs and $90 million in local economic benefits. Large battery installations are also planned around the site as they would ride on the same existing grid connections. But none of this is confirmed yet, since phase 4 needs a green light from Minnesota regulators.

End of Article

title: Democrats' 'climate hushing' prompts activists to turn up the volume - The Guardian
description:
Research makes clear that global warming is making extreme weather events more frequent and severe.
“It’s the broadest brush that we are working with,” said Margie Alt, director of the Climate Action Campaign.
“The message is, talk about climate, climate can’t wait, and we want to see action.” Actions began on Thursday and will take a variety of forms.
And one month earlier, a Yale survey found that roughly two-thirds of Americans are worried about global warming.
“I don’t think that ignoring the climate crisis is smart politics,” she said.
text:
This summer, torrential rains have washed away Texas neighborhoods, dangerous heat has blanketed swaths of the country, and smoke from Canadian wildfires has choked communities as far south as Florida.

Research makes clear that global warming is making extreme weather events more frequent and severe. Yet the climate crisis has largely disappeared from the political agenda, with many Democrats who once described it as an existential threat now shying away from talking about it.

Now US activists are pushing back against this trend of “climate hushing”, arguing it is misguided. During the summer’s federal recess, during which lawmakers leave the nation’s capital to work directly within their home states or districts, demonstrators organized by the environmental advocacy coalition Climate Action Campaign are calling on representatives to put climate back on the political agenda.

“The long history of the climate movement proves that we move fastest when there’s real pressure from the grassroots,” said Bill McKibben, the environmental author and activist who co-founded climate non-profit 350.org, “All the evidence shows those grassroots are as worried about [the] climate crisis as they ever were.”

The events, set to take place over the next month in at least 20 states during the House and Senate recess periods, will mobilize members of groups including local Sierra Club chapters, the senior citizen-led climate organization Third Act, which McKibben founded, and local affiliates of the racial justice group the NAACP.

“It’s the broadest brush that we are working with,” said Margie Alt, director of the Climate Action Campaign. “The message is, talk about climate, climate can’t wait, and we want to see action.”

Actions began on Thursday and will take a variety of forms. In Michigan, participants will demonstrate against the Republican representative Bill Huizenga who voted for Trump’s so-called big beautiful bill, which boosted planet-heating fossil fuels.

In Arizona, young activists will meet with the Democratic representative Adelita Shirley Grijalva, a climate champion, and encourage her to continue talking about global warming. In other districts, organizers have circulated petitions calling on the House Democratic leader, Hakeem Jeffries, and Senate Democratic leader, Chuck Schumer, to prioritize climate issues or plan to call on their representatives to connect the climate crisis to recent heatwaves.

The activists’ campaign comes as new polling challenges the need for “climate hushing”, a trend that took off as some policy wonks argued that talking about global warming could alienate voters and distract from the message of affordability. July research from the University of California, Santa Barbara found that emphasizing climate change was neutral to beneficial for Democratic candidates, suggesting that talking more about the issue does not alienate voters and can even increase support in competitive races.

Though the Trump administration frequently derides climate policy as a “scam” and a “hoax”, polling indicates most Americans are not onboard with that view. Another July poll from Data for Progress found that 61% of likely voters believe extreme weather has become more frequent over the past five years, including nearly half of Republicans. And one month earlier, a Yale survey found that roughly two-thirds of Americans are worried about global warming.

“Smart politicians will grab on this issue,” said McKibben. “There’s perhaps no other question where the gulf between Maga and the general public is higher.”

Alt said she saw climate-hushing as “the climate denial of 2026”.

“I don’t think that ignoring the climate crisis is smart politics,” she said. “I think that it is dropping the ball on the biggest threat the US and the world faces.”

text:
With El Paso residents continuing to face high electricity bills during another summer of extreme heat, U.S. Rep. Veronica Escobar, D-Texas, is renewing her call for Congress to pass a package of bills designed to reduce energy costs, expand assistance programs and increase oversight of utility companies.

Escobar announced her support for three pieces of legislation that she said would address rising energy costs through utility regulation, expanded financial assistance and investments in lower-cost energy sources.

Families should not have to choose between keeping the lights on, cooling their homes during dangerous heat, and paying for other basic necessities," Escobar said in a statement. "At a time when utility bills are rising, Congress should be focused on delivering meaningful relief—not protecting excessive utility profits or making it harder and more expensive to build the affordable energy our communities need.

The legislative package includes the Lowering Utility Bills Act, introduced by Rep. Greg Casar of Texas, which would establish stricter federal and state standards for how investor-owned utilities and electric transmission providers determine their authorized rates of return. According to Escobar's office, the proposal is intended to increase oversight of utility rate-setting and prevent consumers from paying unnecessarily high electricity bills.

The second proposal, the Heating and Cooling Relief Act, sponsored by Rep. Yassamin Ansari of Arizona, would expand and modernize the Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program (LIHEAP). The bill would broaden eligibility and better account for the increasing financial burden of extreme weather, helping more low-income households pay for heating and air conditioning.

Escobar said the measure is particularly relevant for communities like El Paso, where prolonged periods of triple-digit temperatures make access to affordable cooling a public health concern.

The third measure, the Energy Bills Relief Act, introduced by Reps. Mike Levin of California and Sean Casten of Illinois, seeks to reduce household energy costs through several initiatives. The legislation would restore clean energy tax credits created in 2022 that were later eliminated, encourage utilities to invest in more efficient energy systems, provide assistance to families at risk of having their electricity disconnected and strengthen protections against energy price gouging.

The proposal also would require large energy users, including data centers, to cover a greater share of the costs associated with the electricity they consume rather than shifting those expenses to residential customers. It also includes provisions intended to increase community input on energy projects.

RECOMMENDED: Escobar introduces bill to stop eminent domain seizure of Mount Cristo Rey area

Escobar also criticized actions taken by the Trump administration and congressional Republicans, arguing that the rollback of clean energy incentives and delays in permitting renewable energy projects could lead to higher long-term energy costs.

Her office pointed to the phaseout of clean energy tax credits under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, as well as delays affecting renewable energy projects, including offshore wind developments in Texas, as examples of policies she said could reduce affordable electricity generation.

The legislation would need approval from both chambers of Congress before it could become law.

title: $307M solar project planned for Eastern Kentucky wins state tax incentive
authors: Austin R. Ramsey, Ryan C. Hermens
description:
The Kentucky Economic Development Finance Authority approved a tax refund through the Kentucky Enterprise Initiative Act, which provides incentives for certain investments in research and development and electronic processing equipment.
A 111-megawatt solar project on the site of a former coal mine in Martin County began operating in 2024.
But state economic development officials say access to renewable energy is increasingly important to companies considering where to invest.

text:
A renewable energy company is preparing to build one of Kentucky’s largest solar farms in Fleming County after a state economic development board approved a $400,000 tax refund for the project Thursday.

ACCIONA Energy plans to invest about $307 million to build a roughly 1,200-acre solar installation capable of generating 188 megawatts of electricity. The company says construction will begin soon, and the project could be operational by as soon as 2028.

The project is expected to create about 300 construction jobs, though it was not immediately clear how many permanent jobs the solar farm would support.

The project comes as Kentucky faces a widening tension over its energy future. Coal remains the backbone of the state’s power grid, while solar is rapidly expanding nationwide and businesses are increasingly seeking access to renewable energy. The Fleming County project would be one of the largest solar installations in Kentucky and comes as the Trump administration pushes to revive coal-fired generation even as solar recently surpassed coal nationally.

The Kentucky Economic Development Finance Authority approved a tax refund through the Kentucky Enterprise Initiative Act, which provides incentives for certain investments in research and development and electronic processing equipment.

The electricity generated at the Fleming County project will be sold into the broader PJM electric grid through East Kentucky Power Cooperative’s transmission system, according to an economic impact and land use analysis.

A 111-megawatt solar project on the site of a former coal mine in Martin County began operating in 2024. That project has 11 full-time Kentucky employees. Last year, state utility regulators OK’d a $1 billion three-county solar project on another reclaimed mine that is expected to generate as much as 800 megawatts of electricity at full capacity.

Solar generated 12.8% of U.S. electricity in May, surpassing coal at 12.2%, according to Ember, a global energy policy group. Coal supplied nearly 20% of the nation’s electricity just five years ago.

The shift comes as the Trump administration seeks to bolster the nation’s coal industry, including by directing federal money toward coal plants in Kentucky and West Virginia. Kentucky Power’s Mitchell plant near Moundsville, West Virginia, is receiving $51 million for a new cooling tower, while East Kentucky Power received $90 million to allow its Spurlock and Cooper coal plants to co-fire with natural gas.

Despite those efforts, solar remains the nation’s fastest-growing electricity source.

Kentucky has been slower to embrace solar than many other states, with coal continuing to dominate the state’s power generation. But state economic development officials say access to renewable energy is increasingly important to companies considering where to invest.

Jeff Noel, secretary of the Kentucky Cabinet for Economic Development, said companies are increasingly looking for renewable power as they make commitments to shareholders, customers and employees about their energy use.

The Fleming County project would add to a small but growing number of large-scale solar installations in Kentucky. The Martin County project received a $600,000 state tax refund through the same incentive program in 2021.
